stories.headline: A personalized cancer vaccine passes its biggest test

sources.title: Moderna and Merck say mRNA cancer vaccine succeeded in late-stage melanoma trial (STAT News)
Moderna, Merck unveil mRNA-based cancer vaccine that cuts spread (Al Jazeera)
Cancer breakthrough as personalised mRNA vaccine stops melanoma returning (Gavi VaccinesWork)
Moderna reaches 'landmark moment' in melanoma vaccine trial (video, CBS News)

chunks.text: For years, scientists have dreamed of a [[vaccine]] against cancer. This week, that dream took a giant step forward. Drug companies Moderna and Merck, which {{teamed up}} years ago, announced that their [[personalized]] [[melanoma]] vaccine passed its biggest test yet. The news {{came out}} on August 19, and doctors around the world are calling it a possible [[turning point]]. It is the first time a vaccine of this kind has succeeded in a large, final-stage [[trial]].

verbs.correct: To join forces with someone
verbs.wrong: To compete against a rival
verbs.why: Team up means two people or companies join forces to work on something together. Moderna and Merck teamed up years before this vaccine succeeded.

verbs.correct: To be published for the public
verbs.wrong: To be kept secret for years
verbs.why: Come out means information becomes public, like news, a report, or a movie. Here it is the announcement that a vaccine trial finally succeeded.

chunks.text: Here is how it works. First, [[surgeons]] {{cut out}} the patient's [[tumor]] and send a piece to a [[laboratory]]. Scientists read the cancer's [[genetic code]] and {{pick out}} up to 34 tiny changes, called [[mutations]], that are most likely to alert the body's defenses. Next, a personal [[dose]] is {{put together}} piece by piece for that one patient and nobody else. The shot trains the [[immune system]] to {{hunt down}} escaped cancer cells the way police chase a runaway prisoner.

verbs.correct: To remove something by cutting
verbs.wrong: To measure something exactly
verbs.why: Cut out means to remove a part by cutting it away, literally with scissors or, as here, a surgeon's knife. Surgeons cut out the tumor before scientists study it.

verbs.correct: To choose from a larger group
verbs.wrong: To count every single item
verbs.why: Pick out means to choose specific items from a larger group, like the riskiest changes in a tumor's genetic code. It is a careful, deliberate choice, not a random one.

verbs.correct: To build from separate parts
verbs.wrong: To divide into small pieces
verbs.why: Put together means to build something whole from separate pieces. Each vaccine dose is put together from mutations unique to that one patient.

verbs.correct: To search for until found
verbs.wrong: To frighten from far away
verbs.why: Hunt down means to keep searching until you find your target. The immune system hunts down cancer cells that escaped the original tumor.

chunks.text: The numbers behind the announcement are strong. More than 1,000 patients with serious melanoma joined the [[Phase 3]] trial after surgery. Patients who received the vaccine together with Keytruda, a famous cancer [[drug]], stayed [[cancer-free]] longer than patients who got the drug alone. For many of them, the melanoma has not {{come back}} at all. The [[combination]] also {{slowed down}} the disease's spread to other [[organs]]. An earlier, smaller study had already cut the risk of return in half. [[Investors]] noticed too: Moderna's [[stock price]] {{shot up}} within hours of the announcement.

verbs.correct: To return after going away
verbs.wrong: To disappear forever
verbs.why: Here come back means a disease returns after treatment seemed to work. For many patients in this trial, the melanoma has not come back at all.

verbs.correct: To make something less fast
verbs.wrong: To stop something completely
verbs.why: Slow down here means to make something else move or spread less quickly. The drug combination slowed down how fast the cancer spread to other organs.

verbs.correct: To rise very fast
verbs.wrong: To fall little by little
verbs.why: Shoot up means to rise very quickly and sharply, often about numbers or prices. Moderna's stock price shot up within hours of the announcement.

chunks.text: What happens next? The companies are already talking with [[regulators]], and independent [[experts]] will {{go over}} the full numbers line by line at a coming medical meeting. Nobody knows yet how long the [[protection]] lasts. But if everything holds, the companies hope to {{roll out}} the treatment to thousands of patients as early as next year. And researchers are ready to {{take on}} the next challenge: using the same method against lung, kidney, and [[pancreatic]] cancer. One cancer expert said it best: this is where things begin.

verbs.correct: To examine something carefully
verbs.wrong: To forget to check something
verbs.why: Go over means to examine something closely, point by point, before trusting it. Experts will go over the full trial results at a medical meeting.

verbs.correct: To make available to many people
verbs.wrong: To test on a small group first
verbs.why: Roll out means to gradually make something available to many people, like a new treatment. Companies hope to roll out the vaccine to thousands of patients next year.

verbs.correct: To accept a difficult challenge
verbs.wrong: To avoid a hard task politely
verbs.why: Take on means to accept a hard challenge and commit to it. Researchers hope to take on other cancers next, using the same method.

mainIdea.s: A personalized cancer vaccine passed a large final-stage trial for the first time, keeping melanoma from returning in many patients. The treatment could reach patients next year.
mainIdea.why: The vaccine, built for each patient and given with Keytruda, kept people cancer-free longer and slowed the disease's spread.

mainIdea.s: A new cancer vaccine protects healthy people from ever developing melanoma, like a flu shot. Doctors will soon offer it to everyone who spends too much time in the sun.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the vaccine treats patients who already had melanoma removed. It is not a shot for healthy people.

mainIdea.s: Regulators quietly approved a cheap new pill this week that cures every type of skin cancer within a month. Hospitals say the demand is already far bigger than the supply.
mainIdea.why: There is no pill and no approval yet. The vaccine passed a trial, and talks with regulators have just started.

stories.headline: Rage bait: the trick that turns your anger into money

sources.title: The Oxford Word of the Year 2025 is rage bait (Oxford University Press)
Don't get angry, but the 2025 Oxford Word of the Year is 'rage bait' (NPR)
Oxford University Press picks 'rage bait' as its word of the year (CBS News)
Why 'Rage Bait' is Oxford's Word of the Year (video, Firstpost)

chunks.text: You see a post so wrong that your face gets hot. A cooking video that [[ruins]] a famous [[dish]] on purpose. An opinion nobody could truly believe. Before you type your [[furious]] reply, stop: it may be [[rage bait]], content made [[deliberately]] to {{stir up}} anger. The trick works because rage bait {{relies on}} one simple fact: angry people click, comment, and share more than happy ones.

verbs.correct: To cause strong feelings or trouble
verbs.wrong: To calm a group of people
verbs.why: Stir up means to deliberately cause strong emotions, usually anger or excitement, in a group of people. Rage bait is content made just to stir up anger.

verbs.correct: To need something to work or succeed
verbs.wrong: To copy something step by step
verbs.why: Rely on means to depend on something for a system to work as planned. Rage bait relies on the fact that angry people click and share more.

chunks.text: Here is how the game works. A creator posts something designed to feel [[unfair]] or completely wrong. Readers {{give in}} to the [[temptation]] to [[correct]] it, and soon hundreds of [[strangers]] {{pile on}} in the comments. Every reply pushes the post higher, so the crowd {{winds up}} paying the creator with the one thing he wanted: [[attention]]. The [[outrage]] is real, but the [[opinion]] often is not. Some rage baiters [[admit]] they do not believe a word of their own posts.

verbs.correct: To stop fighting a feeling or demand
verbs.wrong: To make a promise to yourself
verbs.why: Give in means to stop resisting a temptation or a pressure and finally act on it. Readers give in to the urge to correct a stranger's wrong opinion.

verbs.correct: To join many others in attacking
verbs.wrong: To leave a group one by one
verbs.why: Pile on means to join a large group already criticizing or attacking someone. Hundreds of strangers pile on in the comments once a post goes viral.

verbs.correct: To reach an end you did not plan
verbs.wrong: To start something with energy
verbs.why: Wind up means to reach an end you never intended. Angry commenters wind up giving the rage bait creator exactly what he wanted.

chunks.text: The word had a big year. In December 2025, dictionary experts at Oxford picked rage bait as their [[word of the year]], beating aura farming and biohack. More than 30,000 people voted, and use of the term [[tripled]] in just twelve months. The phrase {{caught on}} quickly, but the idea is older: it first appeared in an online [[forum]] back in 2002. The [[editors]] define rage bait as content built to cause anger and raise a site's [[traffic]] and [[engagement]]. Angry readers who {{call out}} the trick in the comments often just make it stronger.

verbs.correct: To become popular with many people
verbs.wrong: To confuse almost everyone
verbs.why: Catch on means an idea, word, or trend becomes widely known and used. The phrase rage bait caught on fast, though the idea itself is decades old.

verbs.correct: To publicly say something is wrong
verbs.wrong: To whisper a secret to a friend
verbs.why: Call out means to say publicly that something or someone is wrong. Readers who call out rage bait in the comments often make the post stronger.

chunks.text: So what should you do when a post [[makes your blood boil]]? Experts say the hardest step is to {{pass up}} the chance to tell a stranger he is wrong. Try to {{hold back}} your first hot reply until the anger cools, and ask a simple question: who [[profits]] from my anger? The [[storm]] around a rage bait post usually {{blows over}} in a day, but the views remain forever. If a post exists only to make you angry, the smartest answer is quiet: do not [[take the bait]], and just {{log off}}.

verbs.correct: To choose not to take a chance
verbs.wrong: To grab an offer with both hands
verbs.why: Pass up means to deliberately not take an opportunity that is right in front of you. Here it means resisting the chance to correct a stranger online.

verbs.correct: To keep a strong feeling inside
verbs.wrong: To express a feeling loudly
verbs.why: Hold back means to keep a strong emotion from showing, at least for a moment. Experts suggest you hold back your first angry reply until your anger fades.

verbs.correct: To pass and be forgotten soon
verbs.wrong: To grow bigger every hour
verbs.why: Blow over means a wave of anger or trouble fades away on its own. Online outrage usually blows over in a day, but the video stays online forever.

verbs.correct: To stop using an app or website
verbs.wrong: To create a new online account
verbs.why: Log off means to close an app or website and stop scrolling for a while. The simplest answer to rage bait is often just to log off.

ex: The coach's speech stirred up the whole team.

ex: He would not admit that he was lost.

ex: The editors cut the story in half.

mainIdea.s: Rage bait, online content made on purpose to cause anger, was named word of the year after its use tripled. The article explains how it earns money and how to resist it.
mainIdea.why: Oxford picked the term in December 2025. Angry clicks raise traffic, and experts say the best answer is to log off.

mainIdea.s: Dictionary editors gave their 2025 prize to a term describing posts made to spread calm and kindness online. Use of that friendly phrase tripled in just twelve months.
mainIdea.why: Close, but rage bait is the opposite of friendly. It is built to stir up anger, and clicks turn that anger into money.

mainIdea.s: A famous chef lost his cooking show this winter after fans discovered that he ruined popular dishes on purpose. He says the angry comments have destroyed his whole career.
mainIdea.why: The ruined dish is only an example of rage bait. Nobody loses a show in the article.

tf.why: That is the engine. Every furious reply pushes the post higher in the feed.

tf.s: The idea of rage bait first appeared in 2025

stories.headline: US debt passes 40 trillion dollars

sources.title: The U.S. debt tops a record-shattering $40 trillion (NPR)
U.S. government debt passes $40 trillion, more than doubling in a decade (CNBC)
US debt hits $40 trillion: Who does Washington owe? (Al Jazeera)
US debt hits 40 trillion dollars: the price per American (video, CNN)

chunks.text: The United States government has never [[owed]] this much money. Its [[debt]] has been {{piling up}} for [[decades]], and in August it passed 40 [[trillion]] dollars for the first time. Divide that by [[every man, woman, and child]] in the country, and it {{works out to}} more than 115,000 dollars each. The [[pace]] is {{speeding up}}, too: the last trillion arrived in only about five months.

verbs.correct: To grow into a large amount
verbs.wrong: To be counted one more time
verbs.why: Pile up means to grow steadily into a very large amount over time. The government's debt has been piling up for decades and just passed 40 trillion dollars.

verbs.correct: To equal after the math is done
verbs.wrong: To round down to a lower number
verbs.why: Work out to means to equal a certain amount once you do the math. This giant debt works out to about 115,000 dollars for each person in America.

verbs.correct: To happen faster than before
verbs.wrong: To become easier to stop
verbs.why: Speed up means to happen faster than before, at a quicker pace. The nation's debt growth is speeding up too: the most recent trillion arrived in only five months.

chunks.text: How does a country build a debt like that? Every year, the government {{takes in}} far less in [[taxes]] than it spends, and the [[gap]] is now more than two trillion dollars a year. To [[cover]] it, the government [[borrows]], and borrowed money is never free. The government must now {{set aside}} more than one trillion dollars from its [[budget]] every year just to pay [[interest]] on the old debt.

verbs.correct: To receive as income
verbs.wrong: To spend on programs
verbs.why: Take in means to receive money as income, especially for a government or a business. Each year the government takes in far less in taxes than it spends.

verbs.correct: To save for one special use
verbs.wrong: To borrow at a lower rate
verbs.why: Set aside means to save a certain amount for one specific use, not for spending elsewhere. The government must now set aside over one trillion dollars a year just for interest.

chunks.text: Why should [[ordinary]] people care? Because heavy government borrowing can {{drive up}} [[interest rates]] for everyone else. When the government needs to borrow so much, families who {{take out}} a [[loan]] for a house or a car feel it too. The [[average]] rate on a 30-year US home loan is now near 6.7 percent, and [[long-term]] borrowing costs recently reached their highest level in almost twenty years.

verbs.correct: To force something higher
verbs.wrong: To spread something evenly
verbs.why: Drive up means to force a price or a rate higher than before. Heavy government borrowing can drive up interest rates for everyone, including families buying homes or cars.

verbs.correct: To arrange to borrow money
verbs.wrong: To pay a debt very slowly
verbs.why: Take out means to arrange to borrow a specific amount of money. Families who take out a loan for a house or a car feel higher rates too.

chunks.text: Experts from both political parties call the [[path]] [[unsustainable]], and, so far, the country's leaders keep {{putting off}} the [[hard choices]]. But the problem will not {{go away}} on its own, and the longer the country waits, the more expensive the [[fix]] becomes. In the end, the [[options]] {{boil down to}} spending less, collecting more in taxes, or both. [[One way or another]], someone will have to {{pick up}} the [[bill]], and it may be today's students.

verbs.correct: To delay until later
verbs.wrong: To argue about loudly
verbs.why: Put off means to delay something until a later time, often because it feels hard. The country's leaders keep putting off the hard choices about spending and taxes.

verbs.correct: To stop existing
verbs.wrong: To become smaller
verbs.why: Go away means to stop existing or disappear completely on its own. A debt problem this large will not go away by itself, and waiting only makes it worse.

verbs.correct: To reduce to the main choices

stories.headline: Did social media hook kids? A trial begins

sources.title: Meta heads to court in a landmark trial about kids and social media addiction (NPR)
Landmark trial accusing social media companies of addicting children begins (NBC News)
A Meta trial loss could end the social media we know (CNBC)
Meta hooked children on Facebook and Instagram, court hears (video, BBC News)

chunks.text: Were [[likes]], [[endless]] feeds, and [[constant]] notifications designed [[on purpose]] to [[hook]] children? That is the question [[at the heart of]] a huge [[trial]] that began in mid-August in a [[federal court]] in California. Four US states have {{teamed up}} to {{take on}} Meta, the company behind Facebook and Instagram, in one of the biggest tech cases in American history.

verbs.correct: To join others to work together
verbs.wrong: To share the costs of a case
verbs.why: Team up means to join with others so you can work toward a shared goal. Four US states have teamed up to bring this case against Meta together.

verbs.correct: To fight against someone strong
verbs.wrong: To copy someone's business
verbs.why: Take on means to challenge or fight against someone much bigger or more powerful than you. The states are taking on Meta in one of the largest tech cases in American history.

chunks.text: The case is about app features everyone knows. [[Notifications]] {{pop up}} on the screen [[at all hours]], so young users return [[again and again]]. The [[feed]] never ends, so there is no natural place to stop. Likes and other small rewards {{draw in}} teenagers and keep them [[scrolling]]. Many teens say they cannot {{put down}} the phone, even at dinner or late at night. The states [[argue]] that these [[designs]] were built to hold children's [[attention]], [[whatever the cost]].

verbs.correct: To appear suddenly
verbs.wrong: To sound louder at night
verbs.why: Pop up means to appear suddenly on a screen, without any warning. In the case, notifications pop up at all hours and repeatedly interrupt young users.

verbs.correct: To attract and hold interest
verbs.wrong: To confuse and then bore
verbs.why: Draw in means to attract someone's attention and hold it so they keep engaging. Likes and small rewards draw in teenagers and keep them scrolling for hours.

verbs.correct: To stop holding something
verbs.wrong: To charge something at night
verbs.why: Put down means to stop holding something and set it aside. Many teens say they cannot put down their phone, even at dinner or late at night.

chunks.text: The states want big changes. They ask the court to make Meta {{do away with}} some of these features for young users, and they demand up to 1.4 trillion dollars, one of the largest amounts ever requested in a US court. Meta {{pushes back}} hard against the [[claims]]. The company {{stands by}} its [[record]], saying it has built strong [[protections]] for teens and that the [[demands]] are [[unfair]].

verbs.correct: To remove something completely
verbs.wrong: To improve something slowly
verbs.why: Do away with means to remove something completely so it no longer exists. The states want the court to make Meta do away with certain features built for young users.

verbs.correct: To resist and disagree strongly
verbs.wrong: To ignore every question
verbs.why: Push back means to resist firmly and refuse to accept something. Meta is pushing back hard against the states' claims and denies that its designs are unfair.

verbs.correct: To keep supporting something
verbs.wrong: To quietly change something
verbs.why: Stand by means to keep supporting a decision or statement even when it is challenged. Meta stands by its record on teen safety and insists the demands are unfair.

chunks.text: The trial is expected to {{go on}} for about six weeks, and the whole tech world is watching. A loss could change how social media looks and feels for everyone. An entire [[generation]] has {{grown up}} with likes, notifications, and endless feeds, and courts are only now deciding what that means. In the end, the case may {{come down to}} one question: did the company know its designs could hurt young users?

verbs.correct: To continue for some time
verbs.wrong: To pause again and again
verbs.why: Go on means to continue happening for a period of time. The trial is expected to go on for about six weeks.

verbs.correct: To spend your childhood
verbs.wrong: To learn from mistakes
verbs.why: Grow up means to spend the years of your childhood in a particular situation. An entire generation has grown up with likes, notifications, and endless feeds.

verbs.correct: To depend on one main thing
verbs.wrong: To end without any answer
verbs.why: Come down to means that a complicated question really depends on one main point. In the end, the case may come down to whether Meta knew its designs could harm young users.

stories.headline: A cheaper robotaxi opens to everyone

sources.title: Waymo's cheaper, next-gen robotaxi is now open to all riders in these three cities (TechCrunch)
Waymo's New Robotaxi Minivans Are Now Taking Paying Passengers (InsideEVs)
Emerging Tech Watch, August 2026 (Mikesai Library)
Waymo begins public rides in Ojai as it shifts to lower-cost robotaxis (video, CNBC)

chunks.text: In three big US cities, a taxi with no driver just became normal. Waymo's newest robotaxi, a [[roomy]] electric [[minivan]] called the Ojai, is now open to everyone in Los Angeles, Phoenix, and San Francisco. The vans have been {{showing up}} in [[traffic]] next to regular cars all summer, but riders could not choose one until now. Today, anyone with the app can {{hop in}} when their car arrives, with no one [[behind the wheel]].

verbs.correct: To appear in a place
verbs.wrong: To make a loud noise
verbs.why: Show up means to appear somewhere, becoming a normal, familiar sight over time. The driverless vans have been showing up in traffic next to regular cars all summer.

verbs.correct: To enter a car quickly
verbs.wrong: To wait beside the road
verbs.why: Hop in means to get into a vehicle quickly and casually. Anyone with the app can now hop in when their robotaxi arrives, with no driver at all.

chunks.text: The Ojai is built to cost less. The base van comes from China, but it arrives without its Chinese internet [[software]]: Waymo {{takes out}} that system and {{puts in}} its own [[self-driving]] brain at a [[factory]] in Arizona. Each van is cheaper to build and run than the Jaguar cars the company used before. There is one problem: [[import taxes]] {{push up}} the price of every van that crosses the ocean.

verbs.correct: To remove something from inside
verbs.wrong: To test something one more time
verbs.why: Take out means to remove something from inside a machine or a device. Waymo takes out the Chinese software, though you can also say take the software out.

verbs.correct: To place something inside
verbs.wrong: To design something new
verbs.why: Put in means to place something inside, filling a space left by whatever was removed. At a factory in Arizona, Waymo puts in its own self-driving system instead.

verbs.correct: To make a price higher
verbs.wrong: To keep a price steady
verbs.why: Push up means to make a price rise, usually because of an outside cost. Import taxes push up the price of every van that has to cross the ocean.

chunks.text: Riding in one feels simple. [[Passengers]] sit down, {{buckle up}}, and press a button. The van joins traffic [[on its own]]. A talking [[assistant]] answers questions during the ride. For now, the app [[decides]] which car you get, so riders {{end up}} with either the new van or an older Jaguar. Soon, riders will be able to {{pick out}} the [[model]] they want right in the app.

verbs.correct: To fasten your seat belt
verbs.wrong: To choose the safest seat
verbs.why: Buckle up means to fasten your seat belt before a vehicle starts moving. In the Ojai, passengers sit down, buckle up, and press a button to begin the ride.

verbs.correct: To finally have something
verbs.wrong: To trade one thing for another
verbs.why: End up means to finally have or get something, not always by your own choice. For now, riders end up with either the new van or an older Jaguar model.

verbs.correct: To choose from a group
verbs.wrong: To pay extra for something
verbs.why: Pick out means to choose one specific thing from a group of options. Soon, riders will be able to pick out the exact robotaxi model they want in the app.

chunks.text: Waymo is [[moving fast]]. About 300 of the new vans are [[on the road]] today, and one [[analyst]] expects the [[fleet]] to reach 5,000 [[by the end of the year]]. The company also plans to {{roll out}} the service in Denver, Las Vegas, and San Diego later this year. [[Driverless]] rides are [[no longer]] a science [[experiment]]. The question now is price: will cheaper vans mean cheaper rides, and will lower prices {{win over}} people who still {{hold back}}?

verbs.correct: To offer something widely
verbs.wrong: To test something in secret
verbs.why: Roll out means to introduce a service to more people or places over time. Waymo plans to roll out its robotaxi service in Denver, Las Vegas, and San Diego next.

verbs.correct: To gain someone's support
verbs.wrong: To beat someone in a race
verbs.why: Win over means to convince someone to support or trust something they doubted before. The question now is whether cheaper prices will win over people who are still unsure.

verbs.correct: To wait because of fear or doubt
verbs.wrong: To save money for later
verbs.why: Hold back means to stop yourself from trying something because of doubt or fear. Some people still hold back from riding in a car with no driver at all.

Construction workers in Belgium uncover $10 million in gold at work (CNN)
$10 million gold treasure discovered during renovation of Belgian brewery (WSB-TV)
Workers discover gold bars and coins worth $10 million at former brewery (video, CBS News)

chunks.text: It started as a normal workday in Dendermonde, a town in the Belgian region of East Flanders. A construction [[crew]] was digging under an old building, once home to a [[brewery]], to lay new [[sewer pipes]]. Then a worker's [[drill]] {{broke through}} an old [[cellar]] wall, and something yellow appeared in the dust. While doing one of the least [[glamorous]] jobs in construction, the crew had {{come across}} it [[by pure chance]]: a [[fortune]] in gold.

verbs.correct: To make a hole in something
verbs.wrong: To knock on something loudly
verbs.why: Break through means to make a hole in something solid, often by force. A drill breaking through a wall, or sunlight breaking through clouds, are both classic uses.

verbs.correct: To find something by chance
verbs.wrong: To dig for something for years
verbs.why: Come across means to find something by pure luck, not because you were searching for it, like finding an old coin in a drawer.

chunks.text: The [[find]] was huge: about 50 gold bars and pile after pile of old gold coins, [[hidden]] inside the walls. Together, the [[treasure]] {{comes to}} about nine million euros, or more than ten million dollars. The news {{got out}} fast, and photos of the shining bars soon appeared on the local police's own Facebook page.

verbs.correct: To reach a total amount
verbs.wrong: To lose value over time
verbs.why: Come to means to reach a certain total, especially with money, like a restaurant bill or a pile of treasure.

verbs.correct: To spread to many people
verbs.wrong: To stay quiet for a while
verbs.why: News gets out when it spreads to many people, often faster than anyone expected. We use it for secrets, rumors, or big discoveries becoming public.

chunks.text: The workers did not [[think twice]]. They called the police [[at once]] and {{handed over}} [[every last]] coin to the [[officers]]. Nobody tried to {{walk off with}} a fortune in their pockets. The treasure was moved to a high-security government [[vault]], where it is now {{locked away}}. The building [[site]] itself has been {{fenced off}}, and police warned [[treasure hunters]] that digging there would be [[pointless]].

verbs.correct: To give something to someone
verbs.wrong: To count something slowly
verbs.why: To hand over something means to give it to someone in charge, like the police. People often hand things over because it is the honest choice, not because they must.

verbs.correct: To steal something easily
verbs.wrong: To carry something heavy
verbs.why: Walk off with means to take something and leave, almost like a light way of saying steal. It works well for small thefts, like a stranger walking off with your umbrella.

verbs.correct: To keep something in a safe place
verbs.wrong: To melt something into new bars
verbs.why: Lock away means to put something in a very safe place where it stays protected, like a vault or a locked drawer. We use it for valuable things nobody should touch.

verbs.correct: To close an area with a barrier
verbs.wrong: To search an area with dogs
verbs.why: Fence off means to surround an area with a barrier so people stay outside it. Police fence off crime scenes, and crews fence off dangerous building sites.

chunks.text: One question remains: who does the gold {{belong to}}? The building is owned today by a local [[charity]], but nobody knows who hid the treasure, or when. Old [[records]] about the house might {{clear up}} the [[mystery]]. If the original owner's family never {{turns up}}, the [[courts]] will have to decide. For now, no one can say where the gold will finally {{end up}}, but everyone agrees on one thing: the workers who found it did [[the right thing]].

verbs.correct: To be owned by someone
verbs.wrong: To be made by someone
verbs.why: Belong to means that something is owned by a particular person, group, or place. We use it for objects, but also for feeling part of a team or a family.

verbs.correct: To explain something confusing
verbs.wrong: To create a new mystery
verbs.why: Clear up means to explain something that was confusing, so people finally understand it. Old records, new evidence, or an honest witness can all clear up a mystery.

verbs.correct: To appear after some time
verbs.wrong: To ask for a big reward
verbs.why: Turn up means to appear somewhere after being missing or unknown for a while, often unexpectedly. A lost key, an old friend, or a missing owner can all turn up.

verbs.wrong: To be sold at an auction
verbs.why: End up means to finally arrive at a result or place, often without planning it that way. Court cases, lost items, and long arguments can all end up somewhere surprising.

stories.headline: Dogs can read the feelings on your face

sources.title: Brain scans show that dogs can distinguish emotions in human faces (University of Vienna)
Dogs can tell fear from sadness (ScienceDaily)
Dogs can tell when you're happy, scared or sad (The Washington Post)

chunks.text: Does your dog know when you are sad? Many [[owners]] feel that their pets can [[sense]] their [[moods]], and new [[brain scans]] point to an answer: yes, more than we thought. Scientists at the University of Vienna {{set out}} to test what really happens inside a dog's head when it looks at a human face.

verbs.correct: To begin a job with a plan
verbs.wrong: To finish a long project
verbs.why: Set out means to begin a task with a clear goal already in mind. The scientists set out to discover what really happens in a dog's brain when it looks at a human face.

chunks.text: The team {{signed up}} 12 friendly family dogs whose owners wanted to help. Each dog {{went through}} careful [[training]] so it could [[lie still]] and [[stay awake]] inside the [[scanner]]. [[Treats]] and soft words helped the dogs {{settle down}} in the [[noisy]] machine. The researchers then {{put together}} sets of photos showing four feelings on human faces: happiness, anger, fear, and sadness.

verbs.correct: To add someone to a program
verbs.wrong: To pay someone for their work
verbs.why: Sign up here means to add someone as a participant in a study or program. The researchers signed up twelve friendly family dogs whose owners agreed to help.

verbs.correct: To complete a whole process
verbs.wrong: To skip an important part
verbs.why: Go through means to complete every step of a process from start to finish. Each dog went through careful training before it could lie still inside the noisy scanner.

verbs.correct: To become calm and quiet
verbs.wrong: To fall into a deep sleep
verbs.why: Settle down means to become calm after being excited or nervous. Treats and soft words helped the dogs settle down inside the machine.

verbs.correct: To prepare a set of things
verbs.wrong: To choose one favorite thing
verbs.why: Put together means to gather several separate pieces into one complete set. The researchers put together sets of photos showing four different feelings on human faces.

chunks.text: When the dogs saw a happy face, a [[reward]] area deep in the brain {{lit up}} like a Christmas tree: the same area that becomes active for food and play. Smiles clearly matter to dogs. With help from a [[computer program]], the scans also showed that dogs could {{pick up on}} the [[difference]] between fear and sadness, two feelings that even people sometimes [[confuse]]. The brain [[pattern]] for fear {{stood out}} from the patterns for anger and sadness.

verbs.correct: To become active and bright
verbs.wrong: To slowly stop working
verbs.why: Light up means to suddenly become bright and active. The dogs' reward area lit up when they saw a happy face, the same area active for food and play.

verbs.correct: To notice something not obvious
verbs.wrong: To guess without any proof
verbs.why: Pick up on means to notice a small detail that is easy to miss. The scans showed that dogs could pick up on the difference between a fearful face and a sad one.

verbs.correct: To be clearly different
verbs.wrong: To disappear from view
verbs.why: Stand out means to be clearly different from everything around it. The brain pattern for fear stood out from the patterns for anger and sadness.

chunks.text: The study came out this month in a science [[journal]], and it is the first clear [[evidence]] that dogs can read several human feelings in a face. Still, the scientists are careful. All the dogs were [[well-loved]] pets, and real life gives dogs much more than [[still photos]]: dogs also read [[body language]], voices, and [[smell]]. The team wants to {{follow up}} with tests closer to daily life. One thing is sure: the [[friendship]] between people and dogs {{goes back}} thousands of years, and dogs may understand us better than we knew.

verbs.correct: To continue with more work
verbs.wrong: To argue against a result
verbs.why: Follow up means to continue a piece of work with a next step, often to check or add to earlier results. The team wants to follow up with tests closer to daily life.

verbs.correct: To have existed since a time
verbs.wrong: To improve year after year
verbs.why: Go back means to have existed continuously since a certain time in the past. The friendship between people and dogs goes back thousands of years.

chunks.text: Just after [[dawn]] on August 10, the ground in western Colombia began to shake. The earthquake, with a [[magnitude]] of 7.4, was one of the strongest in the country's modern history. People {{rushed out}} of their homes in cities as far away as Bogota and Medellin, and the [[shaking]] was felt in Ecuador and Panama. In several cities, buildings {{came down}}, and more than 290 people [[lost their lives]].

verbs.correct: To leave a place very fast
verbs.wrong: To lock the doors and hide
verbs.why: Rush out means to leave a building or a place very quickly, often because of danger. People rushed out of their homes the moment the ground began to shake.

verbs.correct: To fall to the ground
verbs.wrong: To shake from side to side
verbs.why: Come down describes something falling from a higher position, like a wall or a roof collapsing. Several buildings came down when the earthquake struck.

chunks.text: The worst problems are in Choco, a [[region]] of mountains and deep forest near the [[epicenter]]. The quake {{set off}} [[landslides]] that [[buried]] the roads, and some villages were completely {{cut off}}: no cars, no trucks, no help. [[Rescue teams]] are trying to {{get through}} to them, but with the roads gone, even reaching the smallest towns can take days. Helicopters may be the only [[way in]].

verbs.correct: To cause something to happen

stories.headline: Sharks may help predict the next hurricane

sources.title: US scientists turn to sharks for help with hurricane prediction (France 24)
Sharks Equipped with Sensors Provide New Clues for Hurricane Forecasting (MARACOOS)
Scientists turn to sharks to improve hurricane predictions (The Japan Times)
Scientists attach sensors to sharks to track hurricanes (video, ABC News)

chunks.text: What does a [[hurricane]] eat? Warm ocean water. Big storms {{feed on}} heat near the sea [[surface]], and a [[patch]] of unusually warm water can {{set off}} rapid growth in a passing storm. To [[predict]] that growth, [[forecasters]] need to know how warm the ocean is, and not just at the top. The problem: the open sea is huge, and much of it is never measured.

verbs.correct: To use something as food
verbs.wrong: To make something much colder
verbs.why: Feed on means to use something as a source of food or energy to grow. Hurricanes feed on warmth stored in the upper layer of the ocean, which fuels their winds.

verbs.correct: To make something start
verbs.wrong: To measure something exactly
verbs.why: Set off means to cause something to begin suddenly, like an alarm or a reaction. One small pocket of extra warm water can set off a sudden burst of storm strength.

chunks.text: Now scientists in the United States are getting help from an [[unusual]] team. Researchers at the University of Delaware {{went over}} more than 20 years of shark-tracking [[records]], species by species, and {{settled on}} two kinds that often swim near the surface: shortfin mako sharks and blue sharks. Small [[sensors]] on their [[fins]] measure the temperature, [[depth]], and [[saltiness]] of the water. Whenever a shark {{comes up}} to the surface, the tags {{send back}} the [[measurements]] to scientists on [[shore]] by [[satellite]].

verbs.correct: To check something carefully
verbs.wrong: To throw something away
verbs.why: Go over means to check or review something carefully, often from start to finish. The team spent time going over two decades of old shark tracking data before picking which species to use.

verbs.correct: To choose after some thought
verbs.wrong: To find something by chance
verbs.why: Settle on means to finally choose one option after thinking about several others. In the end, the scientists settled on makos and blue sharks, since both spend a lot of time near the surface.

verbs.correct: To return information to a place
verbs.wrong: To keep information secret
verbs.why: Send back means to transmit information from one place to another, often over a distance. Each time a shark rises near the top, its tag sends back fresh readings to researchers based on land.

verbs.correct: To rise to a higher place
verbs.wrong: To swim quickly from danger
verbs.why: Come up means to rise toward the surface or to a higher position. These sharks come up to the surface roughly twice each day, giving their tags a window to transmit.

chunks.text: Why sharks? Machines have limits. A research [[robot]] can {{break down}}, and a weather [[buoy]] stays in one place. Sharks never stop swimming, and they travel [[up and down]] through the water all day, taking the sensors with them. Makos {{turned out}} to be a [[perfect fit]], because they visit the surface about twice a day, which gives the tags a [[chance]] to send their data home.

verbs.correct: To stop working suddenly
verbs.wrong: To become too hot to touch
verbs.why: Break down means to stop working suddenly, especially for a machine or a vehicle. Unlike sharks, an underwater robot can break down and simply stop functioning while out at sea.

verbs.correct: To prove to be something
verbs.wrong: To refuse to do something
verbs.why: Turn out means something proves to be true or becomes clear only after some time. Mako sharks turned out to be an ideal choice, since they visit the surface so regularly.

chunks.text: The project is {{starting out}} small, with only a [[handful]] of tagged sharks so far, and the [[engineers]] are still [[improving]] the tags. But every measurement counts. More tagged sharks could {{fill in}} the empty spots on the ocean map, in waters that storms pass [[on their way to]] land. Better maps of ocean heat mean better [[forecasts]], and better forecasts give [[coastal]] towns more time to prepare or {{get out}} before a storm arrives.

verbs.correct: To begin in a small way
verbs.wrong: To fail at an early stage
verbs.why: Start out means to begin something in a small or simple way, before it grows. This whole effort is starting out small, since only a few sharks currently carry the sensors.

verbs.correct: To complete missing parts
verbs.wrong: To color a simple drawing
verbs.why: Fill in means to add the missing pieces so a picture or a record becomes complete. Adding more tagged sharks could help fill in the gaps in what we know about ocean heat.

verbs.correct: To leave a dangerous place
verbs.wrong: To hide in a safe building
verbs.why: Get out means to leave a place quickly because it has become dangerous. With more warning, people living near the coast get extra time to prepare or get out safely.

mainIdea.why: Tagged makos and blue sharks carry sensors that send back temperature, depth, and saltiness data that forecasters need.

mainIdea.s: Sharks with sensors already guide every single hurricane warning in the United States. Thanks to the animals, forecasters predicted each storm this summer perfectly.

stories.headline: Walkable streets help people stay healthy

sources.title: Built to Move: The Benefits of Walkable Communities (NIH News in Health)
Walkable, greener neighborhoods linked to better physical and mental health (Phys.org)
Walkable Neighborhoods Can Boost Physical Activity (Washington State University)
The design of your city can help make you healthier (video, CBC News)

chunks.text: How far can you walk from your [[front door]]? In some [[neighborhoods]], people can {{get around}} on foot all day: the school, the store, and the park are just minutes away. In others, every little [[errand]] means a car trip that {{eats up}} time. This month, the National Institutes of Health {{put out}} its regular health [[newsletter]] with a big question: can the [[design]] of your street make you healthier?

verbs.correct: To move from place to place
verbs.wrong: To travel a very long way
verbs.why: Get around means to move easily from one place to another. In some neighborhoods, people can get around on foot for almost every daily errand.

verbs.correct: To use a lot of something
verbs.wrong: To make something go faster
verbs.why: Eat up means to use a large amount of something, especially your time. A car trip for every small errand eats up minutes that a short walk would not.

verbs.correct: To publish something for readers
verbs.wrong: To research something closely
verbs.why: Put out means to release something so readers or the public can see it. The National Institutes of Health put out its regular newsletter with this month's big question.

chunks.text: The answer seems to be yes. One large study found that people who moved to more [[walkable]] cities {{ended up}} walking about 1,100 extra steps every day. Those steps {{add up}} to almost one extra hour of [[movement]] every week. Over the years, that movement helps people stay at a healthy weight and lowers the [[risk]] of [[heart disease]], [[diabetes]], high [[blood pressure]], and depression.

verbs.correct: To finally be in a situation
verbs.wrong: To try very hard to change
verbs.why: End up means to finally arrive at a result, sometimes without planning for it. People who moved to walkable cities ended up walking about 1,100 extra steps a day.

verbs.correct: To slowly become a big total
verbs.wrong: To be too small to matter
verbs.why: Add up means small amounts slowly combine into something much bigger. Those extra daily steps add up to almost one extra hour of movement every week.

chunks.text: Streets can change, and [[residents]] can [[lead the way]]. In one Stanford University project, neighbors {{team up}}, walk their own streets, and {{point out}} problems to local leaders: missing [[crosswalks]] or dark corners. They also {{send in}} photos to [[city planners]] through a phone app. The project has spread to more than 30 US states and 30 countries, and many [[fixes]] are cheap: paint a crosswalk, add a [[bench]], improve the [[lighting]].

verbs.correct: To join others to work together
verbs.wrong: To have a friendly contest
verbs.why: Team up means to join with other people to work toward the same goal. In this project, neighbors team up to walk their own streets and check for problems.

verbs.correct: To show something to someone
verbs.wrong: To repair something broken
verbs.why: Point out means to show or mention something so another person notices it too. Neighbors point out problems like missing crosswalks or dark corners to local leaders.

verbs.correct: To submit something to a group
verbs.wrong: To print something on paper
verbs.why: Send in means to submit something, often by mail or an app, to a group that will use it. Residents send in photos of street problems to city planners.

chunks.text: You do not have to wait for your city to change. Doctors suggest small moves: park a little farther away, [[take the stairs]], or walk to the store [[instead of]] driving. Try to {{map out}} a short walking [[route]] near your home, then {{stick to}} your plan even on busy days. The [[effort]] {{pays off}} with a stronger heart and a better [[mood]].

verbs.correct: To plan something in detail
verbs.wrong: To measure a long distance
verbs.why: Map out means to plan every step of something in detail before you start. Try to map out a short walking route near your home for daily exercise.

verbs.correct: To keep following a plan
verbs.wrong: To change a plan quickly
verbs.why: Stick to means to keep following a plan without changing it. Once you choose a walking route, stick to it even on your busiest days.

verbs.correct: To bring a good result
verbs.wrong: To cost more than expected
verbs.why: Pay off means an effort finally brings a good result. The small effort of walking more pays off with a stronger heart and a better mood.

stories.headline: A short video game may spot depression

sources.title: Depression screening using video games (NIH Research Matters)
3-Minute Video Game Identifies Patients Who Have Depression (NYU Langone)
This 3-Minute Video Game Is Surprisingly Good at Spotting Depression (Gizmodo)

chunks.text: A short video game on a phone may help doctors spot [[depression]] in about three minutes. The illness is hard to [[measure]], so a team at New York University had to {{come up with}} a [[fresh]] way to test for it: two simple games. The team {{carried out}} a study where 120 people played the games, 50 with the illness and 70 without. The results were published in May in a major science [[journal]], and this month the National Institutes of Health [[featured]] the study in its health news for the public. One day, doctors could use short games like these [[instead of]] long [[questionnaires]].

verbs.correct: To invent a new idea or method
verbs.wrong: To copy an older way of testing
verbs.why: Come up with means to invent a new idea or method, especially to solve a difficult problem. The NYU team came up with two short games to test for depression in just minutes.

verbs.correct: To do a piece of planned work
verbs.wrong: To pay for a piece of research
verbs.why: Carry out means to do a piece of planned research or work from beginning to end. The scientists carried out a study with 120 people to test their new depression screening idea.

chunks.text: The first game asks players to pick apples from a tree on the screen. Every pick gives fewer apples, so each tree slowly {{runs low}} on fruit, and the player must decide when to {{move on}} to a fresh tree. [[On average]], healthy players {{held out}} until a tree was almost empty. Players with depression {{walked away from}} their trees much sooner, and the worse their illness was, the earlier they left. The game measures the moment when picking apples stops feeling [[rewarding]]. About 70 percent of people with depression lose [[pleasure]] in things they [[used to]] enjoy.

verbs.correct: To have less and less left
verbs.wrong: To become full again slowly
verbs.why: Run low means to have less and less of something left, until supply is almost gone. In the apple game, each tree runs low on fruit the longer a player keeps picking.

verbs.correct: To leave and go to the next thing
verbs.wrong: To rest before starting again
verbs.why: Move on means to leave one thing behind and go to the next, without staying too long. In the game, players must decide when to move on to a fresh tree.

verbs.correct: To continue for as long as possible
verbs.wrong: To count the apples one by one
verbs.why: Hold out means to continue for as long as possible before quitting something. On average, healthy players held out until a tree was nearly empty of apples.

verbs.correct: To leave something without finishing it
verbs.wrong: To shake something to get more fruit
verbs.why: Walk away from means to leave something before it is finished, often because you have lost interest. In the study, players struggling with depression walked away from their trees noticeably earlier than others.

chunks.text: In the second game, players looked at 30 [[snacks]] and said what each one should cost. Then the game showed some players only the cheapest items, [[over and over]]. Healthy players changed their minds: seeing cheap snacks {{brought down}} the price they expected to pay, [[little by little]]. Players with depression mostly {{stuck with}} their first numbers. The scientists say their [[expectations]] did not [[adjust]] to the new situation, and that this stuck feeling may be an important part of the illness.

verbs.correct: To make something lower
verbs.wrong: To make something fair
verbs.why: Bring down means to make something lower, like a price, a number, or a fever. In the snack game, seeing cheap items again and again brought down what healthy players expected to pay.

verbs.correct: To keep using the same thing
verbs.wrong: To forget something quickly
verbs.why: Stick with means to keep using the same choice or opinion, without changing it. Players with depression mostly stuck with their first price guess, even after seeing new information.

chunks.text: The team hopes to {{roll out}} the game to [[clinics]] one day and plans to ask US [[regulators]] for official [[approval]] as a medical [[device]]. Patients could also play at home once a week, so doctors can {{keep track of}} how well a [[treatment]] is working [[within]] two or three weeks instead of months. The researchers are careful about the [[limits]]. Not everyone with depression plays the same way, and a game cannot {{rule out}} that a player is simply tired or stressed. [[For now]], the game's job is to {{back up}} a doctor's opinion with extra information, not to [[replace]] the doctor.

verbs.correct: To make something widely available
verbs.wrong: To keep something secret for a time
verbs.why: Roll out means to make something newly available to more people or places, often in stages. The team hopes to roll out this game to clinics once it earns official approval.

verbs.correct: To follow and record changes
verbs.wrong: To make something change faster
verbs.why: Keep track of means to follow and record how something changes over time. Doctors could keep track of a patient's progress in a few weeks instead of waiting months.

verbs.correct: To decide something is not possible
verbs.wrong: To treat something with medicine
verbs.why: Rule out means to decide firmly that something is not the explanation. Even a good test result cannot rule out that a person is simply exhausted or having a rough week.

verbs.correct: To support with more evidence
verbs.wrong: To watch someone very closely
verbs.why: Back up means to support something with extra evidence, making it more convincing. This game is meant to back up a doctor's judgment, not replace the doctor's role entirely.

stories.headline: Three midlife risks are linked to dementia

sources.title: Avoiding These 3 Things in Midlife Is Linked to 13 More Dementia-Free Years
3 things to avoid in middle age could mean 13 more years without dementia, study finds
Avoiding 3 risk factors in midlife could add 13 dementia-free years

chunks.text: A long American study {{took in}} 12,409 adults who {{started off}} with [[no sign of]] [[dementia]]. Researchers {{kept track of}} them for about 26 years, and the results were published in the journal Neurology on August 5. The work asked a simple question: how much does health in [[midlife]] change what happens later? It looked at three [[risk factors]]: [[high blood pressure]], [[diabetes]] and [[smoking]].

verbs.correct: To include people in a study
verbs.wrong: To follow a patient for one year
verbs.why: Take in means to include people as participants in a study or program. This long study took in more than 12,000 adults with no sign of dementia.

verbs.correct: To be in a state at the beginning
verbs.wrong: To leave a study before it ends
verbs.why: Start off means to be in a certain state right at the beginning. Every adult in the study started off with no sign of dementia at all.

verbs.correct: To follow something over a long time
verbs.wrong: To treat an illness with medicine
verbs.why: Keep track of means to follow and record something over a long period. Researchers kept track of the group for about 26 years to see what happened.

chunks.text: Adults who had none of the three in middle age {{went on}} to live about 30 years without dementia after the study began. Adults who had all three [[managed]] about 17. The [[gap]] {{adds up to}} roughly 13 years. People with all three were also about 2.7 [[times more likely]] to [[develop]] dementia [[at some point]]. The same [[pattern]] {{came through}} for men and women, with only small differences.

verbs.correct: To continue living for a period
verbs.wrong: To join a different research study
verbs.why: Go on here means to continue living for a certain period afterward. Adults with none of the three risks went on to live about 30 more years without dementia.

verbs.correct: To reach a total of a certain amount
verbs.wrong: To count the years without dementia
verbs.why: Add up to means to reach a certain total once everything is combined. The gap between the two groups adds up to roughly 13 extra years of health.

verbs.correct: To show clearly in the results
verbs.wrong: To appear in men but not in women
verbs.why: Come through means to appear clearly in the results of a study. This same pattern came through for both men and women, with only small differences.

chunks.text: The three factors were measured together, so the study cannot {{single out}} which one matters most. It also cannot {{tell apart}} a real [[cause]] from a [[coincidence]]. This is [[observational]] work: it watched what happened to people who already smoked or already had [[raised]] blood pressure. Money, education and [[genes]] shape health [[as well]], and they may {{make up}} part of the gap.

verbs.correct: To choose one thing out of a group
verbs.wrong: To measure two things at once
verbs.why: Single out means to pick one thing from a group as the most important. Because the risks were measured together, the study cannot single out which one matters most.

verbs.correct: To see the difference between two things
verbs.wrong: To explain a result to the public
verbs.why: Tell apart means to see a real difference between two similar things. Notice the word order: we say tell two things apart, not tell apart two things.

verbs.correct: To form one part of a whole
verbs.wrong: To disprove an earlier finding
verbs.why: Make up means to form one part of a larger whole. Money, education and genes may also make up part of the gap between these two groups.

chunks.text: The numbers are real, but they are not a promise. Nobody can say that if you {{steer clear of}} cigarettes today, or {{cut out}} sugar, or {{get into}} walking, your own dementia will be {{pushed back}} [[by]] 13 years. What the study does show is that doctors already treat these three conditions in [[middle age]], and the same conditions are linked to dementia [[decades]] later. The [[funders]] were the National Institutes of Health.

verbs.correct: To keep away from something harmful
verbs.wrong: To improve your health very slowly
verbs.why: Steer clear of means to keep away from something harmful on purpose. The study does not promise that if you steer clear of cigarettes, your own risk drops by exactly 13 years.

verbs.correct: To stop eating a type of food
verbs.wrong: To measure blood sugar every day
verbs.why: Cut out means to stop eating or using something on purpose, usually for your health. The study cannot promise that if you cut out sugar today, dementia arrives 13 years later.

verbs.correct: To begin doing an activity often
verbs.wrong: To reach an older age in good health
verbs.why: Get into means to begin doing an activity regularly, until it becomes a habit. The study cannot promise that if you get into walking now, your risk changes exactly.

verbs.correct: To make something happen later
verbs.wrong: To lower the risk of an illness
verbs.why: Push back means to make something happen later than it otherwise would. The study cannot promise your own dementia risk will be pushed back by exactly 13 years.

mainIdea.s: A 26-year study found that adults with no high blood pressure, diabetes or smoking lived about 13 more years without dementia. It only watched people, so the gap may not be a direct cause.

mainIdea.s: Doctors say quitting smoking or treating blood pressure today will push back a person's dementia risk by 13 years. The study proves these three habits directly cause the illness later in life.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the article says nobody can promise that one person's own risk will be pushed back by 13 years. This is observational work, not proof of a direct cause.

mainIdea.s: A separate study this year found older adults who followed a Mediterranean diet showed slower memory loss over five years. Researchers say the diet may also lower the risk of heart disease.
mainIdea.why: This story is about a different study on diet and memory loss, not about the midlife risks and dementia study.

sources.title: 'You literally can't': AI startup Orchid sparks backlash over its 'second brain' assistant
Orchid AI assistant launches, gets backlash for relationship ad
'Tech people need to stop': Startup faces backlash after suggesting its AI can save bad relationships

chunks.text: An argument {{kicked off}} on July 28, when a short [[advertisement]] for an AI [[assistant]] called Orchid appeared online. The app works [[by text message]] and {{sorts out}} small jobs: [[bookings]], [[reminders]], files. In the [[clip]], a man forgets his [[anniversary]] while he is playing a video game. His partner messages the assistant instead of him, and the assistant {{stands in for}} him by handling the conversation. It books a restaurant and sends lilies, because it remembers that she likes them better than roses.

verbs.correct: To start suddenly and noisily
verbs.wrong: To end a video with a joke
verbs.why: Kick off here means an argument or controversy started suddenly and got loud fast. An argument kicked off on July 28 when a short advertisement for Orchid appeared online.

verbs.correct: To handle small tasks
verbs.wrong: To reply to a message very fast
verbs.why: Sort out means to handle or organize practical tasks so they get done. The Orchid app sorts out small jobs like bookings, reminders, and files by text message.

verbs.correct: To do something in place of someone
verbs.wrong: To send flowers to a partner
verbs.why: Stand in for means to take someone's place and act for them temporarily. In the ad, the assistant stands in for the man by handling his partner's messages.

chunks.text: The video {{blew up}}. It reached 3.2 million [[views]] and more than 600 [[replies]] [[in a few days]]. Many people who had been [[ready to]] {{sign up}} {{turned on}} the company instead. The line that made people angriest was the assistant's own: "You literally can't. [[That's why]] I'm here." Its [[critics]] said the app was selling a way to look [[thoughtful]] without doing any of the caring.

verbs.correct: To suddenly get a lot of attention
verbs.wrong: To delete a post after an argument
verbs.why: Blow up means that something suddenly gets huge attention online, often within days. The video blew up, reaching 3.2 million views and more than 600 replies.

verbs.correct: To join a service as a member
verbs.wrong: To book a table at a restaurant
verbs.why: Sign up means to officially join a service, usually by creating an account. Many people who had planned to sign up criticized the company instead.

verbs.correct: To suddenly attack someone
verbs.wrong: To share a video with a friend
verbs.why: Here turn on means people suddenly attacked or criticized the company instead of supporting it. Be careful: turn on is also very common for switching on a light or a device.

chunks.text: A [[licensed therapist]] {{spoke out}} too. She warned that texting a machine instead of your partner is [[a form of]] [[triangulation]]: a third person {{cuts in}} on a conversation that should happen only between the two partners. Some readers said [[the whole thing]] {{put off}} people who had planned to try the app. Others called it [[ragebait]], made to be shared in anger.

verbs.correct: To say publicly what you think
verbs.wrong: To answer a message in private
verbs.why: Speak out means to publicly share your opinion, especially about something concerning. A licensed therapist spoke out too, warning that texting a machine instead of a partner is risky.

verbs.correct: To interrupt and take a place
verbs.wrong: To lower the price of an app
verbs.why: Cut in means to interrupt and insert yourself into something meant for just two people. The therapist said a machine can cut in on a conversation that should stay between partners.

verbs.correct: To make someone lose interest
verbs.wrong: To remind someone of a date
verbs.why: Put off means to make someone lose interest in something they once wanted. Some readers said the whole controversy put off people who had planned to try the app.

chunks.text: The company has not {{backed down}}. It said it wanted a story built around a real situation [[rather than]] a normal product video, and it {{brushed off}} the criticism by leaving the clip online. A second advertisement, which claimed the app could check food for [[allergens]], was quietly deleted. The fight {{sums up}} a question the [[tech industry]] keeps [[running into]]: people will let software book a table, but they do not want it to do the caring for them.

verbs.correct: To stop defending your position
verbs.wrong: To repeat a claim more loudly
verbs.why: Back down means to abandon your position after facing pressure or criticism. The company has not backed down, and it left the controversial ad online.

verbs.correct: To treat something as unimportant
verbs.wrong: To delete a video from the internet
verbs.why: Brush off means to treat criticism as unimportant and simply ignore it. Orchid brushed off the criticism by leaving the ad online rather than removing it.

verbs.correct: To capture the whole of something
verbs.wrong: To start a new argument online
verbs.why: Sum up means to capture the whole meaning of a bigger situation in one moment. This fight sums up a real tension: people accept AI booking a table, not doing their emotional work.

stories.headline: Heat squeezes Italy's Parmesan cheese

sources.title: Italy's $4.7 billion cheese economy is feeling the heat as climate change threatens its cheese banks
Italy's Parmesan Industry Under Pressure as Extreme Heat Cuts Milk Production
Europe's 40C Heatwave Threatens Parmesan Cheese Production
Italy's cheese banks feel the heat (video, Reuters)

chunks.text: A long [[heatwave]] in northern Italy is {{cutting into}} the country's most famous cheese. When the air goes above 40 degrees Celsius, which is 104 Fahrenheit, [[dairy cows]] eat less and give [[up to]] ten [[percent]] less milk. Parmigiano Reggiano is made from that milk. The [[producers]] who {{stand behind}} the name sell about four [[billion]] euros of cheese a year, and a farmer cannot {{make up}} the milk that a hot summer {{takes away}}.

verbs.correct: To reduce the amount of something
verbs.wrong: To move milk from farm to dairy
verbs.why: Cut into means something reduces an amount that really matters, like income or supply. The heat is cutting into how much milk Italy's dairy cows produce.

verbs.correct: To support and protect something
verbs.wrong: To wait for cheese to be ready
verbs.why: Stand behind means to support something fully, standing ready to guarantee its quality. The producers who stand behind the Parmigiano Reggiano name protect a centuries-old reputation.

verbs.correct: To replace something that was lost
verbs.wrong: To decide the price of a product
verbs.why: Make up means to replace what was lost so the total returns to normal. A farmer cannot make up milk that a hot summer has already cost the herd.

verbs.correct: To remove something a person had
verbs.wrong: To store cheese for a longer time
verbs.why: Take away means something is removed from you, leaving you with less than you had before. A hot summer literally takes away milk the farmers need for their monthly income.

chunks.text: The cheese also [[takes a long time]] to make. A [[wheel]] must [[sit]] for [[at least]] twelve months, and most are kept for two or three years. About four million wheels a year come from around 300 [[dairies]]. While a wheel waits in [[storage]], money has already {{gone out}} for [[feed]], work and power. No money {{comes in}} for years, so the costs {{pile up}}.

verbs.correct: To be spent and leave the farm
verbs.wrong: To be sold in another country
verbs.why: Go out means money leaves your hands and is spent, often before you see any return. Feed, labor, and power costs all go out long before a wheel is ready to sell.

verbs.correct: To arrive as money that is earned
verbs.wrong: To join a group of producers
verbs.why: Come in means money arrives as income, the opposite of spending it. No money comes in from a wheel of cheese for years while it slowly ages.

verbs.correct: To grow into a large amount
verbs.wrong: To be counted at the end of a year
verbs.why: Pile up means costs or problems keep growing larger the longer they are left. With no income for years, a farmer's expenses pile up fast.

chunks.text: Italian banks {{thought up}} an answer to this [[a long time ago]]. One bank has accepted cheese as [[security]] for a loan since 1953. The farmer gives the bank his wheels, the bank {{puts away}} the cheese in a [[vault]], and the farmer {{takes out}} a [[loan]] [[worth]] 60 to 80 percent of what it is worth. One vault holds more than 500,000 wheels.

verbs.correct: To invent a clever answer to a problem
verbs.wrong: To copy an idea from another country
verbs.why: Think up means to invent a creative solution to a real problem. Italian banks thought up a clever system: farmers could borrow against wheels of aging cheese.

verbs.correct: To store something in a safe place
verbs.wrong: To sell cheese before it is ready
verbs.why: Put away means to place something in storage where it will stay safe until it is needed. The bank puts away each farmer's cheese wheels in a locked vault.

verbs.correct: To arrange a loan from a bank
verbs.wrong: To repay money that is owed
verbs.why: Take out means to formally arrange a loan, so it's a common phrase for borrowing money. A farmer takes out a loan worth most of what the stored cheese is worth.

chunks.text: So the extreme heat is now affecting the banks that lend money against cheese. Less milk means fewer wheels, and fewer wheels mean the banks are holding less. Keeping those vaults cool costs about 30 percent more [[electricity]] in the hottest weeks, and the Po River has {{dried up}} to under a third of its normal [[level]]. Farmers can still {{fall back on}} the loans and {{get by}}, but there is less money left [[at the end of the year]].

verbs.correct: To lose most of its water
verbs.wrong: To be measured twice each summer
verbs.why: Dry up means water disappears until barely any is left, which describes rivers just as well as bank accounts. The Po River has dried up to under a third of its normal level.

verbs.correct: To use a support when all else fails
verbs.wrong: To pay a loan later than agreed
verbs.why: Fall back on means to use a backup you know you can trust when other options are gone. Farmers can still fall back on these loans when a bad summer cuts their income.

verbs.correct: To have just enough money to live
verbs.wrong: To sell a farm and leave the business
verbs.why: Get by means to manage with just enough, nothing extra, to cover your needs. Farmers can still get by on these loans, even though there is less left at year's end.

stories.headline: Doctors warn about looksmaxxing

sources.title: Looksmaxxing may point to deeper body image issues in young men, mental health expert says
Looksmaxxing isn't just a TikTok trend, it often reflects severe body image issues in boys and young men

chunks.text: A new word has {{caught on}} online [[among]] teenage boys and young men. Looksmaxxing means improving your [[appearance]] [[as much as possible]]. The soft version is [[grooming]] and a [[daily routine]] of sleep and exercise. The hard version is [[surgery]] on the nose or the [[jawline]]. Many who follow it are still {{growing up}}, and they {{look up to}} influencers who give a face a [[rating]] [[out of ten]].

verbs.correct: To become popular with many people
verbs.wrong: To be noticed by only a few people
verbs.why: Catch on means to become popular and spread among many people, often quickly. This new word caught on fast among teenage boys and young men online.

verbs.correct: To change from a child into an adult
verbs.wrong: To raise a child inside a family
verbs.why: Grow up means to develop from a child into an adult over the years. Many who follow this trend are still growing up themselves, which makes the pressure worse.

verbs.correct: To admire someone you want to copy
verbs.wrong: To study a problem very carefully
verbs.why: Look up to means to admire someone and want to be like them. Many young men look up to online influencers who rate faces out of ten.

chunks.text: A social worker at the University of Michigan wrote in July 2026 that these behaviors [[look like]] the [[signs]] of an [[eating disorder]] or [[body dysmorphia]]. Some young men {{cut out}} [[whole food groups]] or {{give up}} meals for days. A few hit their own face with a [[hammer]]. She says the [[trend]] is not [[harmless]], and that a boy who starts small can {{end up}} in danger.

verbs.correct: To stop eating a type of food
verbs.wrong: To spend less money than before
verbs.why: Cut out means to stop eating a certain food or type of food completely. Some young men cut out whole food groups to try to change how they look.

verbs.correct: To stop having something you want
verbs.wrong: To gain weight in a short time
verbs.why: Give up means to stop having or doing something you actually want, often for a goal. Some young men give up entire meals for days at a time, which can be dangerous.

verbs.correct: To reach a situation you did not plan
verbs.wrong: To close an online account for good
verbs.why: End up means to reach a situation you never planned for, often after a series of small steps. Doctors warn that a boy who starts small can end up in real danger.

chunks.text: Looksmaxxing spreads because it [[pays to]] {{show off}}. A researcher at Northeastern University says the most [[extreme]] [[stunts]] get the most clicks, so the advice keeps getting harder. He also says the [[ideal]] face in these videos copies old European [[beauty standards]]. A [[psychologist]] there says men are a new market for beauty companies. For some boys, looksmaxxing stops being a hobby and can {{take over}} the whole day. Then the wish to {{stand out}} [[turns into]] a fear of being [[judged]].

verbs.correct: To try to impress other people
verbs.wrong: To arrive at a place as planned
verbs.why: Show off here means to try to impress other people, often by posting something extreme online. The most extreme stunts get the most attention, so the advice keeps getting harder.

verbs.correct: To fill all of a person's time
verbs.wrong: To hire a person for a new job

chunks.text: Doctors {{point out}} that the problem is easy to [[miss]] in boys. Most tests ask about a fear of being fat, so a boy who trains hard to look [[lean]] can pass them. Researchers estimate that [[one in three]] people with an eating disorder is male. The [[warning signs]] include [[obsessive]] mirror checks and secret rules about food. Experts say it is healthy to {{work out}}. But they also advise parents to help a son {{open up}} and to [[seek help]] early, since [[self-esteem]] problems can have [[long-term]] effects.

verbs.correct: To tell people about an important fact
verbs.wrong: To argue against a popular opinion
verbs.why: Point out means to tell people about a fact they might not have noticed on their own. Doctors point out that these warning signs are easy to miss in boys.

verbs.wrong: To admit that you did something wrong
verbs.why: Open up means to talk honestly about feelings a person would normally hide. Parents can help a son open up instead of staying silent about what worries him.
