stories.headline: A film of the Odyssey fills movie theaters

sources.title: Box Office: 'The Odyssey' Soars to $652 Million Globally After Two Weekends, Including $140 Million in Imax
'The Odyssey' extends stay in 70mm Imax theaters as shows sell out weeks in advance
Coveted 'The Odyssey' IMAX 70mm Screenings Extended After Weeks Of Sold Out Showings
'The Odyssey' drives summer box office boom through rare IMAX 70mm screenings (video, FOX 5 New York)

chunks.text: The Odyssey is a Greek [[poem]] about 2,800 years old. A film of it has become the biggest movie story of the summer. It {{came out}} on July 17, [[directed]] by Christopher Nolan with Matt Damon as Odysseus, and had {{raked in}} about 652 million dollars [[worldwide]] after only two weekends. About 140 million of that came from IMAX screens alone, which is unusual, because IMAX normally {{makes up}} a small [[share]] of any film's [[earnings]].

verbs.correct: To be released to the public
verbs.wrong: To be shown in only a few theaters
verbs.why: Come out means a movie or an album is released for the public to see. This film based on the Odyssey came out on July 17 and became a huge hit.

verbs.correct: To earn a lot of money
verbs.wrong: To spend a lot of money on ads
verbs.why: Rake in means to earn a very large amount of money quickly. The film had raked in about 652 million dollars worldwide after only two weekends.

verbs.correct: To form a part of a whole
verbs.wrong: To recover money that was lost
verbs.why: Make up means to form one part of a bigger total. IMAX screens usually make up only a small share of a film's total earnings.

chunks.text: The reason is the way it was filmed. This is the first full length film [[shot]] entirely on IMAX film cameras, using more than two million feet of [[70mm]] film. Those cameras are heavy, noisy and rare, so most directors {{stay away from}} them and film [[digitally]] instead. The reward is a picture with [[far more]] detail than an ordinary movie image, and one that fills a tall screen [[from top to bottom]] rather than filling only a wide strip across the middle.

verbs.correct: To avoid using something
verbs.wrong: To be unable to pay for something
verbs.why: Stay away from means to avoid using something on purpose. Most directors stay away from heavy IMAX film cameras and shoot digitally instead.

chunks.text: The problem is that [[hardly anywhere]] can show it that way. Only about 25 theaters in the whole United States can [[project]] 70mm IMAX. Seats at those [[screenings]] {{sold out}} [[as much as]] seven weeks ahead. One theater [[chain]] had to {{set up}} a digital [[waiting list]] on its app when new tickets were released. Some people flew hundreds of miles to reach a screen. On July 30 the [[studio]] {{gave in}} to the [[demand]] and [[extended]] the 70mm [[run]] by a month, to September 16.

verbs.correct: To be completely sold
verbs.wrong: To be offered for sale early
verbs.why: Sell out means every ticket or seat is gone because so many people want it. Seats at the 70mm screenings sold out as much as seven weeks ahead.

verbs.correct: To create or arrange
verbs.wrong: To make a system work faster
verbs.why: Set up means to create something new so people can use it. One theater chain set up a digital waiting list for the sold out screenings.

verbs.correct: To agree after resisting
verbs.wrong: To refuse a request politely
verbs.why: Give in means to finally agree to a request after resisting it for a while. On July 30 the studio gave in to the demand and extended the run.

chunks.text: The money is not really the interesting part. A story that people have been {{passing down}} since before writing was even common has {{filled up}} theaters in 2026. [[Audiences]] {{lined up}} to see it in the oldest [[format]] available, not the newest one. Whether other studios now {{take up}} film cameras again is a separate question, and an expensive one, because only [[a handful of]] these cameras exist anywhere in the world.

verbs.correct: To give to later generations
verbs.wrong: To perform live for large audiences
verbs.why: Pass down means to give something, often a story or a tradition, to later generations. The Odyssey is a story people have been passing down for almost three thousand years.

verbs.wrong: To open more screens in a city
verbs.why: Fill up means to become completely full of people or things. This ancient story has filled up movie theaters all across the country in 2026.

verbs.correct: To wait in a line

verbs.why: Line up means to wait in a row for your turn. Audiences lined up to see this film in the oldest format available, not the newest one.

verbs.correct: To start using again
verbs.wrong: To take control of a company
verbs.why: Take up means to start doing or using something again after a break. Whether other studios take up film cameras again is still an open question.

stories.headline: Birdsong in a forest lowers stress

sources.title: Birdsong and walks in the forest tied to significant mental health benefits
Listening to birdsong in a forest lowered a person's stress during experiment
Birdsong and walks in the forest tied to significant mental health benefits

chunks.text: [[Researchers]] in the United States have found that where a person sits and what that person hears both change how they feel. The surprising part is that the sound matters about [[as much as]] the place. Their [[study]] {{came out}} on July 17 in the [[journal]] Environmental Conservation. It {{set out to}} separate two things that almost always happen together, which are being in nature and hearing nature.

verbs.correct: To be published
verbs.wrong: To be tested by others
verbs.why: Come out means a study or report becomes available to the public. Scientists say a paper comes out when a journal finally publishes it.

verbs.correct: To intend to do something
verbs.wrong: To succeed in proving an idea
verbs.why: Set out to means you have a clear goal before you begin. This team set out to separate the effect of place from the effect of sound in the experiment.

chunks.text: The team recruited 106 [[volunteers]]. Each one sat either on a [[restored]] [[trail]] beside a river or in a [[bare]] [[concrete]] space with no plants at all. Each one wore noise canceling headphones, which {{shut out}} every real sound around them. The headphones then played either recorded birdsong or recorded traffic, chosen [[at random]]. That gave four [[combinations]]. A volunteer could be among trees while hearing cars, or on concrete while hearing birds. Researchers then [[measured]] [[stress]], positive and negative feelings, and how [[rested]] each person said they felt.

verbs.correct: To block from entering
verbs.wrong: To stop a machine working
verbs.why: Shut out means to block a sound or a feeling completely. These headphones shut out every real noise so the researchers could control what people heard.

chunks.text: Trees with birdsong {{won out}} [[on every measure]]. According to the lead researcher, positive feelings {{went up}}, negative feelings {{went down}}, stress {{went down}}, and the sense of feeling rested {{went up}}. Concrete with traffic noise was worst. The two mixed pairs landed [[in between]], and that is the result that {{stands out}}. People on concrete felt better when they heard birds than when they heard cars. People among trees felt worse when they heard cars than when they heard birds. Neither the place [[on its own]] nor the sound on its own decided how they felt.

verbs.correct: To succeed in the end
verbs.wrong: To get support from people
verbs.why: When something wins out, it beats every alternative in the end. Trees with birdsong won out on every single measure the team tracked.

verbs.correct: To become greater
verbs.wrong: To rise and then fall again
verbs.why: Go up just means a number or a feeling rises. Here positive feelings and the sense of feeling rested both went up after birdsong.

verbs.correct: To become smaller
verbs.wrong: To drop to nothing at all
verbs.why: Go down means a number or a feeling gets smaller. Stress and negative feelings both went down when people listened to birdsong instead of traffic.

verbs.correct: To be clearly noticeable
verbs.wrong: To disagree with other results
verbs.why: A result stands out when it surprises you or breaks the pattern you expected. Here the mixed pairs, trees with traffic or concrete with birds, stood out the most.

chunks.text: The practical point is about cities. Not every [[neighborhood]] can afford a new park. This study suggests that an empty concrete area gets better [[as soon as]] natural sound {{comes back}}. That can happen through planting that {{draws in}} birds, or [[simply by]] helping people {{block out}} the traffic. The researchers are careful about how far the [[finding]] goes. It was one study, on one [[campus]], with about a hundred people, and it measured how they felt that day [[rather than]] months [[afterwards]].

verbs.correct: To return to a place
verbs.wrong: To become louder than it was
verbs.why: Come back means to return to a place after being away. When natural sound comes back to a bare space, it can change how people feel there.

verbs.correct: To attract toward a place
verbs.wrong: To stop animals leaving an area
verbs.why: Draw in means to attract something toward a place. Trees and plants can draw in birds, adding natural sound even to a plain city block.

verbs.correct: To stop from being heard
verbs.wrong: To leave a noisy street
verbs.why: Block out means to stop a sound from reaching your ears. City planners could help residents block out traffic noise even without a full park.

mainIdea.s: A new study found that where a person sits and what they hear change how stressed they feel. People felt best among trees with birdsong and felt worst on bare concrete with traffic noise.
mainIdea.why: Trees with birdsong won out on every measure, and concrete with traffic noise was worst. The two mixed pairs landed in between, which is the result that stands out.

mainIdea.s: Researchers found that only the sound a person hears changes their stress, not the place they sit in. People felt best with birdsong and worst with traffic noise, no matter where they sat.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the study found the place also mattered. People on concrete felt better hearing birds than cars, and people among trees felt worse hearing cars than birds.

mainIdea.s: A separate study found that parks with more trees see lower crime rates than areas with less greenery. Researchers said planting more trees could help cities save money on policing.
mainIdea.why: This is about trees and crime rates, a different study entirely. The birdsong study measured stress and mood, not crime.

stories.headline: Hyundai workers strike over robots

sources.title: We Just Had The First Humanoid Robot Strike Ever
Hyundai workers in South Korea strike over humanoids
Hyundai Workers Walk Out in Auto Industry's First Humanoid Robot Strike
How Hyundai's humanoid robot plans are facing fierce opposition from workers (video, KOREA NOW)

chunks.text: About 35,000 workers at Hyundai's car [[plants]] in South Korea {{walked out}} in July over a plan to put [[humanoid]] robots on [[the factory floor]]. Their [[union]] says no car company anywhere has faced a [[strike]] about robots before. The workers are not asking Hyundai to {{call off}} the plan. They want the right to agree before any robot arrives.

verbs.correct: To stop work as a protest
verbs.wrong: To leave a job permanently
verbs.why: Walk out means to leave your job suddenly as a form of protest, usually along with many other workers. About 35,000 Hyundai workers walked out in July over the company's plan to add robots.

verbs.correct: To cancel something planned
verbs.wrong: To delay a plan to a later year
verbs.why: Call off means to cancel something that was already planned or scheduled. The workers are not asking Hyundai to call off its plan for robots, only to be consulted first.

chunks.text: Hyundai owns Boston Dynamics, an American robot maker, and intends to install about 25,000 of its Atlas robots at Hyundai and Kia plants worldwide. The first are due at a factory in Savannah, in the United States, starting in 2028. No date has been [[fixed]] for South Korea. The Korean Metal Workers' Union is {{holding out for}} a written promise that no humanoid robot enters a Korean plant unless the union agrees first. It is also {{pushing for}} [[hourly]] jobs to be {{turned into}} fixed [[salaries]], and for the [[retirement age]] to rise from 60 to 65.

verbs.correct: To refuse to settle without
verbs.wrong: To wait without making any demands
verbs.why: Hold out for means to keep refusing to agree until you get exactly what you want. The union is holding out for a written promise that no robot enters a plant without its approval.

verbs.correct: To demand something strongly
verbs.wrong: To vote in favor of an agreement
verbs.why: Push for means to demand something firmly and keep demanding it. The union is also pushing for hourly workers to receive fixed salaries and a later retirement age.

verbs.correct: To change into something else
verbs.wrong: To be paid at a higher hourly rate
verbs.why: Turn into means to change from one form into a different one. The union wants hourly pay to turn into a fixed yearly salary for workers.

chunks.text: The action {{built up}} slowly. Between July 13 and 15 the workers left their [[shifts]] two hours early. On July 20 they moved to four hour [[stoppages]] every day at the Ulsan [[complex]], which is the largest car factory in the world. Those early two-hour shifts in mid-July alone stopped about 5,000 cars from being built. Hyundai will not promise that [[automation]] costs no jobs. It says workers will {{move into}} [[supervising]] and repairing the machines instead. Managers have {{put forward}} higher pay, large [[bonuses]] and 15 company [[shares]] for each worker.

verbs.correct: To grow gradually stronger
verbs.wrong: To start again after a break
verbs.why: Build up means to grow larger or stronger step by step over time. The strike action built up slowly, moving from short early departures to full four hour stoppages.

verbs.correct: To change to a new role
verbs.wrong: To be trained for a short period
verbs.why: Move into means to change from your current role into a new one. Hyundai says automated workers will move into supervising and repairing the new robots instead.

verbs.correct: To offer for consideration
verbs.wrong: To pay something before it is due
verbs.why: Put forward means to offer an idea or proposal for others to consider. Managers have put forward higher pay, big bonuses, and company shares for every worker.

chunks.text: Neither side has {{backed down}}. What is [[settled]] in Ulsan matters well [[beyond]] South Korea, because other [[carmakers]] are testing the same machines and are watching how this {{works out}}. The union's [[argument]] is not that robots cannot do the job. It is that the people doing the job now were never asked first.

verbs.correct: To stop demanding something
verbs.wrong: To refuse to speak to the other side
verbs.why: Back down means to abandon a demand instead of continuing to insist on it. Neither side in the Hyundai dispute has backed down yet.

verbs.correct: To develop to an end
verbs.wrong: To be decided by a judge
verbs.why: Here work out means how a situation finally develops or ends, not exercise. Carmakers everywhere are watching closely to see how the Hyundai dispute works out.

stories.headline: A T. rex skeleton sells for 50 million dollars

sources.title: Mystery bidder buys T. rex nicknamed 'Gus' for a record $50 million
T. rex sells for $50 million, becoming the most expensive dinosaur fossil ever auctioned
Rare T. rex fossil sells for record $50.1 million at auction
T. rex skeleton Gus sells for a record $50.1 million (video, Reuters)

chunks.text: A skeleton of a Tyrannosaurus rex sold for 50.1 million dollars in New York on July 14. The [[auction house]] had expected it to {{go for}} 20 to 30 million, so the price almost [[doubled]] the highest [[estimate]]. The buyer [[bid]] by telephone and has not been named. No dinosaur has ever sold for more. The old [[record]] was almost 45 million dollars, paid for a stegosaurus in 2024. The sale has {{stirred up}} an old argument about who should be allowed to own a [[fossil]] like this.

verbs.correct: To be sold for a price
verbs.wrong: To be offered for free
verbs.why: Go for means to sell for a certain price at an auction or a sale. The auction house expected the T. rex skeleton to go for 20 to 30 million dollars.

verbs.correct: To cause strong feelings
verbs.wrong: To bring an old argument to an end
verbs.why: Stir up means to bring old, strong feelings back to the surface again. The record sale has stirred up an old argument about who should own rare fossils.

chunks.text: The skeleton is [[nicknamed]] Gus. It is about 67 million years old, 38 feet long and 12.5 feet tall. A team {{dug up}} the bones on a [[ranch]] in South Dakota in 2021. [[Freeing]] them from the rock and then {{cleaning up}} every piece took five years. The ranch belonged to a farmer called Gary Licking, and he died before that work was finished. The team chose the nickname in his [[memory]].

verbs.correct: To remove from the ground
verbs.wrong: To measure before moving it
verbs.why: Dig up means to remove something buried, usually with careful, slow work. A team dug up the T. rex bones on a ranch in South Dakota in 2021.

verbs.correct: To make clean and tidy
verbs.wrong: To repair a broken piece
verbs.why: Clean up here means to carefully remove rock and dirt from each fossil bone. Freeing the skeleton from the rock and cleaning up every piece took the team five years.

chunks.text: About 61 percent of Gus is real bone, which is a lot for a T. rex. Most skeletons in museums are [[largely]] [[plaster]]. The [[skull]] is almost [[undamaged]]. Gus also kept its [[furcula]], a thin V shaped bone across the chest that we call the wishbone in a chicken. That bone is [[fragile]] and it very rarely {{shows up}} in a fossil this old. Those three things together are why the bidding {{shot up}}.

verbs.correct: To appear or be present
verbs.wrong: To be listed in a book
verbs.why: Show up means to appear or be present, here inside a very old fossil. The delicate wishbone bone very rarely shows up in a fossil this old and this complete.

stories.headline: Romania shoots down a drone for the first time

sources.title: Romanian F-16 shoots down drone after airspace breach, marking first for NATO ally
F-16 downs drone in Romania's airspace for first time
Romania says F-16 shot down drone over the country's airspace (video, euronews)

chunks.text: A Romanian air force F-16 {{shot down}} a drone over Buzau County on Friday, July 24. Radar {{picked up}} the [[aircraft]] at 9:39 a.m., about 20 kilometers east of Sulina, and the pilot destroyed it with a [[missile]] at 11:02 a.m. The drone {{came down}} near the village of Padina. Foreign Minister Oana Toiu said it was the first time a drone had been [[intercepted]] and destroyed inside Romania's national [[airspace]].

verbs.correct: To destroy an aircraft by firing at it
verbs.wrong: To fire a warning shot into the air
verbs.why: Shoot down means to destroy something flying, like a plane or a drone, by firing a weapon at it. A fighter jet can shoot down a drone that enters restricted airspace.

verbs.correct: To detect a signal or object
verbs.wrong: To choose one thing from a group
verbs.why: Pick up means equipment like radar or a microphone detects a signal from far away. Radar can pick up a small object long before anyone on the ground sees it.

verbs.correct: To fall from the sky and land
verbs.wrong: To explode into small pieces
verbs.why: Come down means something falls out of the sky and lands somewhere. A damaged aircraft usually comes down fast, with little control over where it lands.

chunks.text: Romania [[borders]] Ukraine and sits on the eastern edge of NATO, the military [[alliance]] whose members agree to defend one another. Romania takes part in a NATO air policing mission, in which allied jets help [[guard]] each other's skies. During the incident, Italian Eurofighter Typhoons were in the air, and two more Romanian F-16s tracked the drone. Reports of drones crossing into Romanian airspace, or of [[debris]] landing on Romanian [[soil]], {{go back to}} 2022, and officials have counted [[dozens of]] them.

verbs.correct: To date from an earlier time
verbs.wrong: To happen only one time before
verbs.why: Go back to means something started at an earlier point and has continued since then. Reports of this kind of incident go back to a date several years earlier.

chunks.text: Romania's army chief said the drone [[appeared to be]] a Shahed-type aircraft, an Iranian design that Russia has used [[in large numbers]] in Ukraine. That is a description of the shape, not [[proof]] of who sent it. Interim Defense Minister Radu Miruta said officials had not been able to {{pin down}} the drone's [[origin]]. He [[praised]] the crews for their "professionalism, [[composure]] and [[rapid]] response." President Nicusor Dan said the area was [[uninhabited]].

verbs.correct: To establish something exactly
verbs.wrong: To write information down on paper
verbs.why: Pin down means to state or identify something with total certainty, leaving no doubt. Investigators could not pin down exactly where the drone had been launched.

chunks.text: Investigators are {{combing through}} the [[wreckage]], and officials are still trying to {{find out}} where the drone was launched. Miruta {{called for}} more [[spending]] on air defense and on equipment [[designed to]] stop drones. For the villages under that airspace, Friday ended with the most basic question [[unanswered]]: no one in the government has said whose drone it was.

verbs.correct: To search something thoroughly

verbs.correct: To discover a fact

verbs.why: Find out means to discover a piece of information you did not know before. Officials are still trying to find out exactly who sent the drone.

verbs.correct: To publicly demand something
verbs.wrong: To cancel a planned event
verbs.why: Call for means to publicly demand that something be done, often as a solution to a problem. Officials called for more spending on defense after the incident happened.

mainIdea.s: A drone was shot down over Buzau County after officials said they had traced its launch to Russia. The aircraft came down near an empty village, and nobody on the ground was hurt.

mainIdea.s: Poland shot down several drones that crossed its border last year, prompting NATO talks on eastern air defense. That event led allied jets to increase patrols near a neighboring war zone.
mainIdea.why: This is about an earlier Polish shootdown, not the Romanian one from July 2026. Romania's case was its first ever and happened on its own.

sources.title: Watch: Stuffed donkey returned to 5-year-old after social media adventure
Happy ending for honorary BC Ferries crew member Churro as owner found
Churro the Burro's adventure on BC Ferries delights thousands
How a BC Ferries crew found the owner of 'Churro' the stuffed donkey (video, CTV News)

chunks.text: A pink [[stuffed]] donkey {{turned up}} on the BC Ferries [[vessel]] Salish Raven on Thursday, July 16. The company believes it was {{left behind}} on an afternoon [[sailing]] from Swartz Bay to the Southern Gulf Islands, British Columbia. No one had {{come forward}} to claim it. The [[crew]] named it Churro the Burro, gave it a staff [[badge]], and began posting photographs of its days [[at sea]]. [[By the time]] the owner was found, the toy had spent a week [[aboard]].

verbs.correct: To appear or be found, often unexpectedly
verbs.wrong: To refuse to accept an offer or request
verbs.why: Turn up means to appear somewhere, often by surprise, whether it is a lost object or a person who is late. A missing sock can turn up months later in the wash.

verbs.correct: To forget something and go without it
verbs.wrong: To not include something in a list
verbs.why: Leave behind means to forget an item and go without it, like a jacket at a restaurant or a phone on a train. It is usually accidental.

verbs.correct: To make yourself known to claim something
verbs.wrong: To be mentioned or talked about online
verbs.why: Come forward means to make yourself known publicly to claim something or share information. Witnesses and owners of lost items both come forward this way.

chunks.text: BC Ferries carries passengers between Vancouver Island, the mainland and the smaller islands. Instead of a [[plain]] [[lost-and-found]] notice, the company asked the public online to help {{track down}} the owner, and the crew {{showed Churro around}} the ship. There are photographs of it on the bridge, in the engine room, on [[deck]], and in the gift shop among the other stuffed animals. Others show it with a book and a soft serve ice cream.

verbs.correct: To search for someone until you find them
verbs.wrong: To follow how something changes over time
verbs.why: Track down means to search patiently until you locate someone or something hard to find, like an old friend or a missing owner. It takes effort and often a little luck.

verbs.correct: To take someone on a tour of a place
verbs.wrong: To let a visitor in at the entrance
verbs.why: Show around means to take a visitor on a tour of a place, room by room. Crews sometimes show even a stuffed toy around for fun, just like a new hire.

chunks.text: The [[posts]] {{racked up}} more than a million views and thousands of comments. Some people [[suggested]] Churro {{stay on}} as a [[mascot]]. On Monday, July 20, the company said the search was over. The donkey [[belonged to]] five-year-old Alfie, whose grandmother had bought it for him in Mexico. His mother, Abigail Broadribb, had not noticed it was [[missing]] [[at all]]. She {{came across}} the story [[in the news]].

verbs.correct: To collect a large number or amount of something
verbs.wrong: To make sense when you look at all the facts
verbs.why: Rack up means to collect a large amount of something quickly, like views, likes, or comments online. A single popular post can rack up millions in a day.

verbs.correct: To remain in a place or role longer than expected
verbs.wrong: To agree to join a company as a new worker
verbs.why: Stay on means to remain in a place or role for longer than people expected, past the usual point of leaving. A popular mascot might stay on well beyond its original purpose.

verbs.correct: To find something by chance
verbs.wrong: To seem or appear a certain way
verbs.why: Here come across means to find something by chance, not on purpose, like a news story you happen to scroll past. You come across all kinds of things online without searching for them.

chunks.text: The company thanked everyone who had commented, tagged friends and shared the posts, then [[arranged]] a [[reunion]] for later that week. Churro was {{handed back}} to Alfie, keeping the name the crew gave it. "We're just really [[grateful]]," Broadribb said. "This is a very special experience for him to have [[a peek behind the curtain]]."

verbs.correct: To return something to the person it belongs to
verbs.wrong: To give something to a younger family member
verbs.why: Hand back means to return something directly to its owner, often after borrowing or finding it. A lost donkey, a graded paper, or borrowed keys can all be handed back.

stories.headline: Japan now has cooling booths for one person

sources.title: Watch: 'Human refrigerator' debuts in Japan amid rising temperatures
Japan now has human refrigerators inspired by vending machines
Japan creates fridge for humans (video, CBS Chicago)

chunks.text: Japan's newest [[refrigerator]] is built for people. The Do Hiemon Box is a [[booth]] the size of a [[vending machine]]. One person steps inside, and air at 41 degrees Fahrenheit blows onto the head, neck, shoulders and back. After 20 minutes the machine {{shuts itself off}}. One of the first units has gone to Maebashi City Hall in Gunma Prefecture, where anyone can {{drop in}} and use it free during [[opening hours]].

verbs.correct: To stop a machine from working
verbs.wrong: To make a machine work faster
verbs.why: Shut off means to stop a machine from working, either by a person or automatically. This cooling booth shuts itself off after twenty minutes, so nobody has to remember a timer.

verbs.correct: To visit a place without arranging it first
verbs.wrong: To leave something at a place for later
verbs.why: Drop in means to visit a place casually, without an appointment or advance planning. Anyone can drop in at the Maebashi city hall booth during opening hours.

chunks.text: SDRS, which makes refrigeration units and vending machines, modeled the booth on the chilled drink machines found on streets across Japan. Inside, the temperature sits at 59 degrees, with three [[airflow]] settings. The booth is [[on wheels]] and needs no {{setting up}}. It is [[aimed at]] construction sites, factories, warehouses and outdoor events.

verbs.correct: To assemble something ready for use
verbs.wrong: To start a journey to another place
verbs.why: Set up means to prepare something so people can use it, like a tent or a new device. This cooling booth needs no setting up: it arrives ready to use immediately.

chunks.text: Temperatures in Japan have reached [[close to]] 100 degrees [[in recent weeks]], and the country has {{brought in}} a new weather category for the hottest days. In Tokyo, 48 people were taken to the hospital with [[heatstroke]] on July 15. SDRS says people feel [[noticeably]] cooler within about five minutes. The company also says ten minutes inside may [[relieve]] the [[symptoms]] of [[heat exhaustion]]. It adds that the booth uses about half the electricity of a spot air conditioner, the [[portable]] kind used on factory floors. Those are the company's own [[claims]], and it has published no independent testing to {{back them up}}.

verbs.correct: To introduce a new rule or system
verbs.wrong: To mention a subject in conversation
verbs.why: Bring in means to introduce something new, like a rule, a system, or in this case a new weather category for extreme heat. Officials bring in new categories when old ones no longer fit reality.

verbs.correct: To support a claim with evidence
verbs.wrong: To repeat a claim more loudly
verbs.why: Back up means to support a claim with solid evidence, such as data or independent testing. A company's own claims about a product need proof to back them up before we trust them fully.

chunks.text: The standard model costs 1.5 million yen [[plus tax]], about $9,300, and is sold to businesses [[rather than]] households. Trusco Nakayama, an industrial equipment supplier, is {{rolling the booths out}} through [[distributors]] [[nationwide]]. The Maebashi unit came as a [[donation]], so the city offers it free. Whether the idea {{catches on}} [[elsewhere]] is [[not yet clear]]. For the builders and road crews working outdoors, the [[appeal]] is simple. Step inside, {{cool off}} for five minutes, then back to work.

verbs.correct: To make a new product available widely
verbs.wrong: To test a product before using it
verbs.why: Roll out means to make a new product available to more people or places, little by little or all at once. Trusco Nakayama is rolling these cooling booths out through distributors nationwide.

verbs.correct: To become popular with many people
verbs.wrong: To reach the same level as others
verbs.why: Catch on means to become popular and spread to many people over time. It is not yet clear whether these cooling booths will catch on outside of Japan.

verbs.correct: To become cooler after being too hot
verbs.wrong: To blow air onto a person's head
verbs.why: Cool off means to become less hot after being too warm, whether that is a person, a room, or an engine. Workers can step into the booth and cool off for a few minutes.

stories.headline: Hot nights cost people a week of sleep a year

sources.title: Climate change is stealing our sleep
India among global hotspots for climate-related sleep loss, highest in TN: Report
Climate Change is Costing People Sleep
Study: warmer nights double global sleep loss since the 1970s (video, WION)

chunks.text: Hot nights are costing the average person about 56 hours of sleep a year, [[close to]] seven nights' [[worth]], according to an [[analysis]] of 1,338 cities published on July 15 by the research group Climate Central. [[Roughly]] six of those hours, about one night, {{come down to}} human-caused [[warming]]. That [[share]] has [[at least]] doubled since the early 1970s, and it is far larger in some regions than others.

verbs.correct: To be explained by one main cause
verbs.wrong: To think of a new plan or idea
verbs.why: Come down to means that a result can be explained by one main cause. About six of those lost hours come down to human-caused warming, the study found.

chunks.text: Heat {{keeps people up}} for a simple reason. Sleep [[depends on]] the body's ability to cool itself, and warm night air {{slows that cooling down}}. [[Rather than]] measure bedrooms, the team applied each city's lowest overnight temperature to a relationship between heat and sleep. An earlier study had [[established]] that relationship using data from nearly 50,000 people wearing [[sleep trackers]]. Kelton Minor of the University of Copenhagen, who led that study, said, "The warmer it gets, the less that people sleep."

verbs.correct: To stop someone from sleeping
verbs.wrong: To stop something from entering
verbs.why: Keep up here means to stop someone from falling asleep, as in keep you up at night. Be careful: keep up more often means to stay at the same pace as someone else.

verbs.correct: To make something happen more slowly
verbs.wrong: To stop a machine from working
verbs.why: Slow down means to make something happen more slowly than usual. Warm night air slows the body's natural cooling down, which makes it harder to fall asleep.

chunks.text: People in parts of southern India and Southeast Asia lose 78 to 91 hours a year to warm nights, [[against]] 36 hours across 253 US cities. Chennai loses more than any other Indian city, 93 hours. The team was [[open about]] one [[weakness]]: the sleep research behind its [[model]] was based mostly on people in higher-[[income]] countries, where [[cooling]] is easier to {{come by}}, so losses in poorer places may be bigger than these [[figures]] [[suggest]].

verbs.correct: To get or obtain something
verbs.wrong: To become known to the public
verbs.why: Come by means to get or obtain something, especially something not always easy to find. In wealthier countries, cooling like air conditioning is much easier to come by.

chunks.text: The effect of warm nights was [[twice as large]] for adults over 65 and three times as large for people on lower-middle incomes. About 35 percent of [[households]] worldwide owned an [[air conditioner]] in 2021, and ownership [[tracks]] income closely. A few lost minutes are easy to {{shrug off}}. Over a year they {{add up}} to a week.

verbs.correct: To treat something as unimportant
verbs.wrong: To raise your shoulders to show doubt
verbs.why: Shrug off means to treat something as unimportant and not think about it again. A few minutes of lost sleep are easy to shrug off, though they matter over time.

verbs.correct: To grow gradually into a larger total
verbs.wrong: To attach an extra part to something
verbs.why: Add up means to grow gradually into a much larger total over time. A few lost minutes each night add up to a whole week of sleep in a year.

stories.headline: Indian students protest after a medical exam leak

sources.title: India opposition leader Gandhi freed after detention at student-led protest

India's 'cockroach' protest continues after police crackdown | BBC News (video, BBC News)

chunks.text: More than 5,000 people [[gathered]] at Jantar Mantar, a protest site in Delhi, on Tuesday, July 22, [[a day after]] [[clashes]] {{broke out}} between police and marchers. The protest is over a national medical [[entrance exam]] whose papers [[leaked]] in May, forcing about two million [[candidates]] to take the test again. Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi and his sister Priyanka Vadra were [[detained]] outside Prime Minister Narendra Modi's [[residence]] and released that evening.

verbs.correct: To start suddenly, as fighting does
verbs.wrong: To stop working completely
verbs.why: Break out means for something sudden and often violent to start, like fighting or a fire. Clashes broke out between police and protesters the day before this large gathering in Delhi.

chunks.text: The protests are organized by the Cockroach Janta Party, which {{grew out of}} an online joke two months ago and has since [[gained]] millions of followers. Led mainly by students, it wants Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan to {{step down}}, the release of Sonam Wangchuk, an [[activist]] on [[hunger strike]] since June 28, and 10 million rupees, about $104,000, for each family of the [[dozen or so]] students who died.

verbs.correct: To develop from something smaller
verbs.wrong: To spend your childhood in a place
verbs.why: Grow out of means to develop naturally from something small or informal into something bigger. This protest movement grew out of a simple online joke just two months ago.

verbs.correct: To leave a position of authority
verbs.wrong: To get involved in order to help
verbs.why: Step down means to leave an important job or position, often under pressure. Protesters are demanding that the education minister step down over the exam leak scandal.

chunks.text: Monday's march toward parliament ended in violence, with police using [[tear gas]] and batons to {{hold back}} the [[crowd]]. Delhi Police said nearly 180 people were hurt, including 118 police and security staff and 60 [[protesters]]. The party's [[founder]], Abhijeet Dipke, said more than 150 protesters were in hospitals. Neither figure has been [[independently]] checked. Modi told [[lawmakers]] that his government acted [[as soon as]] it {{found out}} about the leak, that 13 people had been arrested, and that the re-test {{went ahead}} without problems.

verbs.correct: To stop someone from moving forward

stories.headline: Five cups of coffee a day appears safe for adults

sources.title: Coffee lovers can take heart: Up to 5 cups a day appears safe for most adults, experts say
Coffee: Up to 5 cups a day safe for heart health, AHA says
Coffee and heart health: How many cups of caffeinated coffee are safe to drink each day?
Study: Five cups of coffee per day safe for most adults (video, NPR)

chunks.text: Most healthy adults can drink [[up to]] five cups of coffee a day without raising their risk of heart disease, [[according to]] a scientific statement from the American Heart Association published on July 20 in the journal Circulation. Five 8-ounce cups of black coffee {{add up to}} about 400 milligrams of [[caffeine]], the daily [[figure]] the review {{settled on}}. The number is [[the easy part]].

verbs.correct: To reach a total of a certain amount
verbs.wrong: To increase something by adding more
verbs.why: Add up to means that smaller amounts combine into one final total. Your daily spending, your weekly hours at work, or several small snacks can all add up to a surprising number.

verbs.correct: To decide on something after considering it
verbs.wrong: To become calm and relaxed after a while
verbs.why: Settle on means to finally choose one option after considering others, the way researchers settle on one clear number. It suggests a careful decision, not a rushed guess.

chunks.text: How the coffee is made [[matters]]. Coffee [[brewed]] without a paper [[filter]], including espresso, French press and Turkish-style coffee, contains cafestol, a natural [[compound]] that raises LDL [[cholesterol]], the kind linked to [[clogged]] [[arteries]]. A paper filter {{keeps out}} cafestol, and instant coffee does not contain it, so neither was [[tied to]] higher cholesterol. The caffeine is not [[the issue]]: decaffeinated espresso raised LDL too.

verbs.correct: To stop something from getting into a place
verbs.wrong: To stay within an agreed limit or rule
verbs.why: Keep out means to stop something from entering a place, like a filter keeping cafestol out of your cup. We also use it for keeping cold air, bugs, or noise outside.

chunks.text: Researchers reviewed 28 [[long-term]] studies and linked three and a half to five cups a day with a 20 to 30 percent lower risk of type 2 [[diabetes]]. Almost all of that evidence is [[observational]], meaning it [[tracks]] habits [[rather than]] testing them, so they cannot {{rule out}} that coffee drinkers [[differ]] [[in other ways]]. Caffeine was {{left out}} of the association's 2026 dietary guidance because the evidence was [[not solid enough]]. "What matters most isn't just how much coffee you drink, it is how it's prepared, what you are adding to it, and how your own body responds," said Michelle Routhenstein, a preventive cardiology dietitian.

verbs.correct: To say that something is definitely not possible
verbs.wrong: To give an official judgment on a question
verbs.why: Rule out means to decide that something is definitely not the explanation. Because the coffee studies only observed people, scientists cannot rule out that other habits caused the health difference.

verbs.correct: To not include something in a list or plan
verbs.wrong: To stop doing something for a short time
verbs.why: Leave out means to not include something in a plan or a decision, often on purpose. Something can be left out for lack of proof, for lack of space, or simply by mistake.

chunks.text: Energy drinks and caffeine shots are [[a separate case]], holding three to four times the caffeine by volume and linked to high [[blood pressure]] and irregular heartbeats. Sugar, syrup and cream can {{cancel out}} whatever benefit the coffee brings, and how fast a body {{breaks caffeine down}} [[varies]] with age, medication and genetics. Five cups is a [[ceiling]], not [[a target]].

verbs.correct: To remove the effect of something else
verbs.wrong: To stop an event before it happens
verbs.why: Cancel out means that one thing removes the effect of another, so they balance to nothing. Sugar and cream in your coffee can cancel out any health benefit from the coffee itself.

verbs.correct: To separate a substance into simpler parts
verbs.wrong: To stop working correctly for a while
verbs.why: Break down means to separate something into smaller, simpler parts, especially in chemistry or digestion. Your body slowly breaks down caffeine over several hours, and that speed depends on the person.

mainIdea.s: A major heart health group says adults can safely drink up to five cups of coffee a day. But how the coffee is brewed matters, since unfiltered coffee can raise harmful cholesterol.
mainIdea.why: The American Heart Association's July statement backs up to five cups a day. But it says unfiltered coffee like espresso raises LDL cholesterol, while filtered coffee does not.

mainIdea.s: The review found that drinking coffee actually lowers a person's risk of heart disease and diabetes. It also found that espresso is the safest way to brew coffee for a healthy heart.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the statement says coffee appears safe, not that it lowers heart disease risk. Espresso also raises cholesterol instead of being the safest brewing method.

stories.headline: Britain changes prime minister without an election

sources.title: Andy Burnham becomes U.K. prime minister
Why Britain is getting a new prime minister without a general election
Andy Burnham formally appointed U.K. prime minster (video, NBC News)

chunks.text: Andy Burnham became Britain's prime minister on Monday, July 20, without a single voter casting a [[ballot]]. Keir Starmer {{handed in}} his [[resignation]] to King Charles III at Buckingham Palace, and the king asked Burnham to [[form a government]] soon afterward. Britain has now {{gone through}} seven prime ministers in ten years.

verbs.correct: To give something to a person in authority
verbs.wrong: To give something to each person in a group
verbs.why: You hand in something official to a person with authority, like a resignation, an application, or a report. Starmer handed in his resignation to the king before leaving office.

verbs.correct: To experience one thing after another in a series
verbs.wrong: To continue happening for a long period of time
verbs.why: Go through means to experience a series of things one after another, like jobs, coaches, or in this case, prime ministers. It suggests instability, not just one instance.

chunks.text: Voters in Britain choose members of [[Parliament]], and the leader of the party with a [[majority]] [[takes office]]. If that leader {{steps down}}, the party chooses a [[replacement]], who then moves into [[Downing Street]]. Labour still holds the majority it won in 2024, so the next election is not [[due]] until 2029.

verbs.correct: To leave a position of power
verbs.wrong: To get involved in order to help
verbs.why: When someone steps down, they leave a position of power voluntarily, often under pressure but without being formally removed. We use it for CEOs, coaches, and political leaders alike.

chunks.text: Starmer announced on June 22 that he was quitting as Labour leader. His two years [[in power]] were [[marked by]] [[missteps]], [[most notably]] his choice of [[ambassador]] to the United States, a man with [[close ties]] to [[the late]] sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. After Labour lost seats to a [[populist]] anti-immigration party in May's local elections, more Labour [[lawmakers]] {{turned against}} him. When Burnham won a special election for a seat in Parliament last month, Starmer {{gave in to}} the [[pressure]]. Labour named Burnham leader on Friday, with 379 of its 401 lawmakers [[behind him]].

verbs.correct: To stop supporting someone and begin opposing them
verbs.wrong: To go to someone else for help and support
verbs.why: Turn against describes a real shift in loyalty: people who once supported someone start opposing them instead. Here it was Starmer's own lawmakers, angry after months of mistakes and falling poll numbers.

verbs.correct: To stop resisting and accept something
verbs.wrong: To reveal a secret without meaning to
verbs.why: Give in to means to stop resisting and let something happen, even if you did not want to. Starmer eventually gave in to pressure from his own party to resign.

chunks.text: Burnham was an MP for 16 years and a minister under Tony Blair and Gordon Brown, then {{went on to}} become [[mayor]] of Greater Manchester. Outside Downing Street he promised to be "a [[circuit breaker]] for Britain, {{bringing forward}} the biggest changes in the last 40 years." His first [[instruction]], he said, would be "to end [[rough sleeping]] in our country." He {{takes over}} with no vote of his own behind him. After so much [[turnover]] [[at the top]], voters have heard many promises before.

verbs.correct: To do something after doing something else
verbs.wrong: To explain something in great detail
verbs.why: Go on to shows the next step in someone's career or life, after finishing something else first. Burnham was a minister, then went on to become mayor of Manchester.

verbs.correct: To propose a plan or change for action
verbs.wrong: To force a government out of power
verbs.why: To bring forward a plan or idea means to formally propose it for others to consider. Burnham promised to bring forward major changes soon after starting the job.

verbs.correct: To start doing a job someone else was doing
verbs.wrong: To supervise a project from a distance
verbs.why: Take over means to start doing a job that someone else used to do, especially in leadership. Burnham takes over as prime minister without ever having won a national vote himself.

chunks.text: On July 19, 2026, Spain won the World Cup, beating Argentina 1-0 in the final. After the game, the President of the United States, Donald Trump, walked onto the [[field]] to {{hand over}} the [[trophy]]. He was joined by Gianni Infantino, [[the head of]] FIFA, the group that {{puts on}} the World Cup. Around the world, millions of people {{tuned in}} to watch the winning team [[lift the cup]].

verbs.correct: To give something to someone
verbs.wrong: To shake hands with the winners
verbs.why: Hand over simply means to give something to another person, often in a formal moment. President Trump walked onto the field to hand over the World Cup trophy.

verbs.correct: To organize a big event
verbs.wrong: To compete in a big contest
verbs.why: Put on means to organize and run an event for others to enjoy, like a show, a festival, or a tournament. FIFA is the organization that puts on the World Cup every four years.

verbs.correct: To watch a show on TV
verbs.wrong: To increase the sound of a TV
verbs.why: Tune in means to watch or listen to a broadcast, especially one happening live. Millions of people around the world tuned in to see the final.

chunks.text: Usually, leaders {{step aside}} after the trophy is given, so the winners can enjoy the [[moment]] [[on their own]]. But this time, President Trump {{hung around}} as the Spanish players [[celebrated]]. The team {{carried on}} cheering and dancing, with the president still standing [[close by]]. [[In the end]], Infantino had to {{step in}} and [[gently]] guide him to the side of the [[stage]].

verbs.correct: To leave space for someone else
verbs.wrong: To lead a team off the field
verbs.why: Step aside means to leave the spotlight so someone else can have their moment. Leaders usually step aside once the ceremony begins, letting the winners celebrate alone.

verbs.correct: To stay in one place
verbs.wrong: To dance with the winners
verbs.why: Hang around means to stay somewhere longer than expected, often without a clear reason to. Trump hung around on the field while the Spanish players kept celebrating.

verbs.correct: To continue doing something
verbs.wrong: To lift a teammate up high
verbs.why: Carry on means to continue doing something without stopping, even when there is a distraction nearby. The Spanish team carried on cheering and dancing through the interruption.

verbs.correct: To get involved to help
verbs.wrong: To walk onto the field
verbs.why: Step in means to get involved and take action when something needs fixing right away. Infantino had to step in and guide the president off to the side of the stage.

chunks.text: Not everyone was [[pleased]] to see the president on the field. Earlier, during the [[national anthems]], some fans in the [[crowd]] had {{let out}} loud [[boos]]. It was not the first time he had {{turned up}} at a [[major]] final. A year before, he had done the same thing at another trophy [[ceremony]], and fans quickly {{brought up}} that earlier moment online.

verbs.correct: To make a loud sound
verbs.wrong: To wave a flag in the air
verbs.why: Let out means to release a sound suddenly, like a shout, a laugh, or in this case a wave of disapproval. Fans in the crowd let out loud boos during the national anthem.

verbs.correct: To arrive at a place
verbs.wrong: To win a big match
verbs.why: Turn up means to appear somewhere, often unexpectedly or without much notice. It was not the first time Trump had turned up at a major sports final.

verbs.correct: To mention a topic
verbs.wrong: To question an old memory
verbs.why: Bring up means to mention a topic in conversation, sometimes reminding people of something they had forgotten. Fans quickly brought up his earlier appearance at another trophy ceremony.

chunks.text: In the end, though, the day [[belonged]] to Spain. The players {{held up}} the [[shining]] golden trophy while red and yellow [[flags]] [[waved]] across the [[stadium]]. [[Back home]], thousands of fans {{poured out}} into the [[streets]] to celebrate. For the Spanish team, nothing was going to {{take away from}} their special night, [[no matter]] who else was standing on the stage.

verbs.correct: To raise something up high
verbs.wrong: To carry the cup off the field
verbs.why: Hold up means to lift something high so everyone can see it clearly. The Spanish players held up the golden trophy as flags waved across the stadium.

verbs.correct: To appear in large numbers

verbs.why: Pour out means a crowd appears suddenly, filling a space in huge numbers. Thousands of fans poured out into the streets back home to celebrate.

verbs.correct: To make something seem less good

verbs.why: Take away from means to reduce how good or special something feels, even if it's just a small distraction. Nothing was going to take away from Spain's celebration, no matter who else stood on the stage.

chunks.text: For more than twenty years, Rachid Lazraq has {{looked after}} a small shoe shop called Rich Collection Italia on Hackney Road in East London. The shop sells [[stylish]] Italian shoes, but [[in recent years]] [[business]] had slowly {{dried up}}. Most people had started buying online, and [[fewer and fewer]] [[customers]] [[came through the door]]. Sad and tired, Rachid had almost decided to {{shut down}} the shop [[for good]].

verbs.correct: To protect and help something
verbs.wrong: To sell shoes to customers
verbs.why: Look after means to protect and maintain something over a long time. For more than twenty years, Rachid looked after his small shoe shop in East London.

verbs.correct: To slowly disappear over time
verbs.wrong: To lose money on every sale
verbs.why: Dry up means to slowly disappear or shrink over time until almost nothing is left. His business had slowly dried up as more customers began shopping online instead.

chunks.text: His daughter, who is 25 and works as a [[journalist]], did not want to {{give up}} on the [[family business]]. She had {{found out}} that a French [[influencer]] had shown the shop online, so she {{came up with}} a simple idea. On July 7, she posted a short [[video]] on TikTok about the shop's Y2K [[sandals]], a [[style]] from the early 2000s that is [[popular]] again.

verbs.correct: To stop trying and quit
verbs.wrong: To lose all of your money
verbs.why: Give up means to stop trying and quit on something you care about. His daughter did not want to give up on the family business without a fight.

verbs.why: Find out means to learn a fact you did not know before. She found out that a French influencer had already shown the shop to her followers online.

chunks.text: The video quickly {{took off}}. [[Overnight]], it {{racked up}} 300,000 [[views]], and soon young customers were {{lining up}} outside the shop, sometimes waiting two hours to get inside. [[In just a few days]], the whole business had {{turned around}}. The quiet little shop that was about to close was suddenly [[full of life]].

stories.headline: Spain wins the World Cup

sources.title: Spain is the 2026 World Cup champion, defeating Argentina for its 2nd title
FIFA World Cup 2026 Final: Argentina vs Spain live updates
Spain 1-0 Argentina (Jul 19, 2026) Final Score - ESPN
Spain GAME-WINNING Goal in 2026 FIFA World Cup™ Final 🏆Ferran Torres nets in Extra Time vs Argentina (video, FOX Sports)

chunks.text: On July 19, 2026, Spain {{pulled off}} [[one of the biggest]] wins in their history. At MetLife Stadium near New York, they {{took on}} Argentina in the [[final]] of the World Cup, the biggest event in soccer. After 90 minutes, no one had scored, so the game {{went on}} into [[extra time]]. [[At last]], Spain won 1-0 and {{picked up}} the World Cup [[trophy]] for the second time.

verbs.correct: To succeed at something difficult
verbs.wrong: To score in the final minute
verbs.why: Pull off means to succeed at something difficult, especially when the result was not guaranteed. Spain pulled off a hard fought 1-0 win over Argentina to win the World Cup again.

verbs.correct: To face or compete against
verbs.wrong: To beat a strong rival team
verbs.why: Take on means to compete against an opponent, often one that is strong or well known. Spain took on Argentina in the final, the biggest match in world soccer.

verbs.correct: To continue without stopping
verbs.wrong: To restart after a break
verbs.why: Go on simply means to continue rather than stop or end. Since no one had scored after 90 minutes, the match went on into extra time.

verbs.correct: To lift or collect something
verbs.wrong: To pass the ball to a teammate
verbs.why: Pick up here simply means to lift something up and take hold of it. Spain picked up the World Cup trophy for the second time in their history.

chunks.text: For most of the match, Spain {{kept up}} the [[pressure]] and [[controlled]] the ball. Argentina's [[goalkeeper]], Emi Martinez, was [[superb]] and [[made save after save]]. Then, [[deep into]] extra time, the [[striker]] Ferran Torres {{broke through}}. In the 106th minute, he {{put away}} a shot from [[close range]], and Spain were [[in front]]. Martinez [[set a record]] with 11 [[saves]], but he could not {{keep out}} every shot.

verbs.correct: To keep something at the same level
verbs.wrong: To move the ball up the field fast
verbs.why: Keep up means to maintain something steadily, without letting it drop. For most of the match, Spain kept up the pressure and controlled the ball.

verbs.correct: To force a way past a defense
verbs.wrong: To kick the ball very hard
verbs.why: Break through means to finally get past something that was blocking you, like a strong defense. Deep into extra time, striker Ferran Torres finally broke through against Argentina's defense.

verbs.correct: To score a goal in a game
verbs.wrong: To save a shot on goal
verbs.why: Put away means to score a goal, especially a chance that a player successfully finishes. Torres put away a close range shot in the 106th minute to give Spain the lead.

verbs.correct: To stop something from getting in
verbs.wrong: To kick the ball far away
verbs.why: Keep out means to prevent something from entering, like a shot from going into the goal. Martinez set a save record, but he could not keep out every shot Spain took.

chunks.text: Argentina had [[dreamed of]] winning the World Cup two times [[in a row]]. Their star, Lionel Messi, is now 39, and this was [[almost certainly]] his last World Cup. But on this night, he could not {{take over}} the game the way he once did. Spain's young players never {{let up}}, and their [[defense]] stayed strong. Argentina tried to {{fight back}}, but they could not [[find a way through]].

verbs.correct: To take control of something
verbs.wrong: To argue with the referee
verbs.why: Take over means to take control of a situation, often to change how it is going. Messi could not take over the match the way he once did in past World Cups.

verbs.correct: To become weaker or slower
verbs.wrong: To celebrate too soon
verbs.why: Let up means to become less intense or to relax the effort you are making. Spain's young players never let up, keeping their defense strong until the very end.

verbs.correct: To try hard to recover
verbs.wrong: To leave the field early
verbs.why: Fight back means to make a strong effort to recover when you are losing. Argentina tried to fight back late in the game, but they could not find a way through.

chunks.text: When the final [[whistle]] went, the Spanish players fell to the ground in joy. For many fans, the win {{brought back}} happy memories of 2010, when Spain lifted their first World Cup. Sixteen years later, a new team has {{carried on}} that dream. Now Spanish soccer can {{look forward to}} [[a bright future]], with young stars [[leading the way]].

verbs.correct: To make you remember something
verbs.wrong: To call old players back to play
verbs.why: Bring back means to make someone remember a feeling or event from the past. This win brought back happy memories of Spain's first World Cup title in 2010.

verbs.correct: To keep doing something
verbs.wrong: To carry the cup through town
verbs.why: Carry on means to continue something that started earlier, keeping it going. Sixteen years after Spain's first title, a new generation of players has carried on that same winning tradition.

verbs.wrong: To get ready for the next final
verbs.why: Look forward to means to feel excited about something good that is going to happen soon. With young stars leading the way, Spanish soccer fans can look forward to a bright future.

stories.headline: Scientists find air around a faraway planet

sources.title: Potential Atmosphere Detected on Habitable-Zone Exoplanet LHS 1140b
Astronomers spot first atmosphere around a potentially habitable alien world
Rocky Planet 48 Light-Years Away May Be First in a Habitable Zone With a Confirmed Atmosphere
Atmosphere Confirmed Around Habitable Zone Planet LHS 1140b (video, Anton Petrov)

chunks.text: Scientists have {{picked up}} the first signs of air around a small, rocky planet outside our [[solar system]]. The planet, called LHS 1140 b, sits about 48 [[light-years]] from Earth. It circles its star in the zone where the temperature could be right for water. This is [[a huge deal]], because a planet needs air to {{hold on to}} heat and to give life a chance. But the discovery did not {{end up}} being simple.

verbs.correct: To notice or detect something
verbs.wrong: To collect gas from space
verbs.why: Pick up means to detect a faint signal that might otherwise be missed. Scientists picked up the first signs of air around a small, distant rocky planet.

verbs.correct: To keep something and not lose it
verbs.wrong: To pull heat in from a star
verbs.why: Hold on to means to keep something instead of losing it over time. A planet needs air to hold on to heat, or the surface stays too cold for life.

verbs.correct: To be in a situation in the end
verbs.wrong: To prove an idea was correct
verbs.why: End up describes the final result of something, especially when it is unexpected. The discovery did not end up being simple, since the signal later disappeared completely.

chunks.text: LHS 1140 b is a [[super-Earth]], which means it is rocky like Earth but much bigger. To study it, a team at Harvard University {{set out}} to watch the planet with a powerful [[telescope]] in Chile. In 2024, they {{came across}} [[helium]] [[gas]] escaping from the top of the planet's air. The planet's star {{gives off}} strong [[radiation]], and this slowly {{strips away}} the gas. For the scientists, it was a rare [[privilege]] to [[witness]] this so far from Earth.

verbs.correct: To start trying to do something
verbs.wrong: To aim a telescope at a planet
verbs.why: Set out means to begin a project with a clear goal in mind. A Harvard team set out to watch the planet with a powerful telescope in Chile.

verbs.correct: To find something by chance
verbs.wrong: To calculate the planet's speed
verbs.why: Come across means to find something unexpectedly while you are looking for something else. In 2024, the team came across helium gas escaping from the top of the planet's air.

verbs.correct: To release light, heat, or gas
verbs.wrong: To slowly burn out and die
verbs.why: Give off means to release something, like light, heat, or gas, into the surroundings. The planet's star gives off strong radiation that slowly destroys its atmosphere.

verbs.correct: To slowly remove something
verbs.wrong: To pull something in with gravity
verbs.why: Strip away means to remove something gradually, layer by layer, until little is left. The star's radiation slowly strips away the helium gas from the top of the planet's air.

chunks.text: In a surprising [[twist]], the [[signal]] [[did not last]]. When the team {{went back}} to check the planet in 2025, the helium had completely disappeared. Scientists think the air may [[shift]] and change [[over time]], which is why the signal appeared and then [[vanished]]. [[For now]], the change is a [[mystery]]. The team is not [[certain]] what happened, and more work is needed to {{find out}} what is {{going on}}.

verbs.correct: To return to a place or time
verbs.wrong: To travel back in time
verbs.why: Go back means to return to a place to check on something again. When the team went back to check the planet in 2025, the helium had disappeared.

verbs.correct: To learn something you did not know
verbs.wrong: To solve a problem by thinking
verbs.why: Find out means to learn a fact you did not know before through research. Scientists need more work to find out why the helium signal appeared and then vanished.

verbs.correct: To be taking place right now
verbs.wrong: To continue to the next study
verbs.why: Go on means that something is currently happening, even if the cause is unclear. Right now scientists are not sure what is going on with the planet's disappearing air.

chunks.text: To {{clear up}} the mystery, the team will {{take on}} a bigger study with the James Webb Space Telescope, the most powerful space telescope ever built. Their main goal is to {{track down}} water, which would [[prove]] the air is real. If they {{pull off}} this hard job and [[succeed]], LHS 1140 b could become [[one of the best]] places to look for life. Scientists around the world will follow the results [[closely]].

verbs.correct: To explain or solve something
verbs.wrong: To take a clearer picture
verbs.why: Clear up means to solve a mystery or make a confusing situation clear. To clear up the mystery of the disappearing signal, the team will run a bigger study.

verbs.correct: To begin to handle a task
verbs.wrong: To pay for a space mission
verbs.why: Take on means to accept a difficult or demanding task or project. The team will take on a much bigger study using the James Webb Space Telescope.

verbs.correct: To find something after searching
verbs.wrong: To measure the amount of water
verbs.why: Track down means to search carefully until you finally locate what you need. The team's main goal is to track down water, which would prove the air is real.

verbs.wrong: To barely finish before the deadline
verbs.why: Pull off means to succeed at something that is difficult or unlikely to work. If the scientists pull off this hard job, LHS 1140 b could become a top place to search for life.

mainIdea.s: Scientists picked up signs of air on a distant rocky planet, but the signal vanished when they went back to check. They now plan a bigger study to find out if real air is there.
mainIdea.why: The team found helium escaping from the planet in 2024, but the signal had vanished by 2025. They now plan a bigger study with a powerful telescope to track down water.

mainIdea.s: Scientists have proven that a distant rocky planet holds a stable layer of air that can support life. Their next step, they say, is only to learn more about the planet's size and shape.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the article never says the air was proven or stable. The helium signal disappeared, and the team is not certain what happened.

mainIdea.s: Astronomers announced this year that they found a brand new rocky planet in a far off solar system. Thick clouds and intense heat make this new world a poor place to search for life.
mainIdea.why: This is about a different planet and a different discovery. The real story is about LHS 1140 b and a helium signal that appeared and then vanished.

stories.headline: China says no country should control AI

sources.title: China's Xi Jinping launches new AI alliance: What is it?
Xi offers AI olive branch to the world, calling for 'symphony of global cooperation'
29 Nations Join China-Led World AI Cooperation Organization
Xi Jinping unveils China's global AI vision at Shanghai conference | East Asia Tonight 17 July 2026 (video, CNA)

chunks.text: The world is changing at an [[incredible]] speed because of artificial intelligence, and now China wants countries to work together on it. On July 17, 2026, at a big meeting in Shanghai, President Xi Jinping shared a [[bold]] idea: no single country should control this powerful [[technology]] alone. To {{back up}} his words, China {{set up}} a new international group [[aimed at]] helping poorer nations. Xi warned that the world should not let one country {{take over}} the future of AI.

verbs.correct: To support or prove something
verbs.wrong: To make a copy of computer data
verbs.why: Back up means to support a claim with real action, not just words. China backed up its call for cooperation with an actual program to help developing countries.

verbs.correct: To create or start something
verbs.wrong: To lead a group of countries
verbs.why: Set up means to create something new so it can start working, like a business, a program, or a group of countries. China set up a new international group to help poorer nations with AI.

verbs.correct: To take control of something
verbs.wrong: To earn the most money from AI
verbs.why: Take over means to seize full control of something, often against the wishes of others. Xi warned that no single country should take over the future of artificial intelligence.

chunks.text: Twenty-nine countries have already {{signed up}} to the new group, including Brazil, Indonesia, and South Africa. Its main job is [[governance]], which means making fair rules for how AI is used. [[Right now]], a few rich countries [[lead the way]], and many poorer nations are afraid of being {{left behind}}. China says it wants to {{bring in}} these [[developing countries]] so they can share the [[benefits]] of AI.

verbs.correct: To officially join something
verbs.wrong: To gather for a big meeting
verbs.why: Sign up means to officially put your name on a list and become a member. Twenty-nine countries have already signed up to China's new AI cooperation group.

verbs.correct: To fail to include someone
verbs.wrong: To be ruled by richer nations
verbs.why: Leave behind means to fail to include someone while progress continues without them. Many developing nations worry about being left behind as richer countries dominate the field of AI.

verbs.correct: To include or involve someone
verbs.wrong: To introduce a new law or rule
verbs.why: Bring in means to invite someone to join an activity or a group. China says it wants to bring in developing countries so they finally have a voice in the future of AI.

chunks.text: To show it is serious, China made some big promises. It will {{hand out}} 5,000 [[training places]] so people in poorer countries can {{pick up}} new AI [[skills]]. But this is not [[purely]] about kindness. China is also {{looking out for}} its own [[interests]], because it is in a [[fierce]] [[race]] with the United States, which has {{cut off}} China from some advanced computer [[chips]].

verbs.correct: To give something to many people
verbs.wrong: To give control to another person
verbs.why: Hand out means to give something to a large number of people, usually for free. China promised to hand out 5,000 training places so people in poorer countries can learn new AI skills.

verbs.correct: To learn something informally
verbs.wrong: To teach others a new skill
verbs.why: Pick up means to learn something naturally through practice, without a formal course. The training program lets people in developing countries pick up new AI skills quickly.

verbs.correct: To protect your own interests
verbs.wrong: To copy technology from rivals
verbs.why: Look out for here means to protect your own interests while helping someone else. China is looking out for itself too, since it is racing against the United States over AI chips.

verbs.correct: To block someone from something
verbs.wrong: To interrupt someone who is talking
verbs.why: Cut off means to block someone from access to something they depend on, like money or supplies. The United States has cut off China from certain advanced computer chips needed to build AI.

chunks.text: China is also thinking about the future. It hopes the new group will help {{draw up}} global rules for AI at the [[United Nations]]. Whether [[rival]] powers like the United States will {{join in}} [[remains to be seen]], and some countries may {{hold back}} and wait. But for millions of people in poorer nations, the message is simple: they will finally [[get a chance to]] shape the future of AI, [[instead of]] watching [[from the outside]].

verbs.correct: To prepare or write something
verbs.wrong: To collect votes from members
verbs.why: Draw up means to prepare a plan or document in an official way. China hopes its new group will help draw up global rules for artificial intelligence at the United Nations.

verbs.correct: To join an activity
verbs.wrong: To lead the whole group
verbs.why: Join in means to add yourself to an activity that others have already started. It remains to be seen whether rival powers like the United States will join in this new effort.

verbs.correct: To wait and not act yet
verbs.wrong: To keep information secret
verbs.why: Hold back means to wait before acting, often because you are unsure or cautious. Some countries may hold back from China's new group and watch how things develop first.

stories.headline: New AI blood test could catch cancer early

sources.title: NHS AI blood test could reduce invasive womb cancer checks
Thousands of women could avoid painful cancer exam with new AI blood test
Thousands of women could be spared painful cancer exam by new NHS AI blood test

chunks.text: Scientists in Britain have {{come up with}} a new blood test that can help find cancer. The test uses artificial intelligence, [[a kind of]] smart computer program, to {{pick up}} [[early signs]] of the [[disease]]. Doctors hope it will {{rule out}} cancer in many patients quickly, so they do not need [[painful]] [[exams]]. It could be good news for women who [[worry about]] [[womb]] cancer.

verbs.correct: To think of a new idea or plan
verbs.wrong: To face a difficult problem
verbs.why: Come up with means to think of a new plan or solution, often after real effort. Scientists come up with tests, and teams come up with fresh ideas.

verbs.correct: To notice or detect something
verbs.wrong: To take a blood sample from a patient
verbs.why: Here pick up means to notice or detect something small, the way this test picks up early signs of cancer in a blood sample.

verbs.correct: To decide something is not the cause
verbs.wrong: To place a patient in a higher risk group
verbs.why: When doctors rule out cancer, they decide it is not the cause of the symptoms and can stop worrying about it. This new test helps them do that fast.

chunks.text: The test works [[in a simple way]]. A [[nurse]] takes a small [[sample]] of blood from the patient. Then the computer {{looks over}} about 30 [[chemical]] signs in the blood and {{breaks down}} the results into three groups: low [[risk]], medium risk, and high risk. This helps doctors {{narrow down}} which patients [[truly]] need more tests.

verbs.correct: To examine something carefully
verbs.wrong: To print a copy of the results
verbs.why: Look over means to examine something carefully, checking each detail one by one. Here the computer looks over dozens of chemical signs in a blood sample.

verbs.correct: To separate something into parts
verbs.wrong: To suddenly stop working
verbs.why: Break down means to separate something into smaller parts so it is easier to understand. The computer breaks the results down into three simple risk groups.

verbs.correct: To reduce something to fewer choices
verbs.wrong: To make a test more accurate
verbs.why: Narrow down means to reduce a large group of options to just a few. Doctors use this test to narrow down which patients truly need further exams.

chunks.text: For many patients, this test could {{cut out}} [[the need for]] painful exams. [[Right now]], women with worrying [[symptoms]] often have to {{go through}} an [[uncomfortable]] check at the hospital. The new test is very [[accurate]], and in one large study it [[correctly]] found more than 99 percent of real cancers. It can also {{speed up}} the whole process, so patients do not wait and worry [[for so long]].

verbs.correct: To remove something completely
verbs.wrong: To perform surgery to remove tissue
verbs.why: Cut out means to remove something completely, so it no longer happens at all. This test could cut out the need for many painful hospital exams.

verbs.correct: To experience something difficult
verbs.wrong: To wait a long time for a result
verbs.why: Go through means to experience something difficult, from a hard illness to an uncomfortable medical exam. Many women go through this kind of check to detect cancer early.

verbs.correct: To make something happen faster
verbs.wrong: To repeat a test more often
verbs.why: Speed up means to make a process happen faster than before. This test can speed up diagnosis, so patients do not wait and worry for weeks.

chunks.text: In a large [[trial]], the test was used on more than 16,000 patients in England, and it costs only about 30 pounds. Some British hospitals have already begun to {{roll out}} the test for their patients. [[Over time]], doctors hope it will {{take on}} other kinds of cancer too, [[such as]] lung and stomach cancer. If it keeps working well, this cheap and simple test may {{catch on}} in hospitals [[around the globe]].

verbs.correct: To introduce something new to people
verbs.wrong: To withdraw a service from hospitals
verbs.why: Roll out means to introduce something new to a group of people, usually gradually. Some British hospitals have already begun to roll out this new blood test.

verbs.correct: To begin to handle something
verbs.wrong: To be replaced by a different test
verbs.why: Take on means to begin to handle a new task or responsibility. Doctors hope this test can take on other cancers too, such as lung and stomach cancer.

verbs.correct: To become popular or widely used
verbs.wrong: To be recalled by the manufacturer
verbs.why: Catch on means to become popular and widely used, often faster than people expect. If it keeps working well, this cheap test may catch on in hospitals everywhere.
