stories.headline: New England's forests grow back after 150 years

sources.title: The Spectacular Regrowth of New England's Forests
What went right this week: the good news that matters
The Spectacular Regrowth of New England Forests

chunks.text: New England is a [[region]] in the northeastern United States. Long ago, [[settlers]] {{cleared away}} most of its trees, but today the forests have {{come back}} in an [[amazing]] way. Green [[woodlands]] have slowly {{taken over}} the old, empty [[farmland]]. In Massachusetts, [[one of the most]] [[crowded]] states in the country, about 60 percent of the land is now [[covered with]] trees, and one scientist called it the greatest forest [[recovery]] [[in the history of]] the world.

verbs.correct: To remove things to make an area empty
verbs.wrong: To cut a narrow path through a forest
verbs.why: Clear away means to remove everything from an area until it is empty and open. Early settlers cleared away entire forests to make room for farms and towns.

verbs.correct: To return after being gone
verbs.wrong: To grow taller than before
verbs.why: Come back means to return after being away or gone, whether it is a person, a habit, or nature itself. Forests can come back on their own if people simply leave the land alone.

verbs.correct: To take control of an area and fill it
verbs.wrong: To briefly do a job for someone else
verbs.why: Take over means to gradually spread across a space until it fills it completely. Young trees took over the old fields until forest replaced farmland across the whole region.

chunks.text: The forests were not always so healthy. In the 1800s, settlers {{cut down}} [[huge numbers of]] trees to build farms, homes, and towns. Later, the [[railroads]] burned even more wood for fuel, which quickly {{used up}} much of the forest. By the year 1850, most of the trees in New England were gone, and some areas had been almost [[completely]] {{wiped out}}.

verbs.correct: To cut through a tree so it falls
verbs.wrong: To chop something into small pieces
verbs.why: Cut down means to make a tree fall by cutting through its trunk. Notice the word order: we can say cut down a tree or cut a tree down.

verbs.correct: To use all of something until it is gone
verbs.wrong: To make careful use of something
verbs.why: Use up means to consume all of something so nothing is left. Trains once burned so much wood for fuel that they used up huge stretches of forest.

verbs.correct: To destroy something completely
verbs.wrong: To be cleared and then planted again
verbs.why: Wipe out means to destroy something so completely that almost nothing remains. By 1850, logging and farming had nearly wiped out the forests of New England.

chunks.text: Then something [[surprising]] happened. [[Around]] 1850, many farmers {{gave up}} their rocky New England [[fields]] and {{moved away}} to the west, where the [[soil]] was [[richer]] and easier to farm. With [[no one left]] to work the [[abandoned]] land, young trees {{sprang up}} [[on their own]] and turned the empty fields back into forest.

verbs.correct: To let go of something you own or use
verbs.wrong: To offer your place to someone else
verbs.why: Give up means to stop keeping or working with something you own, like land, a habit, or a plan. Many farmers gave up their rocky New England fields for richer soil out west.

verbs.correct: To leave and go live somewhere else
verbs.wrong: To step back to avoid danger
verbs.why: Move away means to leave a place for good and settle somewhere else. Whole families moved away from New England to farm better land in the west.

verbs.correct: To appear and grow very quickly
verbs.wrong: To be planted in neat rows
verbs.why: Spring up means to appear suddenly and grow fast, almost overnight. Once fields were abandoned, young trees sprang up across New England without anyone planting them.

chunks.text: The new forests [[do more than]] look beautiful. They give homes to [[wildlife]], clean the air, and even {{cool down}} [[nearby]] cities during hot summers. [[Still]], the forests are not completely safe. As towns grow, people sometimes clear the land again to build new houses and roads. Experts say the region must {{look after}} its trees and {{hold on to}} this rare success.

verbs.correct: To make something less hot
verbs.wrong: To become calm after feeling angry
verbs.why: Cool down means to make the temperature of something lower, not to calm your emotions. Trees cool down nearby cities by giving shade and releasing moisture into the air.

verbs.correct: To protect and help something
verbs.wrong: To try to find something you lost
verbs.why: Look after means to protect something and care for it so it stays healthy. Experts say the region must look after its new forests or risk losing them again.

verbs.correct: To keep something and not lose it
verbs.wrong: To plant new trees to replace old ones
verbs.why: Hold on to means to keep something and refuse to lose it, especially something valuable or rare. The article says New England must hold on to this rare forest success.

mainIdea.s: Settlers cut down most of New England's trees, and by 1850 the forests were almost gone. After farmers left and moved west, trees grew back on their own, and forests now cover much of the region.

mainIdea.s: New England officials recently announced a new program to plant more trees in city parks as part of a climate plan. The program will run for five years and will focus on cities, not old farmland.

stories.headline: White House worker bet on Trump's words

sources.title: Officials probe whether White House teleprompter operator profited off Trump's words
Trump suspends teleprompter operator over Kalshi bets allegations, White House says
White House teleprompter operator investigated over alleged Kalshi trades on Trump speeches
White House teleprompter operator being investigated after alleged bets on Trump speeches (video, NBC News)

chunks.text: [[Regulators]] in the United States are {{digging into}} a White House worker who ran the president's [[teleprompter]]. His job was to load the words that President Trump reads during his [[speeches]]. [[Because of this]], the worker could {{find out}} [[exactly]] what the president would say before anyone else. Officials say he used this [[early access]] to [[bet money]], and the bets {{panned out}}, [[earning]] him almost $100,000.

verbs.correct: To search deeply for the facts about a topic
verbs.wrong: To officially punish a person for wrongdoing
verbs.why: Dig into means to search deeply into the facts of a situation, more than a quick check would. Regulators are digging into a White House worker who may have used his job unfairly.

verbs.correct: To learn a fact that you did not know before
verbs.wrong: To solve a hard problem by thinking carefully
verbs.why: Find out means to learn a fact you did not know before, often through some kind of search. Because of his job, the worker could find out the president's exact words before anyone else.

verbs.correct: To have a successful outcome
verbs.wrong: To become known to the public
verbs.why: Pan out means to succeed in the end, the way someone had hoped it would. His bets on the president's exact words panned out, earning him almost $100,000.

chunks.text: The bets were placed on a [[prediction]] website called Kalshi. On the site, users try to [[predict]] which exact words a speaker will use. Because the worker had already {{gone through}} the president's scripts, he could easily {{cash in on}} what he knew. This gave him an [[unfair]] [[advantage]] over other users, who were only [[guessing]].

verbs.correct: To read or examine something carefully in full
verbs.wrong: To photocopy every single page for filing
verbs.why: Go through here means to read or study something carefully from start to finish. Because the worker had gone through the president's scripts, he knew exactly what was coming.

verbs.correct: To use a situation to make money or profit
verbs.wrong: To exchange something like a ticket for money
verbs.why: Cash in on means to use a situation or piece of knowledge to make money from it. The worker cashed in on early access to the president's speeches to place winning bets.

chunks.text: The [[scheme]] did not stay secret [[for long]]. Kalshi's security team {{picked up on}} the [[strange]] [[betting]] pattern and {{handed over}} the case to a government agency, the CFTC. The company also {{closed down}} his account and kept about $90,000 of his [[winnings]].

verbs.correct: To notice something that is not obvious
verbs.wrong: To learn a new skill slowly through practice
verbs.why: Pick up on means to notice something small or unusual that other people might miss. Kalshi's security team picked up on a strange pattern in the worker's bets.

verbs.correct: To give something or someone to another person
verbs.wrong: To photograph the entire case file quickly
verbs.why: Hand over means to give something, often a case or responsibility, to someone else in charge. Kalshi handed the case over to the CFTC, and you can also say handed it over.

verbs.correct: To stop a business or service from operating
verbs.wrong: To briefly pause something and start it again
verbs.why: Close down means to stop a business or account from operating, often suddenly. Kalshi closed down the worker's account and kept most of his winnings.

chunks.text: [[For now]], the worker has been {{put on}} [[unpaid leave]] while the [[investigation]] {{keeps on}} running. Officials want to know whether he [[broke any rules]] by using private information. [[In the end]], the CFTC may make him {{give back}} most of the money he won.

verbs.correct: To place someone into a certain status or condition
verbs.wrong: To give someone an extra job or duty to do
verbs.why: Put on here means to place someone into a certain status, like a type of leave from work. The White House put the teleprompter operator on unpaid leave during the investigation.

verbs.correct: To continue doing something without stopping
verbs.wrong: To start something again after it has stopped
verbs.why: Keep on means to continue doing something without any pause or stop. The investigation into the worker keeps on running while officials try to learn more.

verbs.correct: To return something to the person it belongs to
verbs.wrong: To publicly sign a written apology letter
verbs.why: Give back means to return something, usually money or an object, to the person it belongs to. The CFTC may eventually make the worker give back most of what he won.

stories.headline: Cuba's power grid fails for the third time

sources.title: Cuba's power grid collapses again, triggering third blackout in 10 days
Analysis: Rocked by string of blackouts, Cubans' ability to endure reaches a limit
Cuba plunged into third nationwide blackout in two weeks as power grid collapses
Cuba slowly gets power back after third blackout in 10 days (video, France 24)

chunks.text: Cuba's national power [[grid]] has {{broken down}} [[yet again]]. On Tuesday, the whole island suddenly lost electricity, {{cutting off}} power for around 10 million people. It was the third major [[blackout]] in about two weeks. The Ministry of Energy said the system had completely {{shut down}}, and millions of families were left [[in the dark]] [[in the middle of]] the day.

verbs.wrong: To begin suddenly, like a fire
verbs.correct: To suddenly stop working
verbs.why: Break down means a machine or system suddenly stops working, whether it's a car, a printer, or an entire power grid. Cuba's grid broke down for the third time in two weeks.

verbs.wrong: To keep a place separate so that no one can reach it
verbs.correct: To stop the supply of something, like power or water
verbs.why: Cut off means to stop a supply completely, like power, water, or phone service. The failure cut off electricity for around ten million people at once.

verbs.wrong: To stop someone from entering a place
verbs.correct: To stop working or operating completely
verbs.why: Shut down means the whole system stops operating at once, not just one part of it. The Ministry said the entire grid had shut down that day.

chunks.text: The blackouts [[come from]] two deeper problems. First, the island is {{running out of}} fuel to power its plants, [[partly because of]] new US [[sanctions]] on countries that sell oil to Cuba. Second, many [[power stations]] are very old, built long ago in the 1960s and 1980s. On Tuesday, a single unit in the east of the country failed, and that quickly {{set off}} the wider [[collapse]].

verbs.wrong: To use something too quickly and waste it
verbs.correct: To have almost none of something left
verbs.why: Run out of means you have almost nothing left of something you need. Cuba is running out of the fuel its power plants need to work.

verbs.wrong: To begin a journey to a place
verbs.correct: To cause something to start or happen
verbs.why: Set off means one small event triggers something much bigger, like a spark starting a fire. A single failed unit set off the whole nationwide collapse.

chunks.text: [[Repair crews]] got to work [[right away]]. Engineers slowly {{turned on}} small 'islands' of electricity and then joined them together into a bigger network. Hospitals and food factories were the [[priority]], so workers {{dealt with}} them first. In the capital, Havana, teams began to {{bring back}} power before reaching [[the rest of]] the island.

verbs.wrong: To raise a machine's power to its highest level
verbs.correct: To start a machine or make power flow
verbs.why: Turn on means to start a machine or let electricity flow through it. Engineers turned on small sections of the grid one at a time before connecting them.

verbs.wrong: To decide which building gets power first
verbs.correct: To take action to handle or fix something
verbs.why: Deal with means to take direct action to handle a problem instead of ignoring it. Crews dealt with hospitals and food factories first, since they mattered most.

verbs.wrong: To carry something home with you from a trip
verbs.correct: To make something work or exist again
verbs.why: Bring back means to restore something to how it was, so it works or exists again. Teams worked to bring back power to Havana before the rest of the island.

chunks.text: For [[ordinary]] Cubans, these blackouts make [[daily life]] very hard. Without power, people cannot cook, pump water, or {{log on}} to the internet, and many hospital [[surgeries]] were {{called off}}. Anger is [[growing]] as families {{put up with}} one [[outage]] after another. mainIdea.s: Cuba's power grid failed for the third time in about two weeks, cutting power to about 10 million people. Old power stations and a fuel shortage caused the collapse.
mainIdea.why: This was the third blackout in about two weeks, cutting power for about 10 million people. The cause was a fuel shortage and old power stations, the story says.

mainIdea.s: Cuba's grid failed only because its power stations are old, and crews restored the whole island at once. Officials say fuel has already arrived, ending the crisis.
mainIdea.why: Close, but crews restored power in stages, joining small areas together, not the whole island at once. The article also says fuel is still short, so few people expect a quick end to the crisis.

mainIdea.s: Cuba announced a new plan to build solar stations across the island to cut down on future blackouts. The project will take years and will not fix the current crisis.
mainIdea.why: This is about a future plan for new solar power, not the blackout itself. The real story is about the power grid failing three times in about two weeks.

tf.s: Cuba's national power grid has broken down for the third time in about two weeks.
tf.why: The story says this was the third major blackout in about two weeks after the grid collapsed again.

tf.s: Engineers turned on power to the whole island all at once.
tf.why: Engineers slowly turned on small 'islands' of electricity and then joined them together, rather than powering the whole island at once.

tf.s: Officials called off the repairs and told people to wait a week.
tf.why: Repair crews got to work right away and began to bring back power, so the repairs were not called off.

tf.s: Hospitals and food factories were dealt with first when power came back.
tf.why: They were the priority, so workers dealt with them first before the rest of the island.

tf.s: The blackouts come from a fuel shortage and very old power plants.
tf.why: The story says the crisis comes from a lack of fuel and power stations built back in the 1960s and 1980s.

tf.s: Cubans could still log on to the internet easily during the blackouts.
tf.why: Without power, people cannot log on to the internet, so this is false.

stories.headline: China turns off AI companion chatbots

sources.title: China's new AI crackdown on virtual companions leaves heartbreak behind
Chinese users bid farewell to beloved AI companions
China's AI companion rules: what Beijing is really going after
China says no to AI boyfriends - BBC World Service (video, BBC World Service)

chunks.text: In China, a new [[regulation]] has {{shut down}} [[one of the most]] personal uses of AI. Millions of people had been chatting with [[virtual]] "[[companion]]" apps that could [[act like]] a close friend or even a [[romantic]] partner. Now the government wants technology companies to {{turn off}} these [[features]]. Officials say the apps were [[built to]] {{reel in}} [[lonely]] users and [[keep them coming back]].

verbs.correct: To close or stop something completely
verbs.wrong: To make a rule that limits an activity
verbs.why: Shut down means to close or stop something completely, with nothing left running. A new rule in China shut down a very personal use of AI chatbots.

verbs.correct: To stop a machine or feature from working
verbs.wrong: To lower the volume or strength of something
verbs.why: Turn off means to stop a machine or a feature from working, like flipping a switch. Chinese companies had to turn off the romantic chat features in their apps.

verbs.correct: To attract someone and pull them into something
verbs.wrong: To bring something under control and limit it
verbs.why: Reel in means to attract someone and slowly pull them closer, the way a fisherman reels in a fish. Officials say these apps were built to reel in lonely users.

chunks.text: Several big companies quickly {{gave in}} to the new law. ByteDance, which runs the popular app Doubao, {{took away}} its romantic-companion feature on July 15. Alibaba and Tencent removed similar tools even earlier in the year. The rules also {{keep out}} anyone under 18, so [[minors]] can [[no longer]] form these [[bonds]].

verbs.correct: To finally agree to something you were resisting
verbs.wrong: To stop trying and abandon something completely
verbs.why: Give in means to finally agree to something after resisting it for a while. Several big tech companies gave in to the new law and removed their chatbot features.

verbs.correct: To remove something so it can no longer be used
verbs.wrong: To hide something from view for a short time
verbs.why: Take away means to remove something so people can no longer use it. ByteDance took away its romantic companion feature from the app Doubao in mid July.

verbs.correct: To stop someone from entering or joining
verbs.wrong: To require a signed parental form
verbs.why: Keep out means to stop someone from entering or joining something. The new rules keep out anyone under 18, so minors cannot form these emotional bonds.

chunks.text: For many users, the change was hard to {{deal with}}. Some had {{grown attached to}} their [[chatbots]] over months or even years. One person wrote that their AI companion [[felt like]] family, and that saying goodbye left their heart feeling [[hollow]]. Others {{broke down}} online, sharing long [[farewell]] messages before the apps closed [[for good]].

verbs.correct: To handle or cope with a difficult situation
verbs.wrong: To fully solve a problem so it never returns
verbs.why: Deal with means to handle a difficult situation, not necessarily to solve it fully. For many users, saying goodbye to their chatbot was hard to deal with.

verbs.correct: To develop a strong emotional bond with someone or something
verbs.wrong: To gradually lose all interest in real friendships
verbs.why: Grow attached to means to slowly develop a strong emotional bond with someone or something. Some users had grown attached to their chatbots over months or even years.

verbs.correct: To lose control of your emotions and start crying
verbs.wrong: To stop working suddenly, like a machine or a car
verbs.why: Break down here means to lose control of your emotions and start crying. Be careful: break down is also very common for a car or machine that stops working.

chunks.text: The government says the rules will {{look after}} people's [[mental health]] and stop apps from {{taking advantage of}} [[loneliness]]. Doubao will let users save their chat history until October. [[Still]], many people [[wonder whether]] a machine can ever {{make up for}} real [[human connection]].

verbs.correct: To protect and help someone or something
verbs.wrong: To find information in a book or online
verbs.why: Look after means to protect and support someone or something. Officials say the new rules will look after people's mental health and reduce online harm.

verbs.correct: To unfairly use someone's weakness for gain
verbs.wrong: To make good use of a helpful opportunity
verbs.why: Take advantage of means to unfairly use someone's weakness for your own gain. Regulators worried these apps were taking advantage of people's loneliness to keep them paying.

verbs.correct: To do something good to balance out a loss
verbs.wrong: To copy someone's feelings very closely
verbs.why: Make up for means to do something good that balances an earlier loss or disappointment. Many people wonder whether a chatbot can truly make up for real human connection.

stories.headline: Ancient painted tomb uncovered near Egypt's Luxor

sources.title: Archaeologists uncover 3,000-year-old tomb near Egypt's Luxor
3,000-year-old tomb of ancient Egyptian official Paser discovered in Luxor's Theban Necropolis
3,000-year-old Egyptian tomb with vivid afterlife paintings uncovered near Luxor

chunks.text: Archaeologists in Egypt have {{dug up}} an [[ancient]] [[tomb]] near the city of Luxor. A Dutch team from Leiden University {{teamed up with}} Egypt's [[antiquities]] authority to [[explore]] the west bank of the Nile. The tomb is about 3,000 years old, and it [[belonged to]] an [[official]] named Paser. Experts believe it {{dates back}} to the Ramesside period, a great age of Egyptian [[pharaohs]].

verbs.correct: To bring something out of the ground by digging
verbs.wrong: To search old records in order to find hidden facts
verbs.why: Dig up means to remove something from underground by digging, often something valuable or historic. Archaeologists dig up ancient objects that have been buried for thousands of years.

verbs.correct: To join with someone to work together
verbs.wrong: To reach someone who is ahead of you
verbs.why: Team up with means to join forces with another person or group to work on something together. A university team can team up with a local authority to run a long excavation.

verbs.correct: To have existed since a particular time in the past
verbs.wrong: To be old-fashioned and no longer in style
verbs.why: Date back means something has existed since an earlier period in history. Many objects found at ancient sites date back thousands of years.

chunks.text: What makes the tomb special is that its walls still {{show off}} [[colorful]] painted scenes. Time has not {{worn away}} the bright images, which show Paser worshiping the gods inside sacred [[shrines]]. Another painting shows him seated [[beside]] his wife, in front of a table [[piled with]] [[offerings]]. The art really {{leaps out}} because its colors have [[lasted]] for more than 3,000 years.

verbs.correct: To display something proudly for people to see
verbs.wrong: To behave in a boastful way to get attention
verbs.why: Show off means to display something proudly, often something impressive or beautiful. A newly opened tomb can show off paintings that still look almost fresh.

verbs.correct: To slowly damage or remove something over time
verbs.wrong: To make something look shiny and new again
verbs.why: Wear away means something is slowly damaged and removed over a very long time. Wind, water, and light can wear away paint on old stone walls.

verbs.correct: To be very noticeable and catch the eye at once
verbs.wrong: To appear suddenly from a hidden place
verbs.why: Leap out means something is so striking that you notice it the instant you see it. Bright, well preserved colors on an ancient wall can leap out at any visitor.

chunks.text: The team did not {{come across}} the tomb [[by luck]]. They have worked at this [[site]] since 2018, and this season their [[careful]] [[digging]] finally {{paid off}}. As they {{cleared away}} sand and fallen stone, a [[courtyard]], a rock [[chapel]], and underground [[burial chambers]] slowly appeared.

verbs.correct: To find or meet something by chance
verbs.wrong: To change your opinion and agree
verbs.why: Come across means to find something unexpectedly, without having planned or searched for it specifically. Archaeologists sometimes come across a whole new chamber while digging for something else.

verbs.correct: To bring a good result after a lot of effort
verbs.wrong: To finish repaying money that you owe
verbs.why: Pay off means years of hard work finally bring a good result. Careful, patient digging at a site can pay off with a major discovery.

verbs.correct: To remove things to leave a clean, empty space
verbs.wrong: To add more sand and stone to a structure
verbs.why: Clear away means to remove material, like sand or stone, to reveal what lies underneath. Workers clear away centuries of sand before a hidden room can be seen.

chunks.text: News of the find has [[drawn attention]] [[from around the world]]. Officials hope the painted walls will {{shed light on}} Paser's life and his [[exact]] role in Egyptian society. Researchers still need to {{pore over}} the writing on the walls to learn his full [[titles]]. The discovery is [[a reminder of]] how much history still [[lies buried]] under Luxor's sands.

verbs.correct: To give new information that helps explain something
verbs.wrong: To give final proof that something is definitely true
verbs.why: Shed light on means new information helps explain something that was previously unclear or unknown. Wall paintings can shed light on the daily life of someone who died long ago.

verbs.correct: To read or study something very carefully
verbs.wrong: To photograph a surface in fine detail
verbs.why: Pore over means to study something in careful, close detail, usually written text. Researchers will pore over the wall inscriptions to learn the official's exact titles.

sources.title: House passes bill to make daylight saving time permanent

House passes Trump-backed bill that would make daylight saving time permanent
House passes Sunshine Protection Act to make daylight saving time permanent (video, NBC Connecticut)

chunks.text: The US House of Representatives wants to {{do away with}} the twice-a-year clock changes. On Tuesday, [[lawmakers]] {{voted for}} a [[bill]] called the Sunshine Protection Act by 308 votes to 117. The plan would {{lock in}} [[permanent]] [[daylight saving time]] all across the country. Many [[supporters]] say the change is [[long overdue]].

verbs.correct: To remove something completely
verbs.wrong: To escape punishment for a bad action
verbs.why: Do away with means to end something completely so it no longer happens at all. The House voted to do away with the twice yearly ritual of changing every clock in the country.

verbs.correct: To officially support or choose something in a vote
verbs.wrong: To formally suggest a new law for others to study
verbs.why: Vote for means to officially choose or support something, usually by raising a hand or marking a ballot. Most lawmakers voted for the plan, and only a small group opposed it in the end.

verbs.correct: To make something permanent so it cannot change
verbs.wrong: To close a place with a key so no one can leave
verbs.why: Lock in means to fix something in place so it cannot easily change later. This bill would lock in daylight saving time for good, so clocks would stay the same all year.

chunks.text: So what does 'changing the clocks' [[actually]] mean? In many countries, people turn their clocks forward by one hour in spring and back again in fall. This [[custom]] is called daylight saving time, and it helps people {{make use of}} the extra evening light in summer. The original goal was also to save energy. But twice each year, millions of people must {{get used to}} a new [[schedule]], and [[the switch]] can {{throw off}} their sleep for several days.

verbs.correct: To use something that is available to you
verbs.wrong: To enjoy something in your free time
verbs.why: Make use of means to use something that is available to you instead of ignoring it. Moving the clock forward lets people make use of extra daylight after work each evening.

verbs.correct: To slowly become comfortable with something new
verbs.wrong: To learn how to do something difficult for the first time
verbs.why: Get used to means you slowly stop noticing something new because it feels normal to you now. Every spring and fall, huge numbers of people had to get used to a shifted bedtime and wake time.

verbs.correct: To disturb or upset how something works
verbs.wrong: To make someone feel very tired
verbs.why: Throw off means to disturb a system or a routine so it stops working smoothly. Losing or gaining that one hour can throw off your sleep and leave you tired for almost a week.

chunks.text: Many lawmakers were [[eager to]] {{press ahead}} with the plan, and the vote was [[bipartisan]]. They [[argue]] that lighter evenings could {{cut down on}} car accidents and give families more time outdoors after work. Several doctors add that a [[steady]] clock would be better for people. President Trump has {{come out}} [[in favor of]] the [[measure]] and has promised to sign it into law.

verbs.correct: To continue with a plan in a determined way
verbs.wrong: To hurry to finish something before a deadline
verbs.why: Press ahead means to keep moving forward with a plan even if it is difficult or risky. Supporters in the House were eager to press ahead, even knowing the Senate might resist the idea.

verbs.correct: To reduce the amount or number of something
verbs.wrong: To completely stop doing something
verbs.why: Cut down on means to reduce how much of something you do or use. Supporters believe brighter evenings could cut down on the number of car accidents involving pedestrians.

verbs.correct: To publicly say what you think or support
verbs.wrong: To make a public promise or guarantee
verbs.why: Come out means to publicly state your opinion or support for something. The president has come out strongly in favor of this idea and says he will sign it into law.

chunks.text: The bill now {{moves on}} to the [[Senate]], where its future is [[far from clear]]. Not every lawmaker {{goes along with}} the idea. [[Critics]] [[warn]] that winter mornings would stay dark for much longer, which could be risky for children who walk to school. Others recall that the country tried permanent daylight time back in 1973 but [[gave up on]] it [[within a year]]. For now, Americans must [[wait to see]] whether the Senate will {{take on}} the bill.

verbs.correct: To go forward to the next stage or step
verbs.wrong: To forget about the past and continue with life
verbs.why: Move on means to leave one stage behind and continue to the next one. After passing the House, this kind of bill moves on to the Senate for a separate vote.

verbs.correct: To agree with or accept an idea or plan
verbs.wrong: To pretend to agree while secretly disagreeing
verbs.why: Go along with means to accept someone else's plan or idea, even without much enthusiasm. Some members of Congress refused to go along with the idea, worried about darker winter mornings.

verbs.correct: To accept and start handling a hard task
verbs.wrong: To politely refuse an offer of extra work
verbs.why: Take on means to accept a difficult job or responsibility and begin working on it. It is still unclear whether the Senate will take on this bill anytime soon.

stories.headline: New York pauses giant AI data centers

sources.title: New York to impose the country's first statewide moratorium on data centers
New York becomes first state to impose data center moratorium
First Statewide Moratorium on New Hyperscale Data Centers Launched by Governor Kathy Hochul
New York State pauses new hyperscale data centers for up to a year under Hochul order (video, CNY Central)

chunks.text: New York has become the first American state to {{put off}} the building of giant data centers. On July 14, 2026, Governor Kathy Hochul {{signed off on}} a one-year [[pause]] on new [[permits]] for these huge buildings. The [[facilities]] are [[known as]] hyperscale data centers, and they run the [[servers]] behind AI and cloud computing. State leaders say they want time to study the effects before more of these centers open.

verbs.correct: To delay something until a later time
verbs.wrong: To stop something completely and for good
verbs.why: Put off means to delay something until a later time, often because you need more information first. New York put off new data center permits for a full year to study the risks.

verbs.correct: To officially approve or agree to something
verbs.wrong: To finish a message or piece of work
verbs.why: Sign off on means to give official approval to a plan or a document, usually as the final step. Governor Hochul signed off on the one-year pause in July.

chunks.text: The [[biggest worry]] is that these data centers {{use up}} [[huge amounts of]] electricity and water. The water helps keep the thousands of computers cool, since they run [[day and night]]. Many residents have {{spoken out}} because they [[fear]] the centers will {{drive up}} their [[utility bills]]. Officials are also worried about the extra pressure on the state's [[power grid]].

verbs.correct: To use all of something until none is left
verbs.wrong: To make good use of something you have
verbs.why: Use up means to consume all of something until nothing is left. Giant data centers use up huge amounts of electricity and water to keep their computers running.

verbs.correct: To publicly say what you think against something
verbs.wrong: To talk more loudly so that others can hear
verbs.why: Speak out means to say publicly and clearly what you think, especially when you disagree with something. Many residents spoke out because they feared higher electricity bills.

verbs.correct: To cause something to rise or increase
verbs.wrong: To keep something exactly the same amount
verbs.why: Drive up means to cause a price or a cost to rise. Residents worry that these giant data centers will drive up their monthly utility bills.

chunks.text: During the pause, state agencies will {{look into}} how the centers [[affect]] energy, water, and air quality. Experts will {{press ahead with}} a detailed environmental study before any new rules are made. The state also plans to {{set up}} guidelines so that nearby communities gain real [[benefits]], like better local [[infrastructure]]. The [[moratorium]] only covers the largest projects, those that need 50 [[megawatts]] of power or more.

verbs.correct: To investigate or examine something carefully
verbs.wrong: To find a quick solution to a problem
verbs.why: Look into means to investigate a situation carefully before making a final decision. During this pause, officials will look into the true costs of running these massive facilities.

verbs.correct: To continue something in a determined way
verbs.wrong: To do something quickly and carelessly
verbs.why: Press ahead with means to continue a plan in a determined way, even if it takes time or faces resistance. Experts will press ahead with a full environmental study no matter how long it takes.

verbs.correct: To create or establish something new
verbs.wrong: To prepare and start a machine or device
verbs.why: Set up means to create or establish something new that did not exist before. The state also plans to set up guidelines so nearby communities get real benefits, not just new construction.

chunks.text: Some technology companies have {{pushed back}}, saying the pause could send new investment and jobs to other states. Even so, the [[governor]] [[refuses to]] {{back down}}, and she wants strong rules [[in place]] first. Dozens of cities and counties have already blocked such projects, but no state had {{weighed in}} [[until now]]. If the study [[goes well]], building may {{go ahead}} again next year under [[stricter]] standards.

verbs.correct: To strongly oppose or resist something
verbs.wrong: To move an event to a later date
verbs.why: Push back means to resist or oppose something strongly, often in response to a new rule or plan. Some tech companies pushed back, warning the pause could cost the state jobs.

chunks.text: Every year on July 14, France celebrates Bastille Day, the country's national day. This year, France {{put on}} its yearly military [[parade]] down the famous Champs-Élysées [[avenue]] in Paris. [[Soldiers]], [[tanks]], and planes moved slowly along the wide street while huge [[crowds]] {{turned up}} to watch. The holiday {{looks back}} at [[a key moment]] in French history and gives the whole nation [[a chance to]] feel [[proud]].

verbs.correct: To organize and present a public event or show
verbs.wrong: To suggest a plan for others to think about

verbs.correct: To arrive or come to a place in large numbers
verbs.wrong: To be found by chance after having been lost
verbs.why: Turn up means to arrive somewhere, often in large numbers or without a fixed plan. Huge crowds turned up along the Champs-Elysees to watch the parade this year.

verbs.correct: To think about something that happened in the past
verbs.wrong: To study or examine something in careful detail
verbs.why: Look back means to think about something that happened in the past, often to remember or honor it. This holiday lets the French look back at a key moment in their history.

chunks.text: This year's parade was different from all the others. [[For the first time]], [[troops]] from other European countries {{joined in}} and marched together with the French army. The event was planned to {{stand up for}} Ukraine, which has been fighting a war against Russia for years. Through the parade, these nations wanted to {{show off}} their [[unity]] and [[prove]] to Ukraine that it is [[not alone]].

verbs.correct: To join an activity with other people
verbs.wrong: To officially become a member of the army
verbs.why: Join in means to become part of an activity that other people are already doing together. This year, soldiers from other European countries joined in the French parade for the first time.

verbs.correct: To defend or support someone or something
verbs.wrong: To bravely oppose and confront a powerful enemy
verbs.why: Stand up for means to defend or support someone, especially when they are being attacked or need help. The parade was meant to stand up for Ukraine during its war with Russia.

verbs.correct: To proudly display something you are proud of
verbs.wrong: To pretend to have skills you do not really have
verbs.why: Show off means to display something proudly so other people can see and admire it. The European nations wanted to show off their unity in support of Ukraine.

chunks.text: Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, was invited as a [[guest of honor]] and {{looked on}} from a special [[stand]]. A small group of Ukrainian soldiers {{marched past}} while proudly carrying their national flag. Two Ukrainian [[pilots]], who had trained in France, flew [[fighter jets]] over the crowd. [[In total]], about 6,800 troops {{took part}}, setting [[a new record]].

verbs.correct: To watch something as an observer only
verbs.wrong: To guard and keep someone safe by watching them
verbs.why: Look on means to watch an event happen without doing anything yourself, simply as an observer. Zelenskyy looked on from a special stand while the parade passed in front of him.

verbs.correct: To walk past a place in a formal group

verbs.why: Take part means to be involved in an event alongside other people, rather than just watching it. About 6,800 troops took part in this year's parade, the largest number ever.

chunks.text: For President Emmanuel Macron, this was a special day. It was his last Bastille Day parade before he {{steps down}} as president next year. Around 30 world leaders {{showed up}} to [[stand beside]] him. A heat wave was so strong that many towns had to {{call off}} their [[fireworks]], but the [[mood]] in Paris stayed proud and strong.

verbs.correct: To leave an important job or position
verbs.wrong: To get involved in order to help
verbs.why: Step down means to leave an important job or position, usually by choice rather than force. Macron will step down as president next year after his final term ends.

chunks.text: Scientists have {{come up with}} a new medicine that may bring [[relief]] to people with [[late-stage]] dementia. The medicine [[carefully]] mixes two [[compounds]] from the cannabis plant, known as THC and CBD. Doctors tested it on patients who often [[deal with]] [[agitation]], a state of restlessness and [[distress]]. In early results that just {{came out}}, the treatment {{calmed down}} many patients.

verbs.correct: To invent or create something new
verbs.wrong: To discover something by accident
verbs.why: Come up with means to invent a new idea or solution, often after a lot of effort. Researchers come up with new treatments by testing many combinations of medicine.

verbs.correct: To become known or be made public
verbs.wrong: To make progress and improve
verbs.why: Come out means information becomes public, often after research or a long wait. Early results from a medical trial usually come out months after the study begins.

verbs.correct: To make someone become less upset or less restless
verbs.wrong: To completely cure a person's long-term illness
verbs.why: Calm down means to make a person feel less upset, less anxious, or less restless. A gentle voice or the right medicine can calm down someone who is nervous or afraid.

chunks.text: The researchers {{went about}} the LiBBY [[trial]] [[with great care]], testing about 120 people whose dementia was very [[advanced]]. Their [[average]] age was 80, and most were [[eligible]] for [[hospice]] care. Nurses {{handed out}} the medicine as a [[fast-acting]] oil that patients could swallow. For 12 weeks, the team {{kept track of}} how each person's behavior and mood changed.

verbs.correct: To begin or handle a task in a particular way
verbs.wrong: To travel or move around from place to place
verbs.why: Go about describes the method you use to handle a task, especially a careful or organized one. The team went about the trial with strict rules for every patient.

verbs.correct: To give something to each person in a group
verbs.wrong: To give people advice or instructions
verbs.why: Hand out means to give the same thing to each person in a group, one by one. Nurses hand out medicine to patients according to a strict daily schedule.

verbs.correct: To watch or follow something carefully over time
verbs.wrong: To move at the same speed as everyone else
verbs.why: Keep track of means to follow information carefully over time so you always know the current situation. Doctors keep track of a patient's symptoms throughout a long treatment.

chunks.text: The results {{turned out}} to be very strong. Close to 90 percent of the patients on the medicine got better, while [[far fewer]] improved on a [[placebo]]. That large [[gap]] made the study {{jump out}} at other researchers. One lead doctor said it is [[rare]] to see so many patients respond so well to a new drug.

verbs.correct: To happen or end in a particular way
verbs.wrong: To produce or make something in large amounts
verbs.why: Turn out means an event ends in a certain way, which can surprise you if you expected something different. A new treatment can turn out far more effective than doctors hoped.

verbs.correct: To be immediately noticeable or obvious
verbs.wrong: To physically leap through the air fast
verbs.why: Jump out means something is so clear or unusual that you notice it right away. A huge difference between two groups in a study will jump out to any researcher.

chunks.text: Still, the researchers {{spell out}} that this is a controlled medical treatment, not the same as recreational cannabis products sold in stores. The medicine was made in a lab and given under close [[supervision]]. [[Side effects]] were [[mild]], and doctors could not {{rule out}} that some were caused by the illness itself. As they {{look ahead}}, the team hopes larger trials will [[confirm]] these [[hopeful]] results.

verbs.correct: To explain something clearly and in detail
verbs.wrong: To sum up a result in a few words
verbs.why: Spell out means to explain something in clear, simple detail so there is no confusion. Researchers spell out exactly what a new treatment can and cannot do.

verbs.correct: To decide that something is not possible
verbs.wrong: To fully explain the reason for something
verbs.why: Rule out means to decide, usually after checking carefully, that something cannot be the explanation. Doctors could not rule out that the illness itself caused some symptoms.

stories.headline: US senator Lindsey Graham dies at 71

sources.title: Sen. Lindsey Graham of South Carolina, Trump ally and foreign policy hawk, dies at 71
Senator Lindsey Graham dies at 71 after 'brief and sudden illness'
Lindsey Graham died of aortic dissection, preliminary medical report says
Sen. Lindsey Graham dies at 71 from aortic dissection, examiners say (video, CBS Chicago)

chunks.text: The United States has lost one of its most [[familiar]] politicians. Lindsey Graham, a [[Republican]] [[senator]] from South Carolina, {{passed away}} on Saturday evening at the age of 71. In the days before, he had {{come down with}} a [[sudden]] illness, and his health {{went downhill}} very quickly. His family shared the news late that night and asked people to [[respect]] their [[privacy]].

verbs.correct: To die, in a gentle and polite way of saying it
verbs.wrong: To suddenly lose consciousness for a short time
verbs.why: Pass away is the gentle way to say someone died, often used out of respect for the family. News reports said the senator passed away on Saturday evening.

verbs.correct: To suddenly begin to feel sick or unwell
verbs.wrong: To slowly develop a serious, long-lasting disease
verbs.why: Come down with means an illness starts suddenly, usually something short like a cold or a fever. Here, he came down with a serious illness, one far more dangerous than doctors first realized.

verbs.correct: To get worse in health or condition over time
verbs.wrong: To become weak from a lack of food or rest
verbs.why: Go downhill means a situation, especially health, keeps getting worse instead of improving. Once he fell ill, his condition went downhill within just a couple of days.

chunks.text: [[At first]], doctors were not sure what had happened. Later, a [[medical examiner]] pointed to a problem called an aortic dissection, which is a serious [[tear]] in the body's main [[blood vessel]]. This kind of illness can {{come on}} very fast and give almost no [[warning]]. Only two days earlier, Graham had {{flown back}} from a trip to Ukraine, where he had met the country's leader.

verbs.correct: To begin, especially an illness or a feeling
verbs.wrong: To start suddenly, like a light or machine
verbs.why: Come on describes how a feeling or illness starts, often quickly and without much warning. A sudden pain can come on in minutes, giving almost no time to prepare.

verbs.correct: To return to a place by plane
verbs.wrong: To pass above a place in the air
verbs.why: Fly back simply means to return home or to your starting point on a plane. He had flown back from a trip to Ukraine only two days before he died.

chunks.text: Graham had {{taken up}} politics many years earlier and had {{stayed on}} in public office [[ever since]]. He was first {{voted in}} to the [[Senate]] in 2002. Around the world, he was [[known for]] his strong views on war, peace, and [[foreign affairs]].

verbs.correct: To begin doing a job, hobby, or activity
verbs.wrong: To accept an offer or invitation from someone
verbs.why: Take up means to begin something new, whether it's a hobby, a cause, or in his case a whole career. He took up politics decades ago and never really left it.

verbs.correct: To remain in a job or position
verbs.wrong: To keep a light or device powered
verbs.why: Stay on means to remain in a role instead of leaving it, often longer than people expect. Graham stayed on in the Senate for more than two decades.

verbs.correct: To choose someone for a position by voting
verbs.wrong: To decide something as a group by holding a vote
verbs.why: Vote in means citizens choose someone for office through an election. Voters first voted him in to the Senate back in 2002.

chunks.text: When the Senate returned to work, its members {{came together}} to mark his passing with [[a moment of silence]]. For that day, [[lawmakers]] {{set aside}} their [[usual]] differences. Many [[rose]] to {{look back}} on his long [[career]] and to [[honor]] his [[years of service]].

verbs.correct: To join or gather as one group
verbs.wrong: To slowly form into a finished result
verbs.why: Come together means people gather as one group, often to face something difficult together. When the news broke, the Senate came together for a moment of silence.

verbs.correct: To decide not to let something affect you
verbs.wrong: To throw something away because it is useless
verbs.why: Set aside means to put a disagreement away for the moment so it does not matter right now. For one day, lawmakers set aside their usual political differences.

verbs.wrong: To feel deep respect and admiration for someone
verbs.why: Look back means to think about the past, often to remember or honor someone. Colleagues took time to look back on his long career in the Senate.

stories.headline: Exercise reshapes the nerves that run the heart

sources.title: Exercise doesn't just strengthen the heart. It rewires it
Regular Exercise Doesn't Just Strengthen the Heart, It Reprograms Its Nerves
Regular exercise may reprogram the nerves that control how the heart beats
Exercise Rewires the Heart's Nerve Network Beyond Strengthening It: Study (video, Medical Dialogues)

chunks.text: Scientists in the United Kingdom have {{come across}} something [[surprising]] about exercise. A team at the University of Bristol {{found out}} that regular [[aerobic]] exercise does more than make the heart muscle stronger. It also reshapes the [[tiny]] [[nerves]] that {{take care of}} the heart's [[rhythm]]. The [[discovery]] could [[lead to]] better care for people with dangerous heartbeat problems.

verbs.correct: To find or discover something by chance
verbs.wrong: To search hard for something over a long time
verbs.why: Come across means to find something by accident, not because you were searching for it. This team came across a surprising fact about how exercise affects the heart's nerves.

verbs.correct: To learn something after study or investigation
verbs.wrong: To share news with the public for the first time
verbs.why: Find out means to learn a fact through careful study rather than by guessing. The Bristol team found out that exercise reshapes the heart's nerves, not only its muscle.

verbs.correct: To be responsible for something and control it
verbs.wrong: To develop brand new cells to replace old ones
verbs.why: Take care of means to be responsible for something and keep it working properly. These nerves take care of the heart's rhythm, keeping each beat steady.

chunks.text: To find these changes, the team {{set up}} a study on rats. The animals {{worked out}} on a regular plan for ten weeks, [[a bit like]] a person going to the gym. Using powerful 3D [[imaging]], the scientists could {{zoom in}} on small clusters of nerve cells near the heart. These cells [[act like]] a [[dimmer switch]] that turns the heartbeat up or down.

verbs.correct: To start or organize something new
verbs.wrong: To trick someone into taking the blame
verbs.why: Set up means to organize something new so it is ready to run. The scientists set up a ten week exercise study using rats.

verbs.correct: To do physical exercise to get fit
verbs.wrong: To follow a special diet to lose weight
verbs.why: Work out means to exercise your body to get fit and stronger. In this study the rats worked out on a regular plan for ten weeks, much like a person at the gym.

verbs.correct: To focus closely on one small area to study it
verbs.wrong: To take a photograph from a long distance away
verbs.why: Zoom in means to focus closely on one small detail instead of the whole picture. Powerful imaging let scientists zoom in on tiny clusters of nerve cells near the heart.

chunks.text: The results {{turned out}} to be very [[unusual]]. On the right side of the heart, the trained rats {{wound up with}} about four times more [[neurons]], the special cells that carry nerve [[signals]]. On the left side, the number of cells [[stayed the same]], but each one nearly [[doubled]] in size. Exercise did not shape the two sides in the same way, and that difference intrigued the scientists.

verbs.correct: To happen or be shown to be true in the end
verbs.wrong: To go exactly as the scientists had predicted
verbs.why: Turn out means the final result of something becomes clear, sometimes differently from what you expected. The results turned out to be very unusual, since the two sides of the heart changed in different ways.

verbs.correct: To finally have something as a result
verbs.wrong: To slowly relax after a busy time
verbs.why: Wind up with means to finally have something as a result, often without planning for it. The trained rats wound up with about four times more nerve cells on one side of the heart.

chunks.text: The team hopes these [[findings]] will {{open up}} new ways to [[treat]] heart problems. Doctors already work on these nerves to calm a racing heart, and knowing which side to focus on could make the treatment [[far better]]. This could help people with [[arrhythmias]], chest pain, and other conditions. [[For now]] the work is [[at an early stage]], so scientists must {{follow up}} with studies in humans before any [[therapy]] is ready.

verbs.correct: To create new chances or possibilities
verbs.wrong: To make an existing treatment work faster
verbs.why: Open up means to create new possibilities that did not exist before. These findings could open up better treatments for people with dangerous heartbeat problems.

verbs.correct: To take further action to continue something
verbs.wrong: To repeat the exact same test with no changes
verbs.why: Follow up means to take a further step after the first stage of work is done. Scientists must follow up with studies in humans before any therapy is ready.

mainIdea.s: Researchers found that exercise increased nerve cells equally on both sides of a rat's heart after ten weeks. The team says the discovery already gives doctors a finished treatment for arrhythmias.

stories.headline: Healthy habits keep older minds sharp

sources.title: Lifestyle Program Improves Brain Health in Latin America
From the Alzheimer's Association International Conference 2026: Lifestyle Program Improves Brain Health Among Older Adults at Risk for Dementia Across Latin America
A Two-Year Lifestyle Program Helped Older Adults Sharpen Their Memory
LatAm FINGERS: a multi-domain intervention to prevent cognitive impairment in Latin America (video, VJDementia)

chunks.text: Doctors have long wondered how people can keep their minds [[sharp]] as they grow older. Now, a large study across Latin America has {{set out}} to answer that question. Scientists {{teamed up}} with older adults in 11 countries and {{rolled out}} a two year program to protect memory and slow mental [[decline]]. The results were shared at a major [[dementia]] conference in July 2026.

verbs.correct: To start a task with a clear goal
verbs.wrong: To describe a plan clearly in writing
verbs.why: Set out means to begin working toward a clear goal, like solving a puzzle. Researchers set out to learn how older adults could keep their memory sharp for longer.

verbs.correct: To join with others to work together
verbs.wrong: To split the work fairly among a group
verbs.why: Team up means to join with other people so you can work on something together. For this project, researchers teamed up with everyday people over 60, spread across eleven different countries.

verbs.correct: To introduce a new plan or program
verbs.wrong: To explain every part of a plan in detail
verbs.why: Roll out means to introduce a new plan or program, usually in careful stages. The scientists rolled out a two year plan built around exercise, diet, and brain games.

chunks.text: More than 1,000 adults, aged 60 to 77, {{signed up}} for the study. Half of them followed a [[strict]] plan with [[supervised]] exercise four times a week, healthy [[nutrition]] [[based on]] local foods, computer games for the brain, and [[regular]] [[cardiovascular]] checks. To make it fun, the team added popular dances like salsa and tango. The people in this group had to {{stick to}} the plan and {{keep up}} their new [[habits]] for two whole years.

verbs.correct: To join a program or activity
verbs.wrong: To write your name when you arrive
verbs.why: Sign up means to officially join a program, a class, or an activity. Over a thousand adults between 60 and 77 signed up, knowing they would need to commit for two full years.

verbs.correct: To continue doing something and not quit
verbs.wrong: To talk about only one subject and nothing else
verbs.why: Stick to means to keep following a plan without quitting, even when it gets hard. People in the strict group had to stick to their new routine, even on days when it felt hard.

verbs.correct: To continue doing something at the same level
verbs.wrong: To move as fast as the people around you
verbs.why: Keep up means to continue doing something at the same steady level, without letting it fade. You can say keep up your habits or keep your habits up, both mean the same thing.

chunks.text: The other half {{took part}} in a lighter version. They got only general health [[advice]] at four short meetings and had to manage mostly [[on their own]]. After two years, the difference was clear. The [[structured]] group improved their [[cognition]] about 55 percent more than the flexible group, and those who worked alone often {{fell behind}} on tests of memory. Many of them {{ended up}} with smaller [[gains]] in thinking.

verbs.correct: To be one of the people doing an activity
verbs.wrong: To play a specific role in a performance
verbs.why: Take part means to be one of the people involved in an activity or event. The second group only took part in a much simpler version of the program, with far less guidance.

stories.headline: Giant telescope in Chile turns for the first time

sources.title: Extremely Large Telescope reaches a major milestone | Space photo of the day for July 13, 2026
And yet it moves!
Rotating the Extremely Large Telescope
Rotating the Extremely Large Telescope (video, European Southern Observatory (ESO))

chunks.text: Engineers in Chile's Atacama Desert have {{pulled off}} something [[amazing]]. At the construction site of the Extremely Large Telescope, or ELT, they turned the giant [[telescope]] [[structure]] around its [[axis]] for the very first time. To get it moving, a small team first pushed the machine [[by hand]], just centimeters [[at a time]], while others {{looked on}}. After that, powerful [[motors]] {{took over}} and completed a full turn.

verbs.wrong: To work together well as one team
verbs.correct: To succeed in doing something difficult
verbs.why: Pull off means to succeed at something difficult, often when success seemed uncertain. Engineers pulled off a delicate operation that took years of careful planning.

verbs.wrong: To supervise something in order to keep it safe
verbs.correct: To watch something as an observer only
verbs.why: Look on means to watch something happen without getting involved yourself. A small crowd looked on as workers carefully guided the massive structure into place.

verbs.wrong: To make a loud humming noise all day
verbs.correct: To take control of something from someone else
verbs.why: Take over means to take control of a task from another person or machine. Once workers pushed the structure a little, powerful motors took over the job.

chunks.text: The ELT is a huge machine, but it moves in a very gentle way. The whole structure is {{held up}} by a [[layer]] of oil only 80 microns thin, which lets it [[slide]] almost without any [[effort]]. When it is done, the telescope's main mirror will be {{made up of}} 798 [[segments]] of special glass. Together, they will {{carry out}} the work of one giant mirror, 39 meters [[wide]].

verbs.wrong: To delay something or make it late
verbs.correct: To support the weight of something
verbs.why: Hold up means to support the weight of something so it does not fall or sink. A surprisingly thin layer of oil can hold up a structure weighing thousands of tons.

verbs.wrong: To be cleaned very carefully before use
verbs.correct: To form the whole of something from smaller parts
verbs.why: Made up of means something is built from many smaller parts that together form one whole thing. The telescope's giant mirror will be made up of hundreds of separate glass pieces.

verbs.wrong: To continue without stopping
verbs.correct: To do or perform a task
verbs.why: Carry out means to actually perform a task, often one that is planned or technical. Hundreds of small mirror pieces will carry out the work of one giant mirror.

chunks.text: The numbers behind the project are [[hard to imagine]]. [[Right now]], the metal parts {{add up to}} about 3,500 metric tons. That weight will {{go up}} to more than 4,600 metric tons [[once]] the mirrors and science [[instruments]] are [[in place]]. Because the whole thing can turn, the telescope will be able to point at any area of the sky and study [[faraway]] [[galaxies]].

verbs.wrong: To seem sensible or make sense
verbs.correct: To reach a certain total when combined
verbs.why: Add up to means several smaller amounts combine to reach one total. All the metal parts of the telescope already add up to thousands of tons.

verbs.wrong: To rise above and pass a fixed limit
verbs.correct: To rise or become higher in amount
verbs.why: Go up means an amount increases or becomes higher than before. The total weight will go up even more once the mirrors are installed.

chunks.text: This test was an important [[milestone]] [[on the road to]] finishing the ELT. Builders [[expect to]] {{wrap up}} the work around 2028. When it opens, the telescope's [[enormous]] mirror will make it {{stand out}} as the largest optical telescope in the world. Many [[astronomers]] already {{look forward to}} the first clear images it will [[capture]].

stories.headline: Speaking more languages may keep the brain younger

sources.title: Speaking multiple languages may slow brain aging by years, study finds
Multilingualism Subtracts Up to 13 Years from Brain Age
Speaking another language could slow aging in the brain
Study shows learning another language appears to slow brain aging (video, CBS Chicago)

chunks.text: Scientists have {{come up with}} [[a new way to]] measure how quickly the human brain grows older. At a large science [[conference]] in Europe, a research team from the Basque region of Spain {{pointed out}} that people who speak several languages often have younger brains than their [[chronological]] age would suggest. The team {{set out}} to test [[whether]] knowing more than one language can [[slow]] this kind of [[aging]]. Their [[early results]] suggest that it can.

verbs.correct: To think of or create a new idea or method
verbs.wrong: To face a problem you did not expect
verbs.why: Come up with means to think of a new idea, method, or plan through creativity or research. Scientists came up with a new way to measure how quickly a person's brain is aging.

verbs.correct: To tell people a fact they may not have noticed
verbs.wrong: To prove that something is completely true
verbs.why: Point out means to mention a fact clearly so that other people notice it too. Researchers pointed out that people who speak several languages often have younger looking brains.

verbs.correct: To begin doing something with a clear goal in mind
verbs.wrong: To hope strongly for a particular result
verbs.why: Set out means to begin a project or a journey with a clear goal already in mind. The research team set out to test whether speaking more languages could slow brain aging.

chunks.text: The researchers used [[a form of]] artificial intelligence to {{work out}} each person's 'brain age' from [[patterns]] of brain [[connectivity]]. They looked at 144 people in the Basque region who spoke between one and four languages, such as Spanish, Basque, French, and English. As the number of languages grew, the brains [[appeared]] younger and younger. People who spoke two languages had brains that seemed about six years younger, while those who spoke four {{ended up}} with brains that looked around thirteen years younger.

verbs.correct: To calculate or figure something out
verbs.wrong: To guess an answer without any real evidence
verbs.why: Work out here means to calculate an answer, not to exercise at the gym. Researchers used artificial intelligence to work out each person's brain age from patterns of brain connectivity.

verbs.correct: To finally reach a certain result or state
verbs.wrong: To improve step by step over many years
verbs.why: End up means to finally arrive at a result, often one you did not fully expect. People who spoke four languages ended up with brains that looked around thirteen years younger.

chunks.text: The scientists say the number of languages is not the only thing that {{stands out}}. People who {{picked up}} a second language early in life, and who reached [[a high level of]] [[proficiency]], seemed to {{hold on to}} the benefit more strongly. Being truly [[fluent]] appeared to matter [[just as much as]] speaking many languages. Constantly [[switching between]] languages may give the brain a kind of daily workout that keeps it healthy.

verbs.correct: To be clearly noticed as important
verbs.wrong: To be the main cause of a result
verbs.why: Stand out means to be clearly noticeable compared to everything else around it. The number of languages a person speaks is not the only factor that stands out in this research.

verbs.correct: To learn a skill or language informally
verbs.wrong: To formally study a subject in a class
verbs.why: Pick up means to learn something naturally through practice, not through formal study. People who picked up a second language early in life kept more of the brain benefit.

verbs.correct: To keep something and not lose or give it up
verbs.wrong: To gain even more of something over time
verbs.why: Hold on to means to keep something you already have instead of losing it over time. Early, fluent speakers seemed to hold on to the brain benefit more strongly than others.

chunks.text: These [[findings]] match a much larger project that {{looked into}} the health of 86,149 older people across 27 European countries. In that [[survey]], people who spoke several languages were about [[half as likely]] to show fast, unhealthy aging. Experts say the two studies {{back up}} a simple message: it is [[never too late]] to start. Adults who {{take up}} a new language may slow some of the mental [[decline]] that often [[comes with age]].

verbs.correct: To examine or investigate something carefully
verbs.wrong: To protect and be responsible for something
verbs.why: Look into means to investigate a subject carefully, usually by collecting real data. A separate large project looked into the health of more than 86,000 older adults across Europe.

verbs.correct: To support something and show that it is true
verbs.wrong: To give a short summary of the main points
verbs.why: Back up means to support a claim with evidence that proves it is likely true. Experts say the two studies back up a simple message: it is never too late to start.

verbs.correct: To start doing a new activity, hobby, or study
verbs.wrong: To fill or use a large amount of time or space
verbs.why: Take up means to start a new activity or hobby that you did not do before. Adults who take up a new language later in life may still slow some mental decline.

chunks.text: A [[growing number of]] governments are trying to {{clamp down}} on children's use of social media. The trend {{kicked off}} in Australia, which {{rolled out}} a [[ban]] on the apps for anyone under 16. Now the European Union is thinking about a similar [[policy]] for the young people in its [[member countries]]. Leaders say the plan is [[meant to]] protect [[minors]] from [[harm]].

verbs.correct: To take strong action to stop or control something
verbs.wrong: To punish people who have already broken an existing rule
verbs.why: Clamp down means to take firm, official action to control or stop a problem. More governments are trying to clamp down on how children use social media apps.

verbs.correct: To start or begin an event or activity
verbs.wrong: To become popular very quickly
verbs.why: Kick off means to start something, often in a noticeable or public way. This trend of limiting children's social media use kicked off in Australia, with a ban for anyone under 16.

verbs.correct: To officially start or introduce something new
verbs.wrong: To slowly cancel a rule that is no longer needed
verbs.why: Roll out means to officially introduce a new rule or product to the public. Australia rolled out a ban on social media apps for anyone under 16 years old.

chunks.text: Under the new idea, children under 13 would not be able to {{sign up}} for social media at all. After that age, teenagers would [[gradually]] be allowed to join, but only [[once]] the [[platforms]] {{carry out}} stronger safety checks. Ursula von der Leyen, who {{heads up}} the European Commission, said the plan is not about stopping children from using the apps. She said it is really about deciding when the apps can [[reach into]] children's lives.

verbs.correct: To join or register for a service or activity
verbs.wrong: To formally agree to follow a set of rules
verbs.why: Sign up means to register as a member of a service or platform. Under the new plan, children under 13 could not sign up for social media at all.

verbs.correct: To do or perform a task, often one that was planned
verbs.wrong: To keep doing an activity in the same way as before
verbs.why: Carry out is a formal way to say do something, especially a plan or a check. Platforms must carry out stronger safety checks before older teenagers are allowed to join.

verbs.correct: To be the leader of a group or organization
verbs.wrong: To speak for a group as its main voice
verbs.why: Head up means to be the leader in charge of an organization or a team. Ursula von der Leyen heads up the European Commission, which is behind this proposal.

chunks.text: People who support the rules [[point to]] studies that connect [[heavy]] app use with worse [[mental health]] [[among]] teenagers. They [[argue]] that the apps are built to {{draw in}} young users and keep them scrolling for hours. To deal with this, the EU may make companies {{turn off}} features like [[autoplay]] and [[endless]] scrolling. Many parents also worry about the anxiety and lost sleep that come with [[constant]] use.

verbs.correct: To attract someone and get their interest
verbs.wrong: To trap someone so that they cannot escape
verbs.why: Draw in means to attract people and pull their attention toward something. Critics argue that social media apps are built to draw in young users and keep them scrolling.

verbs.correct: To stop a machine or feature from working
verbs.wrong: To remove something completely and permanently
verbs.why: Turn off means to switch a feature or function so that it stops working. The EU may make companies turn off features like autoplay and endless scrolling for young users.

chunks.text: Not everyone {{goes along with}} the plans. Some experts warn that [[strict]] [[age checks]] could put everyone's [[privacy]] [[at risk]], [[since]] websites would need to gather more personal information. Others say a ban might {{shut out}} young people from useful advice, support groups, and online friends. The EU [[is expected to]] {{put forward}} a formal [[proposal]] after the summer break, and countries around the world are watching to see [[what happens next]].

verbs.why: Go along with means to accept and support a plan, even without much enthusiasm. Not everyone goes along with the EU's plan, since some worry it could hurt privacy.

verbs.why: Shut out means to block someone from having access to something they need. A ban might shut out young people from useful advice, support groups, and online friends.

chunks.text: The Detroit Zoo is celebrating a very special [[new arrival]]. Late in the evening on July 12, 2026, a baby girl gorilla was born to a [[first-time]] mother named Tulivu. This tiny [[infant]] is only the second gorilla to be born at the zoo in its nearly 100-year history. Staff members were [[thrilled]] when the healthy baby {{turned up}}, and they quickly {{gathered around}} to watch mother and baby together.

verbs.correct: To appear or arrive, often when not expected
verbs.wrong: To increase the level or amount of something
verbs.why: Turn up means to appear or arrive, often at a moment you did not expect. The healthy baby gorilla turned up late in the evening, and staff rushed to see her.

verbs.correct: To gather in a group near something
verbs.wrong: To collect and store things for later use
verbs.why: Gather around means to form a group near something interesting to see. Staff members gathered around to watch the new mother and her baby closely.

chunks.text: [[Keepers]] say that Tulivu {{took to}} [[motherhood]] [[right away]]. During her [[pregnancy]], she trained to {{sit through}} [[gentle]] [[ultrasound]] scans so the medical team could [[check on]] her baby. When the [[delivery]] finally came, she knew just what to do and never {{gave up}}. [[Right after]] the birth, she [[cradled]] her daughter and started to {{look after}} her [[with care]].

verbs.correct: To start to like something quickly
verbs.wrong: To carry something to a new place
verbs.why: Take to means to start liking a new activity or role quickly and naturally. Keepers say Tulivu took to motherhood right away, as if she had always known what to do.

verbs.correct: To stay until the end of something long or boring
verbs.wrong: To rest quietly while you think about a problem
verbs.why: Sit through means to stay in place until something long finishes, even if it is a little boring. Tulivu trained to sit through her ultrasound scans calmly, without leaving her spot.

verbs.correct: To stop trying to do something
verbs.wrong: To hand something over to another person

verbs.correct: To protect and support someone or something

chunks.text: The new baby is a western lowland gorilla, a [[species]] that is [[critically]] [[endangered]] [[in the wild]]. Their numbers have {{fallen off}} [[sharply]] because of hunting and lost forests. Zoos [[across the country]] {{team up}} through a special [[breeding program]] to help the population grow. Each new birth [[adds to]] the genetic [[diversity]] that these animals need to [[survive]].

stories.headline: Apple takes OpenAI to court over stolen secrets
