chunks.text: Two of the [[biggest names]] in technology have {{fallen out}}. Apple, [[the company behind]] the iPhone, has filed a [[lawsuit]] against OpenAI, [[the maker of]] ChatGPT. A few of Apple's workers left the company to join OpenAI, and Apple [[claims]] that when they went, they {{walked off with}} [[confidential]] information that helped OpenAI {{come up with}} a new AI [[device]].

verbs.wrong: To become less successful than a rival
verbs.correct: To stop being partners after a quarrel
verbs.why: Fall out means two people, companies, or countries who used to work closely stop trusting each other after a serious disagreement. Apple and OpenAI have fallen out over accusations of stolen secrets, not a small disagreement.

verbs.wrong: To leave a job suddenly, without warning
verbs.correct: To take something that does not belong to you
verbs.why: When someone walks off with something, they take it without permission, often without anyone noticing right away. In the story, workers are accused of walking off with private company files when they left to join OpenAI.

verbs.wrong: To improve a product that already exists
verbs.correct: To think of or create a new idea or plan
verbs.why: Come up with means to think of or invent something new, like an idea, an excuse, or in this case a whole new device. Apple claims OpenAI could not have come up with its new device without stealing information.

chunks.text: In its [[court papers]], Apple {{lays out}} how it believes the [[theft]] happened. It says that before these workers left, they {{sent off}} [[private]] company files to their own personal email accounts. Apple now wants a [[judge]] to {{step in}} and stop OpenAI from using any of its [[trade secrets]].

verbs.wrong: To prove that something really happened
verbs.correct: To explain or describe something clearly
verbs.why: When you lay out something, you explain it clearly, step by step, so other people can follow your reasoning. Apple's court papers lay out exactly how it believes the theft happened.

verbs.wrong: To hide something so that nobody can find it
verbs.correct: To send something to a place, often by email or mail
verbs.why: Send off means to send something on its way, whether it is a letter, a package, or an email. According to the lawsuit, the workers sent off confidential files to their own personal accounts before quitting.

verbs.wrong: To write a long report about a past event
verbs.correct: To get involved in order to help or stop a problem
verbs.why: Step in means to get involved in a situation, usually to help fix a problem or stop something from getting worse. Apple wants a judge to step in and order OpenAI to stop using its trade secrets.

chunks.text: OpenAI quickly {{hit back}} at the claims. A [[spokesperson]] for the company said that OpenAI has [[no interest in]] other companies' secrets, and that its [[lawyers]] are still {{going over}} the papers. [[So far]], [[the two sides]] do not agree, and neither one will {{back down}}.

verbs.wrong: To refuse to answer questions about a problem
verbs.correct: To reply strongly to an attack or criticism
verbs.why: Hit back means to answer criticism firmly, often in the same public way you were attacked. OpenAI hit back at Apple's claims by saying it has no interest in stealing anyone's secrets.

verbs.wrong: To correct the mistakes in a document
verbs.correct: To examine or check something carefully
verbs.why: Go over means to look through something carefully, checking every detail before you respond. OpenAI's lawyers are going over Apple's court papers before deciding what to say next.

verbs.wrong: To admit that you did something wrong
verbs.correct: To stop demanding something or stop arguing
verbs.why: When you back down, you stop insisting on your position in an argument and let the other side win. Neither Apple nor OpenAI will back down, so the dispute looks far from over.

chunks.text: The fight comes as Apple {{moves away}} from OpenAI in another way. Apple has announced that its [[voice assistant]], Siri, will soon {{run on}} Google's Gemini system [[instead of]] ChatGPT. Many people had expected the two companies to {{stick together}} [[for years to come]], so the sudden change has surprised the whole tech world.

verbs.wrong: To end a contract immediately
verbs.correct: To gradually stop using something
verbs.why: Move away here means to slowly stop relying on something you once depended on. Apple is moving away from ChatGPT, giving Siri Google's Gemini system instead.

verbs.wrong: To be owned by another company
verbs.correct: To work using a certain kind of power
verbs.why: Run on describes what powers a machine or device, like a car that runs on gas or a phone that runs on batteries. Soon Siri will run on Google's Gemini system instead of ChatGPT.

verbs.wrong: To share their technology with each other
verbs.correct: To stay united and continue to support each other
verbs.why: Stick together means to stay loyal to each other and keep working as a team, even under pressure. Many expected Apple and OpenAI to stick together for years, so this split surprised the tech world.

stories.headline: A huge typhoon forces a million people from their homes

chunks.text: A powerful storm called Typhoon Bavi has {{moved in}} on eastern China. Before it reached land, [[officials]] {{moved out}} more than 1.7 million people from towns near the coast in Zhejiang [[province]]. China's weather service {{put out}} an orange [[alert]], the second-highest warning level.

verbs.wrong: To grow stronger very quickly
verbs.correct: To come closer in a threatening way
verbs.why: Move in means something threatening gets closer and closer, like a storm or an army. Typhoon Bavi moved in on the coast before making landfall.

verbs.wrong: To warn people that danger is coming
verbs.correct: To make people leave a place
verbs.why: Move out here means officials made large numbers of people leave a dangerous area. They moved out more than 1.7 million residents before the typhoon hit.

verbs.wrong: To close every road across the city
verbs.correct: To produce or release something publicly
verbs.why: Put out means to officially release information for the public, like a warning or a statement. China's weather service put out an alert before the storm reached land.

chunks.text: [[Out at sea]], Bavi had {{built up}} into a huge [[typhoon]] with [[winds]] near 89 miles per hour. [[On its way]], it {{passed by}} the Philippines and Taiwan, where the storm killed and hurt many people. Weather forecasters [[warned]] that it could {{knock down}} trees and [[flood]] streets when it reached the coastal city of Yuhuan late on Saturday night.

verbs.wrong: To move quickly across the ocean
verbs.correct: To slowly become bigger or stronger
verbs.why: Build up means to slowly grow in size or strength over time. Out at sea, the storm built up into a huge typhoon before reaching land.

verbs.wrong: To stop in a place for a short time
verbs.correct: To move past a place without stopping
verbs.why: Pass by means to travel past a place without stopping there. On its way to China, the storm passed by the Philippines and Taiwan.

verbs.wrong: To bend and twist in the strong wind
verbs.correct: To hit something so it falls to the ground
verbs.why: Knock down means to hit something hard enough that it falls over. Forecasters warned the winds could knock down trees across the region.

chunks.text: The typhoon {{shut down}} [[normal life]] [[across the region]]. Airlines {{called off}} [[hundreds of]] flights, and fast trains and [[ferry]] services stopped for the weekend. Officials also {{set up}} [[shelters]] where families could stay safe until the danger passed.

verbs.wrong: To force people to stay in their homes
verbs.correct: To stop something from working or being open
verbs.why: Shut down means to stop something from operating or being open to the public. The typhoon shut down normal life, closing flights, trains, and ferries.

verbs.wrong: To move something to a later date
verbs.correct: To cancel something that was planned
verbs.why: Call off means to cancel an event or plan that was already scheduled. Airlines called off hundreds of flights ahead of the storm's arrival.

verbs.wrong: To pay the cost for other people
verbs.correct: To create or arrange something
verbs.why: Set up means to create or arrange something so it is ready to use, like a tent, a meeting, or a shelter. Officials set up shelters for families before the storm hit.

chunks.text: Rescue teams {{teamed up}} to [[get ready for the worst]]. In Fujian province, more than 17,000 rescue workers were {{standing by}}, [[ready to help]], and the government [[promised]] millions of dollars for [[relief]]. Officials hoped that all of this [[careful planning]] would {{pay off}} and [[keep people safe]].

verbs.wrong: To share information with each other
verbs.correct: To join with others to work together
verbs.why: Team up means to join with others so you can work together toward one goal. Rescue teams teamed up to prepare for the worst before landfall.

verbs.wrong: To promise to support a person no matter what
verbs.correct: To be ready to help or act at any moment
verbs.why: Stand by means to stay ready to act the moment you are needed. More than 17,000 rescue workers stood by in Fujian province alone.

verbs.wrong: To happen exactly the way it was planned
verbs.correct: To bring a good result after hard work
verbs.why: Pay off means careful effort or planning eventually brings a good result. Officials hoped all their preparation would pay off and keep people safe.

stories.headline: China lands a rocket booster on a ship at sea

sources.title: Making history! China lands rocket during an orbital launch for 1st time ever
China becomes second country to recover orbital booster with Long March 10B
China Successfully Launches, Retrieves Reusable Rocket Booster
China catches Long March-10B booster in reusable rocket breakthrough (video, CGTN)

chunks.text: China has {{pulled off}} [[a major step]] in space travel. From the Hainan Commercial Space Launch Site, a new rocket called the Long March-10B {{took off}}, carried a [[satellite]] into [[orbit]], and then [[guided]] its huge lower part, or [[booster]], [[safely]] back to Earth. China became only the second country, after the United States, to [[recover]] an orbital rocket so it can be used again.

verbs.wrong: To try something for the first time
verbs.correct: To succeed in doing something difficult
verbs.why: Pull off means to succeed at something that is hard or risky, when there was a real chance it could fail. China pulled off catching its rocket booster in a net at sea, something only one other country had done.

verbs.wrong: To separate suddenly from another part
verbs.correct: To leave the ground and begin to fly
verbs.why: Take off means to leave the ground and start flying, whether it is a plane, a bird, or in this case a rocket. The Long March-10B took off, carried a satellite into orbit, and then returned its booster safely.

chunks.text: After the rocket climbed high into the sky, its first [[stage]] [[separated]] and {{came down}} toward the sea. About six minutes later, a giant net on a floating [[platform]] caught it. Chinese [[engineers]] had {{set up}} this net capture system, and they had never {{tried out}} such a design in a real flight before.

verbs.wrong: To become slower before landing
verbs.correct: To move down toward a lower place
verbs.why: Come down simply means to move downward, from a high place toward the ground or the sea. After launch, the rocket's first stage separated and came down toward the ocean, where a net was waiting.

verbs.wrong: To repair a machine that had broken
verbs.correct: To create or establish something new
verbs.why: Set up means to build or arrange something new so it is ready to use, like a business or an experiment. Chinese engineers set up a huge net capture system that had never been tested in a real flight.

verbs.wrong: To practice something many times
verbs.correct: To test something to see if it works
verbs.why: Try out means to test something new to see whether it actually works before you rely on it. Engineers had never tried out this exact net design in a real flight before this launch.

chunks.text: Landing a booster is difficult, but it {{pays off}}. [[Normally]], rockets are used only once and then {{thrown away}}. If the same booster can fly [[again and again]], companies can {{cut down}} their costs and launch [[far more]] often. [[For years]], the American company SpaceX has led this [[field]], and China is now [[working hard]] to {{catch up}}.

verbs.wrong: To become easier with practice
verbs.correct: To bring a good result after effort
verbs.why: Pay off means that hard work or a risky effort finally brings a good result. Landing a booster is difficult, but for China it clearly paid off with a successful catch.

verbs.wrong: To keep something for the next launch
verbs.correct: To remove something you do not want
verbs.why: Throw away means to put something in the trash because you no longer want or need it, like old papers or a broken tool. Normally rockets are used once and then thrown away, but reusable boosters change that.

verbs.wrong: To share costs with other companies
verbs.correct: To reduce the amount of something
verbs.why: Cut down means to reduce an amount, often to save money or time. If boosters can fly again and again, companies can cut down their launch costs significantly.

verbs.wrong: To copy another company's design
verbs.correct: To reach the same level as someone ahead
verbs.why: Catch up means to work hard to reach the same level as someone who is currently ahead of you. SpaceX has led reusable rockets for years, and China is now working hard to catch up.

chunks.text: The Long March-10B stands about 63 meters tall, and [[one day]] it may help {{carry out}} China's plan to send [[astronauts]] to the Moon. Engineers now want to {{look over}} the returned booster, and they hope to fly it again [[before the end of]] the year. If everything {{goes ahead}} [[as planned]], [[reusable]] Chinese rockets could soon become normal.

verbs.wrong: To announce a plan to the whole world
verbs.correct: To do or complete a planned task or action
verbs.why: Carry out means to actually perform a task that has already been planned, not just talk about it. This same rocket may one day help carry out China's mission to send astronauts to the Moon.

verbs.wrong: To repair something before using it again
verbs.correct: To examine or check something carefully
verbs.why: Look over means to check something with your eyes, examining it carefully before deciding what to do next. Engineers will look over the returned booster to see if it is ready to fly again.

verbs.wrong: To finish earlier than expected
verbs.correct: To happen or continue as planned
verbs.why: Go ahead means that a plan continues without being canceled or delayed. If everything goes ahead as planned, reusable Chinese rockets could soon become completely normal.

stories.headline: Europe says Instagram and Facebook are too addictive

sources.title: Commission preliminarily finds the addictive design of Instagram and Facebook in breach of the Digital Services Act
EU says 'addictive' features on Instagram and Facebook breach its rules
EU puts 'addictive' design of Facebook, Instagram under the DSA microscope
EU tells Meta to change Facebook and Instagram's 'addictive design' | AFP (video, AFP News Agency)

chunks.text: The European Union has {{spoken out}} against two of the world's most popular apps. Officials said that Instagram and Facebook, which are both [[owned by]] the company Meta, are [[designed]] to be too [[addictive]]. They believe the apps break a European law called the Digital Services Act, because their design can [[harm]] users' health and [[well-being]].

verbs.wrong: To start a legal case against someone
verbs.correct: To publicly say what you think
verbs.why: Speak out means to publicly say what you think, especially against something you believe is wrong. Officials, doctors, and ordinary users can all speak out about a company's actions.

chunks.text: The [[regulators]] {{pointed out}} three [[features]] that keep people using the apps [[for hours]]. One feature, called infinite scroll, lets a feed load forever; videos {{start up}} [[on their own]] through [[autoplay]]; and the app keeps {{serving up}} posts it thinks you will like. Together, officials said, these [[tricks]] push the brain into "[[autopilot]]," so users {{end up}} [[scrolling]] without really deciding to.

verbs.wrong: To officially declare something illegal
verbs.correct: To tell someone about a fact or detail
verbs.why: Point out means to tell someone a fact or a detail they might not have noticed. Regulators pointed out three features that keep people scrolling for hours.

verbs.wrong: To play without any sound
verbs.correct: To begin or start operating
verbs.why: Start up means to begin operating, especially for a machine, an engine, or a piece of software. In this story, videos start up automatically through autoplay, without anyone pressing play.

verbs.wrong: To save something to watch later
verbs.correct: To present or offer something
verbs.why: Serve up means to present something to someone, often food, but here it is used for content an app offers you. Apps serve up posts and videos they think will keep you watching.

verbs.wrong: To lose track of time completely
verbs.correct: To reach a final situation or place
verbs.why: End up means to reach a final situation without really planning it. Here, small design tricks like autoplay make users end up scrolling for far longer than they intended.

chunks.text: Europe now wants Meta to {{turn off}} infinite scroll and autoplay [[unless]] a user chooses them, and to {{cut down}} how much the app decides for each person. Meta does not agree. It says it has already {{brought in}} strong rules to protect [[teenagers]], and that the EU's review does not [[fairly]] show the steps it has taken.

verbs.wrong: To make a feature harder to find
verbs.correct: To stop a machine or feature from working
verbs.why: Turn off means to stop a machine or a feature from working. Europe wants Meta to turn off autoplay and infinite scroll unless a user actively chooses them.

verbs.wrong: To let users make every choice
verbs.correct: To reduce the amount of something
verbs.why: Cut down means to reduce the amount of something, often for health or safety reasons. Europe wants Meta to cut down how much control its algorithm has over what you see.

verbs.wrong: To promise stronger rules for the future
verbs.correct: To introduce a new rule, law, or system
verbs.why: Bring in means to introduce a new rule, system, or law. Meta says it has already brought in strong rules to protect teenagers online.

chunks.text: If Meta cannot [[win the argument]], it may have to {{pay out}} a very large [[fine]], [[up to]] 6% of the money it makes around the world each year. The company can still respond before Europe {{hands down}} [[a final decision]] [[in the coming months]]. Many doctors say that [[endless]] scrolling can {{bring on}} [[anxiety]] and [[low moods]] in young people, and some want the apps to {{take away}} these features [[for good]].

verbs.wrong: To lose money because of falling sales
verbs.correct: To pay a large amount of money
verbs.why: Pay out means to pay a large sum of money, usually as a punishment, a prize, or an insurance claim. If Meta loses, it may have to pay out a huge fine.

verbs.wrong: To discuss a decision in private
verbs.correct: To officially give a decision or judgment
verbs.why: Hand down means to officially give a decision or a ruling, usually from a court or an authority. Europe has not yet handed down its final decision on Meta's case.

verbs.wrong: To make an illness harder to treat
verbs.correct: To cause something unpleasant to happen
verbs.why: Bring on means to cause something unpleasant to start, especially a feeling or an illness. Long hours of scrolling can bring on stress or sadness that a person did not expect.

verbs.wrong: To hide a feature from young users
verbs.correct: To remove something and carry it away
verbs.why: Take away means to remove something so it is no longer there. Some doctors want addictive app features taken away for good, not just quietly reduced.

stories.headline: Ukraine hits Russian oil sites with drones

sources.title: Drone offensive hits Russian oil tankers and refineries at 'industrial scale' as Moscow bans diesel exports
Russia bans diesel exports after Ukrainian attacks, straining already tense global market
Russia Bans Diesel Exports to Ensure Domestic Supply After Targeted Ukrainian Drone Strikes
Ukraine hits Russia's largest refinery in one of its deepest strikes yet | DW News (video, DW News)

chunks.text: Ukraine {{carried out}} a large drone [[offensive]] that [[lasted]] about three days. Ukraine said its forces {{stepped up}} attacks on Russian oil [[tankers]] and [[refineries]]. One Ukrainian [[commander]] [[described]] the campaign as reaching an "industrial scale." [[According to reports]], the drones {{set off}} fires at several energy sites, and Ukraine [[claimed]] it had hit 21 [[vessels]], including 19 oil tankers, near Crimea.

verbs.wrong: To win a battle after long fighting
verbs.correct: To do or complete a planned task or action
verbs.why: Carry out is a formal way to say you do or complete a planned action. Ukraine carried out a multi day drone campaign aimed directly at Russia's energy infrastructure.

verbs.wrong: To aim at more important targets
verbs.correct: To increase or intensify an activity
verbs.why: Step up means to increase the level or intensity of something you are already doing. Kyiv announced that its military had stepped up strikes on Russia's tankers and fuel plants.

verbs.wrong: To destroy something in an explosion
verbs.correct: To cause something to start suddenly
verbs.why: Set off means to cause something to start suddenly, often with force. According to reports, the drone strikes set off fires at multiple fuel and energy facilities.

chunks.text: The strikes {{knocked out}} part of Russia's oil [[production]]. According to reports, the Omsk refinery in Siberia, which is Russia's largest, {{shut down}} some [[operations]] after it was hit. The plant sits about 1,700 miles from Ukrainian [[territory]] and [[normally]] makes around 460,000 [[barrels]] of fuel a day. Two industry sources said work at the site stopped [[for a time]].

verbs.wrong: To reduce something to half its size
verbs.correct: To destroy or stop something from working
verbs.why: Knock out means to destroy something or force it to stop working completely. These attacks knocked out a real share of the country's overall oil output, at least temporarily.

verbs.wrong: To move work to a safer place
verbs.correct: To stop operating or close
verbs.why: Shut down means to stop operating or close completely, whether for a short time or forever. After the strike, Russia's biggest refinery had to shut down part of its work for a while.

chunks.text: Inside Russia, the attacks [[led to]] serious fuel [[shortages]]. Long lines {{built up}} at gas stations in several regions, and some areas {{brought in}} [[limits on]] how much fuel drivers could buy. Prices {{went up}} quickly. One Russian official said the situation at filling stations was "[[causing concern]]" among the public, and reports said some stations {{ran out}} of gasoline.

verbs.wrong: To appear suddenly all at once
verbs.correct: To increase or grow larger gradually
verbs.why: Build up means to grow larger gradually, little by little, over time. Across several regions, long lines slowly built up outside gas stations as fuel grew scarce.

verbs.wrong: To ask people to follow a rule voluntarily
verbs.correct: To introduce a new rule, law, or system
verbs.why: Bring in means to introduce a new rule or system that did not exist before. In response, several local governments brought in rules limiting how much gasoline each car could purchase.

verbs.wrong: To change many times in one day
verbs.correct: To rise or increase in level or amount
verbs.why: Go up means to rise or increase, like a price or a number. As the shortage spread, fuel prices went up fast in the affected regions.

verbs.wrong: To close early for the day
verbs.correct: To have no more of something left
verbs.why: Run out means you have used all of something and none is left. By the worst point, several stations had simply run out of gasoline to sell.

chunks.text: [[In response]], Russia {{hit back}} at the [[pressure]] on its fuel market by cutting [[exports]]. Russian officials said they would {{hold back}} [[diesel]] exports until July 31 to keep enough fuel at home. To {{deal with}} the shortages, reports said Russia planned to buy fuel from other countries and had already started [[importing]] gasoline from India. [[Analysts]] said the export [[ban]] could push global diesel prices higher.

verbs.wrong: To protect your economy from losses
verbs.correct: To respond to an attack or criticism
verbs.why: Hit back means to respond strongly to an attack, a criticism, or a pressure. In turn, Russia hit back at the pressure by reducing some of its fuel exports.

verbs.wrong: To increase the tax rate on diesel fuel
verbs.correct: To keep or stop something from being released
verbs.why: Hold back means to keep something from being released or sent out, at least for now. Moscow said it would hold back diesel shipments abroad for a few weeks to protect the domestic supply.

verbs.wrong: To limit how much fuel drivers could buy
verbs.correct: To take action to solve a problem
verbs.why: Deal with means to take action in order to solve or manage a problem. To deal with the shortage at home, Russia began buying extra gasoline from outside suppliers, including India.

mainIdea.s: Ukraine launched a drone offensive that hit Russian oil tankers and refineries over three days. The strikes caused fuel shortages, so Russia banned diesel exports.

mainIdea.s: Ukraine's drones hit Russian oil sites in a three-day offensive against refineries and tankers. Russia then raised diesel exports to profit from higher world fuel prices.

mainIdea.s: Ukrainian and Russian officials held a new round of peace talks last month but again failed to agree on a ceasefire deal. Officials said the talks would continue.

tf.s: Inside Russia, some gas stations ran out of gasoline during the shortages.

tf.s: Russia stepped up its diesel exports until the end of July.
tf.why: Russia held back (stopped) its diesel exports. Step up means to increase, which is the opposite of what happened.

stories.headline: A tiny parasite makes over 1,000 people sick

sources.title: STAT: Outbreak of diarrhea-causing parasite grows to more than 1,000 cases
CDC: Surveillance of Cyclosporiasis

chunks.text: Health officials say a tiny [[parasite]] called cyclospora has {{broken out}} across the United States. The CDC reported that this [[outbreak]] has made more than 1,000 people sick [[so far this year]]. The parasite is [[microscopic]], so people cannot see it on their food. Health officials are working to {{find out}} where the [[contaminated]] food comes from.

verbs.wrong: To move from animals to people
verbs.correct: To start suddenly and spread
verbs.why: Break out describes something bad, like a disease, a fire, or a fight, starting suddenly and spreading fast. This outbreak of a tiny parasite broke out across dozens of states this year.

verbs.wrong: To test food in a laboratory
verbs.correct: To discover a fact after searching
verbs.why: Find out means to discover a fact you did not know before, often after some searching. Health officials are still trying to find out where the contaminated food originated.

chunks.text: Cyclospora usually [[spreads]] through contaminated fresh [[produce]], [[such as]] fruits and vegetables. When people {{come down with}} the [[illness]], they often have [[long-lasting]] [[diarrhea]] and stomach pain. The [[infection]], which doctors call cyclosporiasis, is not usually dangerous. Still, some patients {{end up}} needing [[medical care]] to {{deal with}} their [[symptoms]].

verbs.wrong: To pass an illness to another person
verbs.correct: To become sick with an illness
verbs.why: Come down with means to become sick with an illness, usually something common like a cold or stomach bug. In this story, people come down with cyclospora after eating contaminated produce.

verbs.wrong: To wait a long time to see a doctor
verbs.correct: To reach a final situation or place
verbs.why: End up describes reaching a final result, often one you did not plan for. Some people who get this parasite end up needing medical care for their symptoms.

verbs.wrong: To take medicine every day
verbs.correct: To take action to handle a problem
verbs.why: Deal with means to take action and manage a problem instead of avoiding it. Patients need to deal with symptoms like long-lasting diarrhea and stomach pain.

chunks.text: Health officials say the [[germs]] can get onto fresh food when [[irrigation]] water on farms is dirty. The CDC is {{looking into}} the outbreak, and its scientists are {{carrying out}} tests to learn more about it. Officials also [[warn of]] [[the danger of]] eating unwashed produce. They want people to be careful at home.

verbs.wrong: To count the number of sick people
verbs.correct: To examine or investigate something
verbs.why: Look into means to investigate or examine something closely to learn more about it. The CDC is looking into this outbreak to find its exact source.

verbs.wrong: To share results with the public
verbs.correct: To do or complete a task
verbs.why: Carry out is the formal way to say do something, especially a task, a plan, or a test. Scientists are carrying out tests to understand how the outbreak started.

chunks.text: [[To stay safe]], health officials tell people to {{wash off}} fresh fruits and vegetables under [[running water]]. Washing can help {{get rid of}} many germs, but it may not [[remove]] every one. Experts also suggest buying whole [[heads of lettuce]] and removing the outer leaves. Cooking vegetables can {{cut down on}} the [[risk]] of getting sick too.

verbs.wrong: To soak food in clean water
verbs.correct: To remove something by cleaning it
verbs.why: Wash off means to remove something, like dirt or germs, by rinsing it with water. Health officials tell people to wash off fresh fruits and vegetables before eating them.

verbs.wrong: To kill germs with high heat
verbs.correct: To remove or discard something
verbs.why: Get rid of means to remove something you do not want, whether it is old furniture or germs on your food. Washing can help get rid of many germs, though not all of them.

verbs.wrong: To remove something completely
verbs.correct: To reduce the amount of something
verbs.why: Cut down on means to reduce how much of something you do or use, often for your health. Cooking vegetables can cut down on the risk of getting sick from this parasite.

stories.headline: A record heat wave hits the United States

sources.title: US heat wave death toll grows
19 deaths in New Jersey likely connected to heat wave, officials say
Heat-related deaths mount after historic Fourth of July heat wave broiled eastern US
July 4 Heat Wave Shatters More Than 148 Records Across The Eastern US (video, FOX Weather)

chunks.text: A dangerous [[heat wave]] {{heated up}} much of the United States over the July 4 holiday weekend. A large [[heat dome]] [[settled]] over the country, and the [[extreme]] heat {{set in}} from the Midwest to the East Coast. Officials said about 40 million people were under a heat [[alert]] on Sunday. Weather [[forecasters]] [[warned of]] a serious danger to people's health.

verbs.wrong: To stay hot for many days
verbs.correct: To become hotter
verbs.why: Heat up means to become hotter over a period of time. A dangerous heat wave heated up much of the United States over the July 4th weekend.

verbs.wrong: To announce a new weather warning system
verbs.correct: To begin and seem likely to continue
verbs.why: Set in means a condition begins and looks likely to continue for a while. Extreme heat set in across the country from the Midwest to the East Coast.

chunks.text: Forecasters said the heat wave [[broke many old records]]. Temperatures {{shot up}} above 100 degrees Fahrenheit in many cities. In Washington, D.C., the temperature reached 103 degrees on July 4, which officials said was a new record. High [[humidity]] made the air feel even hotter. Overnight, the air did not {{cool down}} much, and [[the low]] stayed near 80 degrees, so many people could not {{cool off}}.

verbs.wrong: To stay at a very high level
verbs.correct: To rise very quickly
verbs.why: Shoot up means to rise very fast in a short amount of time. Temperatures shot up above 100 degrees Fahrenheit in many cities during the heat wave.

verbs.wrong: To move more slowly
verbs.correct: To become cooler
verbs.why: Cool down means to become less hot, usually as time passes. Overnight the air did not cool down much, so the heat stayed dangerous even after dark.

verbs.wrong: To take a rest in the shade
verbs.correct: To make yourself less hot
verbs.why: Cool off means to do something that makes your own body feel less hot. With the low staying near 80 degrees overnight, many people could not cool off at all.

chunks.text: Officials said the heat wave was [[blamed for]] [[at least]] 24 deaths [[across the country]] during the week. In New Jersey, state health officials said about 22 deaths were [[linked to]] the heat. Officials also {{pointed out}} that extreme heat is one of the [[deadliest]] kinds of weather in the United States. Officials asked people to {{look out for}} older neighbors and anyone living without [[air conditioning]].

verbs.wrong: To prove something with numbers
verbs.correct: To tell someone a fact they may not know
verbs.why: Point out means to tell someone a fact they might not already know. Officials pointed out that extreme heat is one of the deadliest kinds of weather in the country.

verbs.wrong: To visit someone every day
verbs.correct: To take care to protect someone
verbs.why: Look out for here means to check on someone and make sure they are safe. Officials asked people to look out for older neighbors and anyone without air conditioning.

chunks.text: To help people {{deal with}} the heat, many cities opened a [[cooling center]] where [[residents]] could stay cool. Officials asked people to {{carry on}} drinking water and to rest indoors during the hottest hours. Some [[outdoor]] events were {{called off}} [[for safety]]. By early the next week, forecasters said the heat would finally {{let up}} as cooler air [[moved in]].

verbs.wrong: To collect data about heat-related deaths
verbs.correct: To take action to solve a problem
verbs.why: Deal with means to take practical action to handle a problem or a difficult situation. Cities opened cooling centers to help residents deal with the dangerous heat.

verbs.wrong: To remember to do something important
verbs.correct: To continue doing something
verbs.why: Carry on means to continue doing something without stopping. Officials asked people to carry on drinking water through the hottest days.

verbs.wrong: To move an event indoors for safety
verbs.correct: To cancel a planned event
verbs.why: Call off means to cancel an event that had already been planned. Some outdoor events were called off for safety during the worst of the heat.

verbs.wrong: To move to another region
verbs.correct: To become less strong
verbs.why: Let up means to become weaker or less intense. Forecasters said the heat would finally let up as cooler air arrived from the north.

stories.headline: New cells bring back sight in mice

sources.title: Blind People Offered Hope of Seeing Again After Stem Cell Breakthrough Remakes Retinal Blood Vessels (Good News Network)
Researchers Grow Rare Eye Vessel Cells to Halt Vision Loss (Neuroscience News)
Lab-Grown Retinal Cells Show Promise for New Eye Therapies (Duke Pratt School of Engineering)

chunks.text: Scientists at Duke University said they had {{carried out}} an [[exciting]] experiment. A team led by Professor Sharon Gerecht {{set out}} to grow tiny blood vessels for the [[retina]] using [[stem cells]]. These special cells are very hard to make, but the scientists {{came up with}} a [[clever]] way to grow them in the lab. Their [[goal]] was to help people who are slowly [[losing their sight]].

verbs.wrong: To repeat an experiment to check the results
verbs.correct: To do or perform a task or experiment
verbs.why: Carry out means to perform a task or an experiment from start to finish. The Duke University team carried out this study to test a brand new way of growing eye cells.

verbs.wrong: To promise to finish something important
verbs.correct: To begin a task with a clear goal
verbs.why: Set out means to begin a project with a clear goal in mind. Scientists here set out to solve a hard problem: growing delicate eye cells safely in a lab.

verbs.wrong: To copy a method from another team
verbs.correct: To think of a new idea or plan
verbs.why: Come up with means to think of a new idea or a solution, often after trying hard. The team came up with a smart trick to grow these cells, which scientists usually find very difficult to produce.

chunks.text: The researchers used stem cells that can [[turn into]] almost any cell in the body. In the lab, these cells slowly grew into the [[tissue]] that [[lines]] the blood vessels in the eye. To copy eye disease, the team put the tissue [[under stress]], and it started to {{break down}} [[in the same way]] it does in sick patients. These blood vessel tissue cells normally come only from inside the body, so growing them outside the body in the lab was a real [[breakthrough]].

verbs.wrong: To grow larger and stronger
verbs.correct: To stop working or collapse
verbs.why: Break down means to stop working properly and collapse, the way a machine breaks down when it stops running. Here, the lab-grown eye tissue broke down under pressure, just like in a real disease.

chunks.text: Next, the team tested the new cells in mice, not in people. They [[injected]] the cells into mice with weak, [[damaged]] eyes. The cells joined the tissue and {{built up}} strong, healthy blood vessels. This slowly {{brought the animals' sight back}}, and their [[vision]] got better. Mice that were treated early did not {{end up}} completely [[blind]].

verbs.wrong: To replace old cells with donor tissue
verbs.correct: To make something grow stronger
verbs.why: Build up means to make something grow stronger or larger, gradually over time. In the treated mice, injected cells built up strong new blood vessels, helping damaged eyes heal.

verbs.wrong: To start talking about a topic
verbs.correct: To make something return
verbs.why: Bring back means to make something return, especially something that was lost or missing. In the study, the new cells slowly brought back some of the mice's lost vision.

verbs.wrong: To stay the same without any change
verbs.correct: To finally be in a situation or place
verbs.why: End up means to finally reach a certain state or result, sometimes after a process nobody fully controls. In this study, mice that got treatment early kept far more of their sight and never ended up fully blind.

chunks.text: Professor Gerecht said the results [[point to]] a [[hopeful]] future, but she was [[careful]]. [[So far]] the [[method]] has only been tested in mice, so scientists cannot say yet that it will work in humans. They still need to work on safety before any tests in people. Doctors do not {{rule out}} problems, and they say a real [[treatment]] for [[diabetic retinopathy]], [[a leading cause]] of [[blindness]], may still be many [[years away]].

verbs.wrong: To warn people about a possible danger
verbs.correct: To decide that something is not possible
verbs.why: Rule out means to decide firmly that something is not possible or will not happen. Doctors are careful here: they do not rule out safety problems before human trials even begin.

mainIdea.s: A team at Duke University set out to grow blood vessel cells for the eye using stem cells. When they tested the cells in mice with damaged eyes, some vision came back.
mainIdea.why: The scientists grew the blood vessel cells from stem cells and tested them in mice with damaged eyes. The mice slowly got some of their vision back.

mainIdea.s: Scientists at Duke University used cells taken from healthy human donors to fix mice with damaged eyes. They say the treatment is now ready to help blind people see again.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the cells did not come from human donors, they were grown in the lab from stem cells. The article says a human treatment is still years away.

mainIdea.s: Doctors are running new trials of a laser treatment for diabetic retinopathy in older adult patients. Early results show the therapy slows vision loss without any surgery.
mainIdea.why: This story is about mice regaining sight after a stem cell experiment at Duke University. It is not about a laser treatment trial for older patients.

stories.headline: Italy may put solar panels between train tracks

sources.title: Italy could be the next country to build a solar railway after Switzerland's successful trial
Swiss railway solar panel experiment passes one-year milestone
Solar energy from railways shows first positive results in Switzerland
Italy could be the next country to build a solar railway after Switzerland's successful trial (video, euronews)

chunks.text: News reports said Italy may become the next country to {{roll out}} a solar railway. The idea comes from Sun-Ways, a Swiss [[start-up]] that {{came up with}} [[a way to]] place solar [[panels]] between train tracks. After a Swiss [[pilot project]] passed its [[one-year mark]] with strong results, [[supporters]] say Italy could {{end up}} building its own line that turns unused rail space into clean energy.

verbs.wrong: To test something in one small area first
verbs.correct: To start using or introducing something widely
verbs.why: Roll out means to launch something widely, moving it from a small test into full public use. Companies roll out new products, and now countries may roll out this rail technology nationwide.

verbs.wrong: To be the first to use a new invention
verbs.correct: To think of or produce a new idea or plan
verbs.why: Come up with means to invent an idea or solution through thinking, not by copying someone else. This start-up came up with a clever way to use empty space between train tracks.

verbs.wrong: To reach the same level as another country
verbs.correct: To finally be in a particular situation or place
verbs.why: End up means you finally land in a certain situation, sometimes without planning it. If the trial continues to go well, Italy could end up with its own solar railway.

chunks.text: The Swiss company first {{set up}} the test track in Buttes, in the canton of Neuchatel, in April 2025. Workers [[laid]] 48 special panels between the [[rails]] on the wooden [[sleepers]]. The panels can be {{taken up}} again for [[maintenance]], and a small machine lifts a six-meter module in about ten minutes.

verbs.wrong: To measure the land before construction
verbs.correct: To build and prepare something for use
verbs.why: Set up means to build and arrange something so it is ready for use, like a tent, a stage, or a test track. Sun-Ways set up its first solar track in Switzerland in 2025.

verbs.wrong: To clean something without removing it
verbs.correct: To lift something up and remove it
verbs.why: Take up means to lift something and remove it from where it was fixed, like old flooring or track panels. Workers can take up a solar panel for repairs in minutes.

chunks.text: The one-year results {{came out}} well. Since May 20, 2025, the [[installation]] has [[produced]] more than 16,000 kilowatt-hours of electricity, [[about as much as]] three or four homes use in a year. The company says more than 11,000 trains have passed [[safely]], and the system has {{held up}} well. Engineers also wanted to {{find out}} whether [[reflections]] might [[dazzle]] drivers, but [[so far]] no problems have appeared.

verbs.wrong: To be checked by other scientists
verbs.correct: To end or result in a particular way
verbs.why: Here come out means a result develops a certain way after time or testing, good or bad. The Swiss test's numbers came out strong after a full year.

verbs.wrong: To pass a safety inspection test
verbs.correct: To stay strong and not fail
verbs.why: Hold up means to stay strong under pressure without breaking or failing, like a bridge under heavy traffic. The panels held up well even after thousands of trains rolled across them.

verbs.wrong: To prove that something is dangerous
verbs.correct: To learn a fact or piece of information
verbs.why: Find out means to learn a fact you did not know before, often through testing or research. Engineers wanted to find out whether sunlight reflecting off the panels might blind drivers.

chunks.text: Sun-Ways says it has {{teamed up}} with an Italian [[partner]]. That partner is [[in contact with]] Rete Ferroviaria Italiana, the company that {{looks after}} Italy's rail network. Supporters believe the idea could {{catch on}} in other countries, and France, South Korea, and Indonesia have all [[shown interest]]. Still, experts [[warn]] that safety checks could {{drag on}} [[for up to]] three years before the plan [[moves ahead]].

verbs.correct: To join with someone to work together
verbs.why: Team up means to join forces with another person or company toward a shared goal. Sun-Ways teamed up with an Italian partner to bring the solar railway idea to Italy.

mainIdea.s: A Swiss test track with solar panels between the rails has produced strong results for a full year. Italy could now build its own line, but safety checks might drag on for up to three years.

chunks.text: Eight days after two [[powerful]] earthquakes hit Venezuela, [[rescuers]] have {{pulled a man out}} of a [[collapsed]] building, and he is still alive. The man, a security guard named Hernan Gil, was [[trapped]] when a shopping mall parking lot {{came down}} [[on top of]] him in the coastal town of La Guaira. Doctors say he is now [[in good condition]]. Many people are calling the rescue a [[miracle]].

verbs.wrong: To help someone walk out of a dangerous place

chunks.text: When the building fell, Gil {{ended up}} trapped inside a small concrete booth in the basement. Experts say the strong booth {{held up}} and formed a protective pocket that shielded him from the falling [[debris]]. For eight long days, he {{held on}} under [[tons of]] [[rubble]], with no food and very little water.

verbs.wrong: To hide somewhere to stay safe
verbs.correct: To finally be in a particular situation
verbs.why: End up means you finally land in a situation you did not plan or expect. Gil ended up trapped in a small concrete booth deep under the rubble.

verbs.wrong: To be rebuilt after the earthquake ended
verbs.correct: To stay strong and not fall or fail
verbs.why: Hold up means to stay strong and not collapse under pressure or weight. The concrete booth held up and protected Gil from the falling debris above.

verbs.wrong: To stay calm and quiet in danger

verbs.why: Hold on here means to survive through a hard, painful situation without losing hope. Gil held on for eight days underground with no food and almost no water.

chunks.text: Rescue teams from seven countries {{teamed up}} to save him. According to Chile's fire department, it took more than 70 hours of [[careful]] work to {{dig out}} the security booth. The workers [[refused]] to {{give up}}, [[even though]] [[the best chance]] of finding [[survivors]] usually ends after about three days. [[In the end]], their effort {{paid off}}.

verbs.wrong: To arrive at the same time
verbs.correct: To join together to work with others
verbs.why: Team up means people or groups join forces to work toward one shared goal. Rescue crews from seven countries teamed up to reach the trapped man faster.

verbs.why: Dig out means to remove someone or something buried by digging carefully around it. It took more than 70 hours to dig out the small booth where Gil was trapped.

verbs.wrong: To take a short break
verbs.correct: To stop trying
verbs.why: Give up means to stop trying, even when success seems unlikely or far away. The rescue workers refused to give up, even after the usual survival window had passed.

verbs.wrong: To delay something until later

verbs.why: Pay off means effort or risk eventually brings a good result. The rescuers' more than 70 hours of digging finally paid off when they found Gil alive.

chunks.text: At the hospital, doctors say Gil is slowly {{getting over}} his [[terrible]] [[ordeal]]. The [[twin]] earthquakes have {{turned out}} to be [[among the worst]] in Venezuela's history, killing more than 2,500 people. Thousands of families still do not know what happened to their [[missing]] relatives. For a country [[full of]] sadness, this one rescue has {{brought about}} a [[rare]] moment of hope.

tf.why: Rescue teams from seven countries teamed up (joined together) to save him.

tf.s: Doctors say Gil is slowly getting over his terrible ordeal.
tf.why: At the hospital, doctors say he is slowly getting over (recovering from) the ordeal and is now in good condition.

tf.s: Gil brought about his own terrible ordeal under the rubble.
tf.why: Gil did not cause what happened to him. Bring about means to cause something to happen, but it was the earthquake that trapped him. Doctors say he is getting over the ordeal.

stories.headline: Giraffes can do simple math

sources.title: Study finds giraffes may be capable of rudimentary math - UPI
Giraffes combine quantities similarly to addition - University of Barcelona
Giraffes combine quantities similarly to addition - Phys.org
9@9: Giraffes can do math (video, WGN Living)

chunks.text: Scientists have {{found out}} that giraffes can do simple math. [[Researchers]] at the University of Barcelona {{carried out}} a study with four giraffes at a zoo in Spain. They wanted to see [[whether]] the animals could {{work out}} which [[amount]] of food was bigger. The results [[surprised]] many people.

verbs.wrong: To share a fact with the public
verbs.correct: To learn or discover something
verbs.why: We use find out when you discover information, such as a secret, a price, or a result. Be careful: you learn a skill, but you find out a fact.

verbs.wrong: To plan something in detail
verbs.correct: To do or perform a task
verbs.why: Carry out is the formal way to say do a task that was planned: scientists carry out studies, and companies carry out plans. In everyday talk, people usually just say do.

verbs.wrong: To smell the difference in food type
verbs.correct: To find the answer to something
verbs.why: Here work out means to calculate in your head. Be careful: work out is also very common for exercising at the gym.

chunks.text: In the test, the scientists {{set up}} [[clear]] [[containers]] with different numbers of carrot and vegetable pieces. Sometimes they added more pieces, and sometimes they {{took away}} a few. Each time, the giraffes had to {{pick out}} the container with more food. To get the [[reward]], the animals used their long [[tongues]] to reach it.

verbs.wrong: To hide something from view
verbs.correct: To prepare or arrange something
verbs.why: You set up anything that needs arranging before it is ready to use: an experiment, a tent, a new phone.

verbs.wrong: To put things in a row
verbs.correct: To remove something
verbs.why: Take away is the opposite of add: the scientists sometimes added pieces of food and sometimes took a few pieces away.

verbs.wrong: To point at something you want
verbs.correct: To choose one thing from several
verbs.why: Pick out means to choose after looking carefully at all the options: a shirt in a store, a face in a crowd, the container with more carrots.

chunks.text: When the scientists added pieces, the giraffes did [[far better]] than [[luck]] [[alone]] would explain. [[According to the study]], they chose the larger amount about 68 percent of the time. This helped the team {{rule out}} the idea that the animals were only [[guessing]]. The results [[suggest]] giraffes can {{keep track of}} small numbers and can {{tell apart}} large and small amounts of food. However, the animals could not [[solve]] harder tasks, [[such as]] [[subtraction]].

verbs.wrong: To show that an idea is only partly true
verbs.correct: To decide that something is not possible
verbs.why: When you rule out an idea, you decide it cannot be the answer and stop thinking about it. The giraffes' results were too good to be luck, so the team ruled luck out.

verbs.wrong: To multiply two numbers together quickly
verbs.correct: To follow the number or progress of something
verbs.why: You keep track of things that change, so you always know their number or state: your spending, the score, the days until vacation.

verbs.wrong: To choose the thing that you like best
verbs.correct: To see the difference between things
verbs.why: If you can tell two things apart, you never confuse them. Notice the word order: we say tell them apart, not tell apart them.

chunks.text: [[For a long time]], people thought that only humans and a few [[clever]] animals, such as [[primates]] and crows, had [[a sense of]] numbers. This new study adds to [[a growing list]] of animals that can count [[in some way]]. The researchers now want to {{carry on}} their work with other zoo animals. They hope it will help us {{figure out}} more about how animal minds work.

verbs.wrong: To repeat the same test one more time
verbs.correct: To continue doing something
verbs.why: Carry on means to continue, especially after a pause or a problem. Americans use it too, but it is even more common in British English.

verbs.wrong: To watch something very closely
verbs.correct: To understand or solve something
verbs.why: Figure out means to understand something after thinking hard: a problem, a reason, even a person. It is one of the most common phrasal verbs in American English.

mainIdea.s: Four giraffes usually chose the container with more food, so it seems they can tell small numbers apart. They could not do harder math, such as subtraction.
mainIdea.why: They picked the larger amount about 68 percent of the time, which is better than guessing. But the study says they could not solve harder tasks such as subtraction.

mainIdea.s: Scientists in Spain tested four zoo giraffes and found they can add and subtract small amounts of food. They say the animals are now as clever as primates.
mainIdea.why: Close, but subtraction was too hard for the giraffes. The study only shows they can tell a larger amount of food from a smaller one.

mainIdea.s: Zoos in Spain have started giving giraffes puzzle feeders to keep their minds busy. Keepers say the animals now eat more slowly and seem much calmer.
mainIdea.why: This story is about a test of whether giraffes can compare amounts of food. It is not about how zoos feed them.

tf.s: Researchers carried on a new study with four giraffes at a zoo in Spain.
tf.why: The researchers carried out (performed) a new study. Carry on means to continue something that is already happening.

tf.s: In the test, the giraffes had to pick out the container that held more food.
tf.why: Each time, the giraffes had to pick out (choose) the container with more food to get the reward.

tf.s: Sometimes the scientists picked out a few pieces of food from the containers.
tf.why: Sometimes the scientists took away (removed) a few pieces. Pick out means to choose one thing from several, not to remove one.

tf.s: Scientists found out that giraffes can do simple math.
tf.why: Researchers at the University of Barcelona found out (discovered) that giraffes can do simple math.

tf.s: The researchers want to carry on their work with other zoo animals.
tf.why: The team wants to carry on (continue) their research to learn more about how animal minds work.

tf.s: This new study shows that giraffes cannot count in any way at all
tf.why: The study suggests giraffes can keep track of small numbers, adding them to the growing list of counting animals.
